105487.e: Melanocytes sit in the epidermis. They make melanin and pass it on to the skin cells around them.

105488.q: What does melanin protect the skin from?
105488.e: Melanin absorbs a large part of the UV rays. In this way it protects the genetic material in skin cells from damage.
105488.m: Melanin protects the skin from UV rays.

105489.q: What happens in the skin when you get a tan?
105489.e: UV rays make the melanocytes produce more melanin. So a tan is a protective reaction of the skin.
105489.m: Getting a tan is the skin protecting itself against the sun.

105490.q: What mainly makes dark skin different from light skin?
a: The amount and type of melanin
105490.e: People of all skin colours have about the same number of melanocytes. In dark skin, however, they make more and darker melanin.
105490.m: Skin colour depends on the amount of melanin.

105491.q: What is the name of an inborn condition in which the body makes little or no melanin?
105491.e: In albinism, melanin is missing from the skin, hair and often the eyes. People with it have very pale skin and must protect themselves well from the sun.

105492.q: What is the dangerous skin cancer that develops from pigment cells called?
105492.e: Melanoma develops from melanocytes that have changed abnormally. Switzerland is one of the countries in Europe with the most cases of melanoma, which is why sun protection is important.

105493.q: Apart from the skin, where else is melanin found?
a: In hair and in the iris
105493.e: Melanin also gives hair and the iris of the eyes their colour. When hair turns grey, it hardly makes any melanin any more.
105493.m: Melanin also colours hair and eyes.

a: A skin condition with blackheads and spots
A fungal infection of the feet
105494.e: With acne, blackheads and inflamed spots appear mainly on the face, chest and back. It is very common in teenagers.
105494.m: Acne shows up as blackheads and spots.

105495.q: At what age does acne occur most often?
105495.e: Hormonal changes in puberty encourage acne. That is why very many teenagers have spots at times, which usually clear up later.
105495.m: Acne is most common in teenagers.

105496.q: What is a blocked skin pore that often looks dark at the top called?
105496.e: A blackhead forms when a hair follicle is blocked by sebum and horny cells. If it is open, the tip turns dark.
105496.m: A blocked skin pore is called a blackhead.

105497.q: Why is an open blackhead dark at the top?
a: The contents change colour in the air
A black hair grows inside it
105497.e: The dark colour does not come from dirt. The plug of sebum, horny cells and melanin turns dark when it meets the air.
105497.m: Blackheads are not dark because of dirt.

105498.q: Which glands play the main part in causing acne?
105498.e: In acne, the oil glands make too much sebum and the opening of the hair follicle becomes clogged with horny cells. It gets blocked and blackheads form.
105498.m: Acne starts with blocked oil glands.

105499.q: Why should you not squeeze spots?
a: The inflammation can spread and leave scars
It turns the skin brown for good
Then no hair grows there any more
105499.e: Squeezing can push pus deeper into the skin. The inflammation then often gets worse and scars can remain.

105500.q: What do the bacteria involved in acne spots feed on?
105500.e: These bacteria live in the hair follicles of the skin and feed on sebum. In blocked pores they multiply and encourage inflammation.

105501.e: Severe acne is best treated by a skin doctor, called a dermatologist. There are effective creams and medicines.
105501.m: A skin doctor can help with severe acne.

105502.q: What can severe, untreated acne leave behind?
105502.e: Deep inflammation can destroy tissue in the dermis. After healing, scars then remain, which is why early treatment is worthwhile.

105503.q: With which childhood illness do you get an itchy rash with small blisters all over your body?
105503.e: Chickenpox is caused by a virus. Typical signs are itchy blisters that appear all over the body and later crust over.
105503.m: Chickenpox causes itchy blisters all over the body.

105504.q: Which viral illness in small children causes blisters on the hands, feet and in the mouth?
105504.e: Hand, foot and mouth disease is caused by viruses and mainly affects children under ten. Typical signs are blisters on the palms, soles of the feet and in the mouth.
105504.m: Hand, foot and mouth disease causes blisters on the hands, feet and in the mouth.

105505.q: Which illness can be caused by the same virus decades after chickenpox?
105505.e: After the illness, the chickenpox virus stays in nerve cells. If it becomes active again later, painful shingles develops.
105505.m: The chickenpox virus can cause shingles later.

105506.q: What causes a rash with weals when you touch stinging nettles?
a: The stinging hairs of the plant
105506.e: The stinging hairs of the nettle break off and inject irritating substances into the skin. Itchy, burning weals appear.
105506.m: The stinging hairs of nettles cause weals.

105507.q: What is a rash with itchy weals, often caused by an allergy, called?
105507.e: Hives, technical term urticaria, look like the result of touching stinging nettles. They are often triggered by allergies, for example to foods or medicines.

105508.q: Which metal in belt buckles and jeans buttons often causes a contact rash?
105508.e: Nickel is one of the most common causes of a contact allergy. Where nickel stays on the skin for a long time, an itchy eczema can develop.

105509.q: In which illness does the red rash typically start behind the ears?
105509.e: With measles, the blotchy rash usually starts behind the ears and on the face. Then it spreads over the whole body.
105509.m: The measles rash starts behind the ears.

105510.q: Which illness with a rash is caused by bacteria and often shows a “strawberry tongue”?
105510.e: Scarlet fever is caused by streptococci, which are bacteria. Typical signs are a fine rash and a red, bumpy strawberry tongue.
105510.m: Scarlet fever can often be recognised by the strawberry tongue.

105511.q: What is typical of atopic eczema?
105511.e: In atopic eczema, the protective function of the skin does not work properly. The skin is dry, gets inflamed easily and is very itchy.
105511.m: Atopic eczema causes dry, itchy skin.

105512.e: Atopic eczema is a skin condition that is not contagious. So you cannot catch it from other people.

105513.q: What can trigger a new flare-up of atopic eczema?
a: Stress or dry air from the heating
105513.e: Stress, infections or dry air in winter can irritate the sensitive skin. Then the eczema flares up again.
105513.m: Stress and dry air can make atopic eczema worse.

105514.q: Where does atopic eczema often appear in schoolchildren?
a: In the creases of the elbows and the backs of the knees
On the ends of the hair
105514.e: In children and teenagers, the inner bends of the arms and legs are often affected. There the skin rubs and easily gets damp.
105514.m: Atopic eczema often appears in the elbow creases and the backs of the knees.

105515.q: How does atopic eczema usually progress?
a: In flare-ups with better and worse times
105515.e: Atopic eczema typically comes in flare-ups. A flare-up can be triggered by stress, infections or dry air from the heating, for example.

105516.q: What is especially important for daily skin care with atopic eczema?
105516.e: Rich moisturising creams strengthen the damaged protective layer of the skin and ease the dryness. Hot showers and scrubbing dry the skin out even more.
105516.m: With atopic eczema, the skin needs plenty of rich cream.

105517.q: Which illnesses often occur together with atopic eczema?
a: A broken bone and a strain
105517.e: Atopic eczema, hay fever and allergic asthma are known as atopic conditions. They often occur in the same families or in the same person.
105517.m: Atopic eczema often occurs with hay fever and asthma.

105518.q: Why does scratching make atopic eczema worse?
a: It irritates the skin and makes the itching stronger
It makes the skin too greasy
105518.e: Scratching damages the skin and encourages inflammation. This makes it itch even more, creating a vicious circle.
105518.m: Scratching makes the itching of atopic eczema stronger.

105519.e: Common warts are caused by papillomaviruses. The idea that toads pass on warts is an old myth.

105520.e: Wart viruses are passed on by direct contact or via objects. Small injuries to the skin make infection especially easy.

105521.q: What are warts on the sole of the foot that hurt when you walk called?
105521.e: Verrucas, or plantar warts, grow inwards on the sole of the foot because of the body’s weight. That is why they press and hurt when you walk.
105521.m: Verrucas are on the sole of the foot.

105522.q: Where is it especially easy to catch warts on the feet?
a: Barefoot at the swimming pool and in changing rooms
105522.e: Wart viruses survive well on damp floors in swimming pools and changing rooms. Pool sliders help protect you.
105522.m: Pool sliders protect against warts at the swimming pool.

105523.q: What are the small black dots you often see in a verruca?
105523.e: The dark dots are small blood vessels in which the blood has clotted. Warts do not have real roots.
105523.m: Black dots in warts are tiny blood vessels.

105524.q: What does a skin doctor often use to freeze a stubborn wart?
105524.e: Liquid nitrogen is about minus 196 degrees Celsius. It destroys the wart tissue, which then falls off.

105525.q: What happens to many warts in children, even without treatment?
105525.e: Over time the immune system fights the wart viruses. That is why many warts in children disappear by themselves after months or a few years.
105525.m: Many warts disappear on their own.

105526.q: In which layer of skin do wart viruses multiply?
105526.e: Wart viruses infect cells of the epidermis and make them grow wildly. This creates the hard, rough bump.

a: Pressure and rubbing, for example in tight shoes
105527.e: A corn forms when a patch of skin is pressed or rubbed for a long time. A common cause is shoes that are too tight.

105528.q: Where do corns form most often?
a: On the back of the hand
105528.e: Corns mainly form on and between the toes. There, shoes press on bony bumps.
105528.m: Corns are usually on the toes.

105529.q: Why does a corn hurt when you walk?
a: A hard core presses deep down on nerves
It contains small splinters of bone
105529.e: In the middle of a corn, a hard core grows inwards like a thorn. It presses on the nerves below and hurts with every step.
105529.m: The hard core of a corn presses on nerves.

105530.q: Where does the German name for a corn, “Hühnerauge” (chicken’s eye), come from?
a: From its look, with a pale ring and a dark core
Because it is treated with eggs
105530.e: With its round edge and the core in the middle, it looks like a bird’s eye. Otherwise it has nothing to do with chickens.
105530.m: A corn looks like a bird’s eye.

105531.q: What should you avoid doing with a corn?
a: Cutting it off yourself with scissors
105531.e: If you cut it yourself, you can hurt yourself and get an infection. It is better to take the pressure off the spot and have the core removed by a professional.
105531.m: You should not cut a corn off yourself.

105532.q: What is a wide patch of thickened hard skin without a hard core, caused by pressure, called?
105532.e: A callus is a broad thickening of the horny layer, for example on the hands of craftspeople. Unlike a corn, it has no core pressing down deep.
105532.m: A callus is thickened hard skin without a core.

105533.q: What helps most to stop a corn coming back?
a: Scratching the spot open every day
105533.e: As long as the pressure continues, the corn keeps forming again. Well-fitting shoes and pads take the pressure off the spot.

105534.e: Podiatrists specialise in caring for and treating feet. They remove the hard core gently.

105535.q: Into which layer of skin is the ink injected for a tattoo?
105535.e: The ink has to reach the dermis. If it were only in the epidermis, it would flake off after a few weeks as the skin renews itself.
105535.m: Tattoo ink sits in the dermis.

105536.q: Which people of New Zealand have a long tradition of face tattoos?
105536.e: The traditional tattoos of the Māori are called tā moko. They show a person’s origins and status and are still worn today.
105536.m: The Māori in New Zealand wear traditional face tattoos.

105537.q: Which famous glacier find from the Ötztal Alps has more than 60 tattoos?
105537.e: The glacier mummy Ötzi is more than 5000 years old. More than 60 tattoos made of lines and crosses were found on his skin.

105538.q: From which language does the word “tattoo” come?
105538.e: The word goes back to “tatau” from Tahiti. Sailors with James Cook brought it to Europe in the 18th century.
105538.m: The word tattoo comes from Polynesia.

105539.q: What are tattoos usually removed with today?
105539.e: Laser light breaks the ink particles into smaller pieces. The body can then gradually remove them, which usually takes several sessions.
105539.m: Tattoos are removed with a laser.

a: A painting on the skin that disappears after a while
105540.e: Henna only colours the upper layers of the skin. As the epidermis renews itself, it fades after a few weeks. People are warned against “black henna” with added substances, because it can cause allergies.
105540.m: A henna tattoo does not last for ever.

105541.q: Why should you keep a fresh tattoo out of the sun and not go swimming?
a: It is a wound that has to heal first
It then starts to itch like a wart
105541.e: When you get a tattoo, the skin is injured thousands of times. Until the wound has healed, germs in the water and sunlight can lead to infections and damage to the colours.
105541.m: A fresh tattoo is a wound.

105542.q: Which cells of the immune system take up tattoo ink in the skin?
105542.e: Scavenger cells, also called macrophages, swallow the ink particles. Because they cannot break them down, the ink stays visible in the dermis.
105542.m: Scavenger cells hold the tattoo ink in place.

105543.q: A load of 600 N hangs 0.2 m from the pivot. What force is needed on the 1.2 m effort arm for balance?
105543.e: By the law of the lever, effort times effort arm equals load times load arm. So 600 N times 0.2 m gives 120 Nm, and 120 Nm divided by 1.2 m gives 100 N.
105543.m: The longer the effort arm, the smaller the force needed.

105544.q: With 50 N on a 2 m effort arm you balance a load of 400 N. How long is the load arm?
105544.e: Effort times effort arm gives 50 N times 2 m, so 100 Nm. 100 Nm divided by 400 N gives 0.25 m, which is 25 cm.
105544.m: With a lever, force and arms together decide the balance.

105545.q: Which Greek scholar was the first to describe the law of the lever exactly?
105545.e: Archimedes of Syracuse formulated the law of the lever in the 3rd century BC. He is said to have declared: “Give me a place to stand and I will move the world.”
105545.m: Archimedes described the law of the lever.

105546.q: What happens to the force needed if you double the effort arm and change nothing else?
105546.e: The product of force and effort arm must stay the same. If the effort arm is twice as long, half the force is enough.
105546.m: Twice the effort arm means half the force.

105547.q: You lift a load with a lever and need only a quarter of the force. How far does your hand have to move in return?
a: Four times as far as the load
Half as far as the load
A quarter of the load's distance
105547.e: According to the golden rule of mechanics, what you save in force you must make up in distance. A quarter of the force means four times the distance.
105547.m: What you save in force, you must add in distance.

105548.q: A 1 m bar is pivoted in the middle. 80 N hangs at the left end. What force must pull down on the right 40 cm from the pivot?
105548.e: On the left: 80 N times 0.5 m, so 40 Nm. 40 Nm divided by 0.4 m gives 100 N.
105548.m: A shorter arm needs a bigger force.

105549.q: What does a lever not save you?
105549.e: A lever reduces the force needed but lengthens the distance. Force times distance, the work, stays the same or even gets a little bigger because of friction.
105549.m: A lever saves force but not work.

105550.q: You lift a 2800 N stone with a 1.5 m crowbar. The pivot is 10 cm from the stone. What force is needed at the other end?
105550.e: The load arm is 0.1 m, the effort arm 1.5 m minus 0.1 m, so 1.4 m. 2800 N times 0.1 m gives 280 Nm, divided by 1.4 m gives 200 N.
105550.m: A long crowbar makes heavy stones easy.

105551.q: When is a lever in balance?
a: When effort times effort arm equals load times load arm
When effort and load are equal
When effort arm and load arm are equally long
When the pivot is exactly in the middle
105551.e: What matters is not the force alone but the product of force and arm. If both products are equal, the lever does not move.
105551.m: In balance, effort times effort arm equals load times load arm.

105552.q: What is typical of a one-sided lever (second or third class lever)?
a: Effort and load act on the same side of the pivot
The pivot lies between effort and load
It has no pivot at all
Effort and load are always equal
105552.e: In a one-sided lever, effort and load are on the same side of the pivot. So the pivot is at one end.
105552.m: In a one-sided lever the pivot is at the end.

105553.q: Which tool is a one-sided lever?
105553.e: In a wheelbarrow the wheel axle is the pivot. The load and the hands on the handles are both on the same side of it.
105553.m: The wheelbarrow is a one-sided lever.

105554.q: How do effort and load act relative to each other in a one-sided lever?
105554.e: With a wheelbarrow the load presses down while the hands pull up. In a one-sided lever, effort and load point in opposite directions.
105554.m: In a one-sided lever, effort and load pull against each other.

105555.q: Why is a nutcracker a one-sided lever?
a: The nut lies between the hinge and the hands
The hinge lies between the nut and the hands
105555.e: In a nutcracker the hinge is at the end, then comes the nut, and right at the outside the hands squeeze. So load and effort are on the same side.
105555.m: In a nutcracker the nut lies between the hinge and the hand.

105556.q: A wheelbarrow holds 600 N of soil, 0.4 m from the wheel axle. The handles are 1.2 m from the axle. What force is needed to lift it?
105556.e: 600 N times 0.4 m gives 240 Nm. Divided by the effort arm of 1.2 m, this gives 200 N.
105556.m: In a wheelbarrow the wheel carries part of the load.

105557.q: Why is a wheelbarrow easier to lift when the load is close to the wheel?
105557.e: If the load is close to the wheel axle, the load arm is short. With the same effort arm, you then need less force.
105557.m: In a wheelbarrow, heavy loads belong at the front near the wheel.

105558.q: What do you gain with tweezers, which are a one-sided lever with a short effort arm?
a: Fine, precise movements at the tip
A lot of force at the tip
105558.e: With tweezers you squeeze closer to the pivot than the tip is. You need a little more force, but you can grip small things finely and precisely.

105559.q: Which tool for opening bottles with crown caps works as a one-sided lever?
105559.e: The bottle opener rests on top of the cap, which is the pivot. The edge of the cap and the hand are on the same side of it.
105559.m: A bottle opener is a one-sided lever.

105560.q: What is typical of a two-sided lever (first class lever)?
a: The pivot lies between effort and load
Effort and load are on the same side
It is always made of two parts
105560.e: In a two-sided lever, the pivot lies between the point where the effort acts and the point where the load acts, as on a seesaw.
105560.m: In a two-sided lever the pivot lies between effort and load.

105561.q: Which of these tools is a two-sided lever?
105561.e: With scissors the hinge lies between the handles and the blades. So they are made of two two-sided levers.
105561.m: Scissors are made of two two-sided levers.

105562.q: How do effort and load act in a two-sided lever?
a: Not on the lever at all
105562.e: On a seesaw both children press down, and yet it can balance. In a two-sided lever, effort and load act in the same direction.
105562.m: In a two-sided lever, effort and load push in the same direction.

105563.q: You squeeze the handles of pliers with 100 N, 15 cm from the hinge. The wire is 2 cm from the hinge. What force acts on the wire?
105563.e: 100 N times 15 cm gives 1500 Ncm. Divided by 2 cm, this gives 750 N.
105563.m: Pliers multiply the force of your hand.

105564.q: Why is it best to cut thick cardboard close to the hinge of the scissors?
a: The load arm is short there
The effort arm gets shorter there
105564.e: Close to the hinge the load arm is short, while the effort arm at the handles stays the same. So a bigger force acts on the cardboard.
105564.m: Cut thick material close to the hinge of the scissors.

105565.q: Why must a beam balance have two arms of equal length?
a: So that it balances with equal masses
105565.e: If both arms are equally long, it only balances when the same weight is on each side. That way you can compare masses.
105565.m: A beam balance compares masses using arms of equal length.

105566.q: On a two-sided lever, 60 N hangs on the left 30 cm from the pivot. How far to the right of the pivot must 45 N hang?
105566.e: On the left: 60 N times 30 cm, so 1800 Ncm. 1800 Ncm divided by 45 N gives 40 cm.
105566.m: The lighter weight needs the longer arm.

105567.q: When rowing, which part acts as a two-sided lever if you take the rowlock as the pivot?
105567.e: The rower pulls the handle on one side of the rowlock, and the blade pushes against the water on the other side. The rowlock lies in between.
105567.m: On an oar the rowlock lies between the handle and the blade.

105568.q: Where is the pivot of a grandfather clock's pendulum?
a: At the top where it hangs
At the bottom at the bob
In the middle of the rod
105568.e: The pendulum swings about the point where it hangs at the top. That is the axis of rotation; the weight at the bottom moves along an arc around it.
105568.m: A pendulum turns about the point where it hangs.

105569.q: Where is the pivot when you stand on tiptoe?
a: In the ball of the foot
105569.e: The foot tilts about the ball of the foot. The calf muscles pull on the heel through the Achilles tendon and so lift the whole body.
105569.m: On tiptoe the foot turns about the ball of the foot.

105570.q: What happens if you move the pivot of a lever closer to the load?
105570.e: If the pivot moves towards the load, the load arm gets shorter and the effort arm longer. So the force needed goes down.
105570.m: A pivot close to the load saves force.

105571.q: Where is the pivot when you nod your head?
a: In the joint between the skull and the top neck vertebra
In the middle of the forehead
105571.e: The skull sits on the top neck vertebra, the atlas, and tilts at this joint when you nod. The head acts like a two-sided lever, kept in balance by the neck muscles.
105571.m: When nodding, the head tilts on the top neck vertebra.

105572.q: What must be true of a lever's pivot?
a: It must be made of wood
It must always be exactly in the middle
105572.e: Only if the pivot is fixed can the lever turn about it and pass on force. If it slips away, the lever does not work.
105572.m: A lever needs a fixed pivot.

105573.q: About which axis do the pedals and cranks of a bike turn?
105573.e: The cranks are fixed in the bottom bracket. That is the axis about which the cranks and pedals turn.
105573.m: Bike cranks turn about the bottom bracket.

105574.q: Two children sit at the ends of a 3 m seesaw. One weighs 300 N, the other 600 N. Where must the pivot be for balance?
105574.e: The heavier child needs an arm half as long. With 1 m and 2 m: 600 N times 1 m equals 300 N times 2 m, both 600 Nm.
105574.m: The heavier child sits closer to the pivot.

105575.q: Why does a mobile over a cot tilt when you move one of the hanging pieces?
a: The balance about the hanging point changes
105575.e: Each rod of a mobile is a lever with the thread as its pivot. If you move a piece, one lever arm changes and the rod tilts until a new balance is found.
105575.m: Each rod of a mobile is a small lever.

105576.q: What is the load arm of a lever?
a: The distance from the pivot to where the load acts
The distance from the hand to the pivot
The whole length of the lever
105576.e: The load arm is the distance between the pivot and the point where the load acts. The effort arm, on the other hand, reaches to where you push or pull.
105576.m: The load arm goes from the pivot to the load.

105577.q: A lever has a load arm of 20 cm and an effort arm of 1 m. How many times your hand force can you hold in balance with it?
105577.e: At 100 cm the effort arm is five times as long as the 20 cm load arm. So the load can be five times as big as the force.
105577.m: The ratio of the arms decides how much a lever multiplies force.

105578.q: With 300 N on a 1.2 m effort arm you balance 900 N. How long is the load arm?
105578.e: 300 N times 1.2 m gives 360 Nm. 360 Nm divided by 900 N gives 0.4 m.
105578.m: The load arm is shorter when the load is bigger than the force.

105579.q: 150 N acts on an 80 cm effort arm and the load is 600 N. How long is the load arm?
105579.e: 150 N times 80 cm gives 12,000 Ncm. Divided by 600 N, this gives 20 cm.
105579.m: Four times the load needs a load arm four times shorter.

105580.q: Which distance is the load arm on a wheelbarrow?
a: From the wheel axle to the middle of the load
From the handles to the wheel
From the handles to the ground
From the wheel to the ground
105580.e: The load acts roughly where the centre of gravity of the load is. The distance from there to the wheel axle is the load arm.
105580.m: On a wheelbarrow you measure the load arm from the wheel axle.

105581.q: Why does a fishing rod have a very long load arm?
a: So that the tip moves far and fast
So that you need less force
So that the fish gets lighter
So that the rod does not break
105581.e: The hands act close to the pivot, and the tip is far away from it. A small movement of the hand creates a big, fast movement of the tip.
105581.m: A long load arm gives distance and speed instead of force.

105582.q: What happens to the load arm of a construction crane when the trolley moves outwards?
105582.e: The trolley carries the load on the jib. If it moves further from the tower, the distance between the axis of rotation and the load grows.
105582.m: When the trolley moves out, the load arm gets longer.

105583.q: Why should you hold a box close to your body when lifting it?
a: The load arm to the spine gets shorter
You can see the box better
105583.e: The further the box is from the body, the longer the load arm relative to the spine. Close to the body, the strain on the back and muscles goes down.
105583.m: Carry heavy loads close to your body.

105584.q: What is the effort arm of a lever?
a: The distance from the pivot to where the effort acts
The distance from the pivot to the load
The muscle in the upper arm
105584.e: The effort arm is the distance from the pivot to the point where you push or pull.
105584.m: The effort arm goes from the pivot to the hand.

105585.q: Why do people sometimes slip a pipe over a spanner to loosen a stuck nut?
105585.e: The pipe lengthens the handle and so the effort arm. With the same force this creates a bigger turning effect.
105585.m: A longer handle loosens stuck screws.

105586.q: A load of 1200 N hangs on a 0.3 m load arm. You push with 240 N. How long must the effort arm be?
105586.e: 1200 N times 0.3 m gives 360 Nm. 360 Nm divided by 240 N gives 1.5 m.
105586.m: With little force you need a long effort arm.

105587.q: Why is a door easiest to open when you push far away from the hinges?
a: The effort arm is longest there
There is less air in the way
105587.e: The distance to the hinges is the effort arm. The longer it is, the less force you need for the same turning effect.
105587.m: Door handles sit far from the hinges.

105588.q: How long must the effort arm be for 25 N to produce a moment of 10 Nm?
105588.e: Effort arm is moment divided by force. 10 Nm divided by 25 N gives 0.4 m.
105588.m: You get the effort arm from moment divided by force.

105589.q: Which part of a bike forms the effort arm when you pedal?
105589.e: The foot presses on the pedal at the end of the crank. The length of the crank to its axis is the effort arm.
105589.m: The crank is the effort arm on a bike.

105590.q: Why is a screw easier to turn with a screwdriver that has a thick handle than with a thin one?
a: The thick handle gives a bigger effort arm
105590.e: The hand grips at the edge of the handle. With a thick handle this distance to the axis is bigger, so the same force produces a bigger moment.
105590.m: A thick handle lengthens the effort arm.

105591.q: Why do loppers for thick branches have especially long handles?
a: Long handles form a long effort arm
Long handles make the blades sharper
105591.e: Loppers have long handles so that the effort arm is large. This means even thick branches can be cut with both hands.
105591.m: Long handles give loppers a lot of power.

105592.q: How do you calculate a moment (torque)?
105592.e: The moment is the product of the force and the perpendicular distance to the pivot. It describes how strongly a force can turn something.
105592.m: A moment is force times lever arm.

105593.q: In which unit is a moment measured?
105593.e: Because a moment is force in newtons times length in metres, its unit is the newton metre, Nm for short.
105593.m: Moments are measured in newton metres.

105594.q: You push with 50 N at the end of a 30 cm spanner. How big is the moment?
105594.e: 30 cm is 0.3 m. 50 N times 0.3 m gives 15 Nm.
105594.m: For the moment, use the lever arm in metres.

105595.q: A car's wheel nut needs a moment of 120 Nm. The wheel brace is 40 cm long. What force is needed at the end of the handle?
105595.e: The force is moment divided by lever arm. 120 Nm divided by 0.4 m gives 300 N.
105595.m: A longer spanner needs less force for the same moment.

105596.q: Why does a door not turn if you push directly on the hinges?
a: The lever arm is zero, so the moment is too
The force is too small there
The door is too heavy there
105596.e: If the force acts exactly at the pivot, the lever arm is zero. Force times zero gives no moment, so nothing turns.
105596.m: Without a lever arm there is no moment.

105597.q: On the same lever, 30 Nm acts anticlockwise and 20 Nm clockwise. What happens?
a: The lever turns back and forth
105597.e: The moments only partly cancel. 30 Nm minus 20 Nm, so 10 Nm anticlockwise, is left over, which is why the lever turns anticlockwise.
105597.m: The bigger moment decides the direction of turning.

105598.q: At what angle to a spanner should you pull to produce the biggest moment?
a: At a slant towards the pivot
105598.e: Only the part of the force at right angles to the lever counts for the moment. At 90 degrees the whole force turns.
105598.m: Pulling at right angles to the lever gives the biggest moment.

105599.q: A child weighing 500 N sits 1.5 m from the pivot of a seesaw. What moment does the child produce?
105599.e: Moment is force times lever arm. 500 N times 1.5 m gives 750 Nm.
105599.m: On a seesaw each child produces a moment.

105600.q: What is an object's centre of gravity?
a: The point where you can imagine all its weight is concentrated
The heaviest spot made of the densest material
105600.e: For many calculations you can pretend that all the weight acts at a single point. This point is called the centre of gravity.
105600.m: At the centre of gravity you imagine all the weight combined.

105601.q: Where is the centre of gravity of an evenly made ruler?
105601.e: In a ruler of even thickness the mass is spread evenly. So the centre of gravity is in the middle, and you can balance it there on your finger.
105601.m: An even ruler has its centre of gravity in the middle.

105602.q: How do you find the centre of gravity of a flat, irregular piece of card?
a: Hang it from two points and draw the plumb line each time
105602.e: An object hanging freely settles so that its centre of gravity is directly below the point it hangs from. Where two such plumb lines cross is the centre of gravity.
105602.m: Two plumb lines cross at the centre of gravity.

105603.q: Where is the centre of gravity of a ring?
a: In the middle of the hole, where there is no material
At the heaviest part of the ring
At the edge of the ring
105603.e: The centre of gravity does not have to be in the material. For a ring it lies exactly in the middle of the hole.
105603.m: For a ring, the centre of gravity is in the empty middle.

105604.q: Roughly where is the centre of gravity of a person standing upright?
a: In the chest by the heart
105604.e: When standing upright, the body's centre of gravity is about at the level of the pelvis, slightly below the belly button. If you change your posture, it moves.
105604.m: A standing person's centre of gravity is near the pelvis.

105605.q: In the Fosbury Flop, why can a high jumper clear a bar even though her centre of gravity can stay below it?
a: Her body bends so that the centre of gravity is outside the body
She becomes lighter in the air
105605.e: In the flop the body bends over the bar like an arch. As a result the centre of gravity lies outside the body and can pass just below the bar.
105605.m: In the Fosbury Flop the centre of gravity lies outside the body.

105606.q: Why do racing cars sit very low on the road?
a: A low centre of gravity makes them more stable in bends
So that they use less petrol
So that the drivers can see better
105606.e: Racing cars are built very flat. So their centre of gravity is close to the ground, and they hold the road better in fast bends.
105606.m: A low centre of gravity makes vehicles stable.

105607.q: Why does a roly-poly toy always stand back up?
a: Its centre of gravity is right at the bottom in the heavy, round base
105607.e: The round base contains a heavy weight. If you tip the toy, the centre of gravity rises, and gravity turns it back to the lowest position.
105607.m: A roly-poly toy has its centre of gravity right at the bottom.

105608.q: What is the best way to pack a hiking rucksack?
a: Heavy things close to your back
Heavy things right on the outside
Heavy things at the bottom on the outside
Heavy things in the side pockets
105608.e: Heavy things close to the back keep the overall centre of gravity close to the body. Then the rucksack pulls back less and you walk more safely.
105608.m: In a rucksack, heavy things go close to your back.

105609.q: When does an object tip over?
a: When the vertical line from its centre of gravity falls outside its base
When it weighs more than 10 kg
When it is taller than it is wide
When it is made of wood
105609.e: As long as the vertical line through the centre of gravity stays within the base, the object stands. If it falls outside, it tips over.
105609.m: An object tips when the line down from its centre of gravity falls outside its base.

105610.q: Why does the Leaning Tower of Pisa stay standing despite its tilt?
a: The vertical line from its centre of gravity still falls within its base
It is tied down with ropes
It stands on rocks made of iron
105610.e: The tower leans, but the vertical line through its centre of gravity still meets the ground within the foundations. That is why it does not topple.
105610.m: A leaning tower stands as long as its centre of gravity is over its base.

105611.q: Which change makes an object more stable?
105611.e: The wider the base, the further you have to tilt the object before the line from its centre of gravity falls outside it.
105611.m: A wide base protects against tipping.

105612.q: Why do you put heavy books on the bottom shelf?
a: The bookcase's centre of gravity is then lower
They are easier to see there
The wood is thicker at the bottom
105612.e: Heavy things at the bottom lower the centre of gravity of the whole bookcase. Then it is less likely to tip forwards.
105612.m: Heavy things go at the bottom of a shelf.

105613.q: Why does a lorry loaded high tip over more easily on a tight bend?
a: Its centre of gravity is high
105613.e: With a high centre of gravity, the force on the bend produces a bigger tipping moment. That is why vehicles loaded high must take bends slowly.
105613.m: A high centre of gravity increases the risk of tipping.

105615.q: Why is it so easy to fall backwards when you tip back on your chair?
a: You are balancing on a narrow edge and the centre of gravity is close to it
The chair back is too heavy
105615.e: On two chair legs the base is just a narrow line. Even a small movement pushes the centre of gravity behind it, and you fall.
105615.m: When you tip back on a chair, the base is dangerously narrow.

105616.q: Why should you close an open parasol in strong wind?
a: The wind acts high up with a long lever arm
The fabric always gets heavier in wind
The stand gets lighter in wind
105616.e: The wind acts on the large canopy high up on the pole. Large force times long lever arm gives a large moment, which can blow the parasol over.
105616.m: Wind on an open parasol acts with a long lever arm.

105617.q: A block stands on a base 10 cm wide with its centre of gravity exactly above the middle. How far can the centre of gravity be moved sideways before its vertical line reaches the edge?
105617.e: From the middle to the edge is half of 10 cm, so 5 cm. If the centre of gravity moves further, its vertical line falls outside the base.
105617.m: From the middle to the edge is half the width.

105618.q: Why is it easier to balance a long broom on your hand than a short pencil?
a: The broom has no centre of gravity
105618.e: The higher the centre of gravity above the hand, the more slowly the object tips. With the broom there is enough time to move your hand after it.
105618.m: Long objects tip more slowly and are easier to balance.

105619.q: What kind of equilibrium does a ball lying in a bowl have?
105619.e: If you nudge the ball, it always rolls back to the lowest point. This is called stable equilibrium.
105619.m: In stable equilibrium an object returns by itself.

105620.q: What kind of equilibrium does a pencil standing on its point have?
105620.e: Even the slightest disturbance makes the pencil fall over, and it does not come back. That is unstable equilibrium.
105620.m: In unstable equilibrium a breath is enough to knock it over.

105621.q: What kind of equilibrium does a ball on a level table have?
105621.e: The ball stays wherever you roll it. Its centre of gravity always stays at the same height; this is called neutral equilibrium.
105621.m: In neutral equilibrium an object stays put anywhere.

105622.q: How do you keep your balance when cycling?
a: You steer slightly in the direction you are tipping
You always steer against the direction you are tipping
You hold the handlebars completely rigid
105622.e: If the bike tips to the left, you steer a little to the left. This brings the wheels back under the centre of gravity and you straighten up.
105622.m: When cycling you steer under your centre of gravity.

105623.q: What does your body do when you stand on one leg?
a: It shifts the centre of gravity over the standing foot
It lowers the centre of gravity into the head
It raises the centre of gravity above the head
105623.e: On one leg the base is only as big as one foot. So the body leans so that the centre of gravity is exactly above it.
105623.m: When standing on one leg, your centre of gravity is over your foot.

105624.q: Why does a balancing bird that sits on a fingertip only by its beak not fall off?
a: Its centre of gravity is below the point of support
It is hollow and filled with air
105624.e: Weights in the wing tips pull the centre of gravity below the beak. So the bird hangs in stable equilibrium and rocks back after a disturbance.
105624.m: If the centre of gravity is below the point of support, an object stays stable.

105625.q: In the forearm lever, what is the load when you lift a water bottle?
a: The weight of the bottle in your hand
The force of the upper arm muscle
105625.e: The load is what the lever has to lift, here mainly the bottle in your hand. The weight of the forearm itself is added to that.
105625.m: When lifting, the load is the weight in your hand.

105626.q: Why can a muscle only pull the forearm, not push it away?
a: Muscles are too soft to push
Tendons are too short to push
105626.e: A muscle can only contract and so pull on its tendon. For the opposite movement a second muscle is needed on the other side.
105626.m: Muscles can only pull, not push.

105627.q: What type of lever is the forearm when it is bent by the biceps?
105627.e: The biceps is attached between the elbow and the hand. So the muscle force and the load in the hand are on the same side of the pivot.
105627.m: When bending, the forearm is a one-sided lever.

105628.q: The biceps is attached 4 cm from the elbow, and a ball weighing 50 N is held in the hand 32 cm from the elbow. With what force must the biceps pull?
105628.e: 50 N times 32 cm gives 1600 Ncm. Divided by 4 cm, this gives 400 N.
105628.m: The biceps pulls much harder than the load in the hand weighs.

105629.q: What is the advantage of the biceps being attached so close to the elbow?
a: A small shortening of the muscle moves the hand far and fast
The muscle has to produce less force
The elbow needs no joint fluid
105629.e: The short effort arm needs a lot of force. In return, the hand on the long load arm moves far and fast, which is useful for throwing and grabbing.
105629.m: The forearm trades force for speed.

105630.q: Which muscle straightens the forearm again?
105630.e: The three-headed upper arm muscle, the triceps, lies on the back of the upper arm. It is the opposite partner of the biceps and straightens the elbow.

105631.q: Where is the pivot in the forearm lever?
105631.e: When bending, the forearm turns about the elbow joint. Muscle force and load act on the same side of this pivot.
105631.m: The pivot of the forearm is the elbow.

105632.q: Why is it easier to carry a bag in the crook of your elbow than in your hand with your arm bent?
a: The load arm to the elbow is much shorter
105632.e: In the crook of the elbow the bag hangs almost at the pivot. The load arm is short, and the biceps has to produce much less force.
105632.m: A load close to the elbow spares the biceps.

105633.q: Where is the counterweight of a tower crane?
105633.e: The jib carries the load, and on the other side of the tower is the shorter counter-jib. That is where the heavy counterweights sit.
105633.m: The counterweight sits on the counter-jib.

105634.q: What are the counterweights on construction cranes usually made of?
105634.e: Usually several heavy concrete slabs or blocks are stacked on. They are cheap, compact and can be combined to suit the crane.
105634.m: Crane counterweights are usually concrete blocks.

105635.q: What job does a crane's counterweight do with regard to moments?
a: It balances the moment of the load
It doubles the moment of the load
105635.e: The load on the jib creates a moment that tries to tip the crane forwards. The counterweight creates a moment in the opposite direction on the other side.
105635.m: The counterweight acts against the moment of the load.

105636.q: A crane lifts 20 kN at 25 m from the tower. The counterweight is 10 m from the tower. How heavy must it be for balance?
105636.e: The load creates 20 kN times 25 m, so 500 kNm. 500 kNm divided by 10 m gives 50 kN.
105636.m: The shorter the counterweight's lever arm, the heavier it must be.

105637.q: Why may a crane lift less at the far end of its jib than close to the tower?
a: Further out the load arm is longer and the moment bigger
Further out the cable is thinner
There is always less wind further out
The trolley is weaker further out
105637.e: For the same load, the moment increases with the distance from the tower. That is why the permitted load decreases further out.
105637.m: The further out, the less a crane may lift.

105638.q: Which safety device stops a crane when a load far out becomes too heavy?
105638.e: The load moment limiter monitors the load and its distance out. If the permitted load moment is exceeded, it switches off dangerous movements.
105638.m: A load moment limiter protects the crane from toppling.

105639.q: Where does a tower crane often have extra ballast besides the counterweight?
a: At the top of the tower
105639.e: Heavy ballast blocks at the base lower the centre of gravity and increase the stability. This makes the whole crane stand more securely.
105639.m: Ballast at the base keeps the crane stable.

105640.q: Why is a tower crane left free to turn after work is over?
a: So that it lines up with the wind like a weathervane
So that the motor cools down
So that birds do not land on it
105640.e: With the slewing brake released, the wind turns the jib in the direction of the wind. Then the crane offers the storm the smallest surface and does not topple.
105640.m: A crane free to turn lines itself up with the wind.

105641.q: Which type of fruit has a completely fleshy fruit wall and usually several seeds, but no hard stone?
105641.e: In a berry the whole fruit wall stays juicy and soft. The seeds lie loose in the flesh and are not enclosed in a stone.
105641.m: A berry is fleshy all the way through and has no stone.

105642.q: Which of these fruits is botanically a true berry?
105642.e: The tomato develops from an ovary with a fleshy fruit wall and many seeds, so it is a berry. Strawberry and raspberry are only called berries in everyday language.
105642.m: Not everything called a berry is a berry botanically.

105643.q: Which type of fruit is the banana, botanically?
105643.e: The banana has a fleshy fruit wall without a stone and so counts as a berry botanically. In cultivated bananas the seeds are only tiny dark dots.
105643.m: The banana is botanically a berry.

105644.q: Which type of fruit is the pumpkin, botanically?
105644.e: The pumpkin has a fleshy fruit wall with many seeds and no stone. Its hard skin makes it a special kind of berry.
105644.m: A pumpkin is botanically a berry.

105645.q: What fills the individual segments of an orange?
105645.e: Citrus fruits are special berries. Their segments are filled with many small juice-filled sacs that grow from the innermost layer of the fruit wall.
105645.m: The juice of an orange is held in tiny juice sacs.

105646.q: Which very poisonous plant from Swiss forests has shiny black berries?
105646.e: Deadly nightshade forms shiny black berries the size of cherries, which are life-threatening even in small amounts. That is why you should never eat berries you do not know.
105646.m: Never eat berries you do not know for sure.

105647.q: Which fruit with a brown, hairy skin is botanically a berry with many small black seeds?
105647.e: The kiwi has a fleshy fruit wall and lots of tiny seeds in its green flesh. It has no stone.
105647.m: The kiwi is a berry with many small seeds.

105648.q: The date contains only one single hard seed. Which type of fruit is it all the same?
105648.e: The hard core of the date is the seed itself and not a stone made from the fruit wall. That is why the date is a one-seeded berry.
105648.m: Even a fruit with only one seed can be a berry.

105649.q: Which vegetable is botanically also a berry?
105649.e: The pepper (capsicum) develops from an ovary and has a fleshy fruit wall with many seeds inside. Carrot, leek and kohlrabi, on the other hand, are root, leaves or shoot.
105649.m: The pepper is a vegetable, but botanically a berry.

105650.q: Which type of fruit is the cherry?
105650.e: The cherry has a thin skin on the outside, juicy flesh beneath it and a hard stone inside. These three layers are typical of stone fruits.
105650.m: A cherry is a stone fruit with a hard core.

105651.q: From which part does the hard stone of a stone fruit develop?
105651.e: The fruit wall of a stone fruit has three layers. The innermost layer becomes woody and forms the stone, which protects the seed.
105651.m: The stone is the woody inner layer of the fruit wall.

105652.q: What is inside the hard stone of a plum?
105652.e: The stone is only the protective shell. Inside it lies the actual seed, from which a new tree can grow.
105652.m: The seed lies inside the stone of a stone fruit.

105653.q: Which of these tropical fruits is a stone fruit?
105653.e: The mango has a large, flat stone in the middle that contains the seed. Around it lies the juicy, fibrous flesh.
105653.m: The mango is a stone fruit with a large, flat stone.

105654.q: Despite its name, the coconut is not a true nut. What is it botanically?
105654.e: The hard brown shell of the coconut is the woody inner fruit wall. That is why it counts as a stone fruit, just like the peach.
105654.m: The coconut is botanically a stone fruit.

105655.q: From which stone fruit is a well-known cooking oil pressed?
105655.e: The olive has oil-rich flesh and a hard stone. Sunflower, rape and flax form other types of fruit.
105655.m: Olive oil comes from a stone fruit.

105656.q: Which part of a stone fruit do we eat in the almond?
105656.e: The almond is a stone fruit with a leathery, not juicy, outer layer. We eat the seed that lies inside the stone.
105656.m: With the almond we eat the seed from inside the stone.

105657.q: Which plant family do cherry, plum and apricot belong to?
105657.e: These fruit trees belong to the genus Prunus within the rose family. Apple, pear and rose also belong to this large family.
105657.m: Many kinds of stone fruit belong to the rose family.

105658.q: In everyday language, what is fruit such as plums, peaches and apricots called as a group?
105658.e: Because these fruits have a hard stone, they are grouped together as stone fruit. Apples and pears, on the other hand, are called pome fruit.
105658.m: Fruit with a hard stone is called stone fruit.

105659.q: What is typical of a true nut?
a: The whole fruit wall becomes woody
105659.e: In a true nut the whole fruit wall becomes hard and woody. Inside there is usually only one single seed.
105659.m: In a true nut the whole fruit wall is hard.

105660.q: Which of these fruits is a true nut?
105660.e: The hazelnut has all the features of a true nut: the whole fruit wall is woody and it does not open. Many other so-called nuts are botanically something else.
105660.m: The hazelnut is a true nut.

105661.q: What are the three-sided nuts of the common beech called?
105661.e: The common beech forms small, three-sided nuts in a prickly husk. They are called beechnuts or beech mast.
105661.m: The fruits of the beech are called beechnuts.

105662.q: What do you call the bowl-shaped structure that an acorn sits in?
105662.e: The acorn is a nut whose bottom sits in a scaly cup. This cup grows out of the flower cluster.
105662.m: The acorn sits in a cup.

105663.q: A sunflower seed is really a whole small fruit. What is its striped shell?
105663.e: What we buy as a sunflower seed is a whole fruit. The striped shell is the fruit wall, and the seed lies inside.
105663.m: A sunflower seed is a small nut-like fruit.

105664.q: In a grain of wheat, the fruit wall and the seed have grown firmly together. So what is a grain of wheat really?
105664.e: A cereal grain is not just a seed but a whole fruit. Because the fruit wall and seed coat have grown together, they cannot be separated.
105664.m: A cereal grain is a whole fruit.

105665.q: Nuts are indehiscent fruits. What does that mean?
a: They do not open when ripe
They only grow in the shade
105665.e: Indehiscent fruits stay closed, and the seed is spread together with the fruit. Dehiscent fruits, on the other hand, open and scatter their seeds.
105665.m: An indehiscent fruit stays closed even when ripe.

105666.q: How many seeds does a true nut usually contain?
105666.e: A true nut usually has one seed. That is why you normally find only one kernel in a hazelnut.
105666.m: A true nut usually contains only one seed.

105667.q: What happens to a ripe capsule?
a: It grows together with the receptacle
105667.e: Capsules are dehiscent fruits. When ripe they dry out and open through slits, lids or holes.
105667.m: A ripe capsule opens and scatters its seeds.

105668.q: What does a capsule develop from?
105668.e: A capsule forms from at least two carpels that have grown together. That is why it often has several chambers.
105668.m: A capsule develops from several joined carpels.

105669.q: How do the seeds get out of a ripe poppy capsule?
a: Through small holes at the top when the wind shakes it
The capsule bursts with a bang
The capsule rots in the soil
105669.e: In the poppy, small holes open at the top under the disc of the stigma. When the stem sways in the wind, the seeds are scattered as if from a salt shaker. This is called a pore capsule.
105669.m: The poppy capsule scatters its seeds through small holes.

105670.q: Botanically, the prickly green case of the horse chestnut is a ...?
105670.e: The case of the horse chestnut splits into three parts when ripe. The shiny brown conkers inside are the seeds.
105670.m: The horse chestnut forms a prickly capsule with seeds inside.

105671.e: After flowering, the tulip grows an upright capsule with three chambers. Pea, cherry and hazelnut form other types of fruit.
105671.m: The tulip forms a capsule after flowering.

105672.q: In which crop are the valuable fibres long hairs on the seeds inside a capsule?
105672.e: The cotton capsule bursts open when ripe, and the white seed hairs puff out. Fabrics are made from these hairs.
105672.m: Cotton is made of seed hairs from a capsule.

105673.q: The so-called vanilla pod is not really a pod at all, botanically. What is it?
105673.e: The fruit of the vanilla orchid is a long capsule. In the shops it is still called a vanilla pod.
105673.m: The vanilla pod is really a capsule.

105674.q: Which plant do linseeds come from, which ripen in roundish capsules?
105674.e: Flax, also called linseed, forms small round capsules with shiny seeds. Linen fibres are also made from its stems.
105674.m: Linseeds are the seeds of flax.

105675.q: How does a ripe pod open?
105675.e: A pod develops from a single carpel. When ripe it splits open along the front seam and the back seam.
105675.m: A pod splits open along two seams.

105676.q: Where do the fruits of the peanut ripen?
105676.e: After fertilisation the flower stalk grows downwards and pushes the young ovary into the soil. The fruit ripens there.
105676.m: The peanut hides its pods in the soil.

105677.q: Which type of fruit is the peanut?
105677.e: The peanut is related to the pea and the bean. Its shell is a pod that usually contains two seeds.
105677.m: The peanut is not a nut but a legume.

105678.q: Which plant family do pea, bean and lentil belong to?
105678.e: Peas, beans, lentils and clover belong to the legumes. What they have in common is the pod.
105678.m: You can recognise legumes by their pods.

105679.q: Oilseed rape and mustard form long fruits with a dividing wall in the middle. What are they called?
105679.e: In the cabbage family, siliques develop from two carpels and have a thin dividing wall. Pods have no such wall.
105679.m: The cabbage family forms siliques, legumes form pods.

105680.q: From which legume is tofu made?
105680.e: To make tofu, soya beans are soaked, ground and cooked. The tofu is then set from the soya milk.
105680.m: Tofu is made from soya beans.

105681.q: Which bean with bright red flowers is also called the scarlet runner?
105681.e: The runner bean climbs high and stands out with its scarlet flowers. It forms long pods with large, often speckled seeds.
105681.m: The runner bean has red flowers and long pods.

105682.q: From which legume is hummus made?
105682.e: Hummus is a purée of cooked chickpeas with sesame paste. The chickpea forms short pods with one or two seeds.
105682.m: Hummus is made mainly of chickpeas.

105683.q: What is special about an aggregate fruit such as the raspberry?
a: Many little fruits from one flower form one fruit
It grows together from many trees
It has no pips at all
105683.e: In the raspberry flower many little fruits form side by side. Together they make a single fruit, the aggregate fruit.
105683.m: An aggregate fruit consists of many little fruits from one flower.

105684.q: Botanically, what is a single red bead of a raspberry?
105684.e: Each bead has a tiny hard stone inside. The raspberry is therefore an aggregate of stone fruits.
105684.m: The raspberry consists of many small stone fruits.

105685.q: When picking, how can you tell a raspberry from a blackberry?
105685.e: The raspberry comes away from the cone-shaped receptacle, which stays on the plant. With the blackberry the receptacle is picked too.
105685.m: A picked raspberry is hollow inside.

105686.q: What are the little yellow dots on the outside of a strawberry?
105686.e: Each dot is a tiny nut with a seed inside. The red flesh is only the enlarged receptacle.
105686.m: The real fruits of the strawberry are the little nuts on the outside.

105687.q: Which fruit, like the raspberry, is an aggregate of stone fruits?
105687.e: The blackberry also consists of many small stone fruits that come from a single flower. Bilberry, redcurrant and gooseberry, on the other hand, are true berries.
105687.m: Blackberry and raspberry are aggregates of stone fruits.

105688.q: What does a pineapple develop from?
a: From many flowers that grow together
105688.e: In the pineapple the fruits of many flowers in a whole flower cluster grow together into one single large fruit. This is called a multiple fruit.
105688.m: A pineapple develops from many flowers that have grown together.

105689.q: What colour are the flowers of the meadow buttercup in our fields?
105689.e: The buttercup flowers shiny yellow in spring and summer. After flowering it forms a small head of many little nuts.
105689.m: The buttercup has shiny yellow flowers.

105690.q: What do the split-open fruits of the peony contain in autumn?
105690.e: The fruits of the peony open along a seam. Inside lie shiny black or dark blue seeds.
105690.m: The peony forms fruits with shiny seeds.

a: A fruit that other flower parts help to form
A fruit that only ripens at night
105691.e: A true fruit develops only from the ovary. In a false fruit, other parts such as the receptacle also grow into the fruit.
105691.m: In a false fruit the receptacle also helps to build the fruit.

105692.q: Which part of the apple is the real fruit from the ovary?
105692.e: The juicy flesh of the apple grows from the receptacle. Only the papery core with the pips develops from the ovary.
105692.m: In the apple the core is the true fruit.

105693.q: Which fruit, like the apple, has a core with pips in the middle?
105693.e: Apple, pear and quince are pome fruits with a core. Cherry, plum and peach are stone fruits with a hard stone.
105693.m: Apple and pear are pome fruits.

105694.q: What does the red, juicy flesh of the strawberry develop from?
105694.e: After flowering the receptacle swells up a lot and becomes red and sweet. That is why the strawberry is also a false fruit.
105694.m: Strawberry flesh is an enlarged receptacle.

105695.q: What is the red fruit of the wild rose called?
105695.e: After flowering, the wild rose forms red fruits. They are called rose hips. People make tea and jam from them.
105695.m: The rose hip is the fruit of the rose.

105696.q: What is inside a rose hip?
105696.e: Inside the rose hip there are lots of hard little nuts with fine hairs. These hairs make your skin itch and used to be used as itching powder.
105696.m: Inside the rose hip lie many hairy little nuts.

105697.q: What is the juicy so-called cashew apple made of?
105697.e: On the cashew tree the stalk below the fruit thickens into a juicy ‘apple’. The real fruit is the kidney-shaped nut attached to it.
105697.m: The cashew apple is a thickened stalk and not a true fruit.

105698.q: What does the fig enclose with its fleshy tissue?
105698.e: The fig is a jug-shaped flower cluster with its flowers on the inside. From them come many tiny little fruits that crunch when you eat them.
105698.m: A fig is a flower cluster that has grown inwards.

105699.q: What are seeds that are spread by the wind like?
a: Light, often with wings or hairs
105699.e: Light seeds with wings or fine hairs are carried far by the wind. Examples are the maple and the dandelion.
105699.m: Wind-spread seeds are light and often have wings or hairs.

105700.q: How do dandelion fruits get far away?
a: They fly on a little parachute in the wind
105700.e: Each little dandelion fruit has a parachute of fine hairs. Like a parachute, it floats away on the wind.
105700.m: The dandelion flies with little parachutes.

105701.q: Which tree has winged fruits that spin to the ground like propellers?
105701.e: The fruit of the maple splits into two parts, each with a wing. As they fall they spin and stay in the air longer.
105701.m: Maple fruits spin like little propellers as they fall.

105702.q: What is the large, narrow bract on the fruit cluster of the lime tree for?
105702.e: The bract has grown together with the stalk of the fruits. It makes the whole fruit cluster glide through the air as it spins.
105702.m: Lime fruits glide away with a wing-like leaf.

105703.q: Which plants have especially tiny, dust-like seeds that the wind carries far?
105703.e: Orchid seeds are as small and light as dust. But they contain hardly any nutrients and need the help of fungi to germinate.

105704.q: In early summer, white fluff sometimes flies through the air. Which trees does it often come from?
105704.e: Poplars and willows form seeds with long white hairs. The wind carries them far away as fluffy flakes.
105704.m: The white fluff in early summer often comes from poplar seeds.

105705.q: What are plants called that dry out and are rolled whole by the wind across open land?
105705.e: In tumbleweeds the dry, ball-shaped plant breaks off at the root. As it rolls along it loses its seeds on the way.
105705.m: Tumbleweeds roll with the wind and scatter seeds.

105706.q: How does the poppy spread its seeds with the help of the wind?
a: The wind shakes the capsule like a shaker
105706.e: The poppy capsule sits on a long, springy stalk. When it sways in the wind, the seeds are thrown out bit by bit.
105706.m: The poppy is a wind shaker.

105707.q: Which of these seeds is typically spread by animals?
a: The burdock with its little hooks
105707.e: The burdock catches in the fur of animals with its little hooks and is carried far. Dandelion and maple use the wind, the coconut uses water.
105707.m: Burrs travel in the fur of animals.

105708.q: How do the fruits of the burdock get to new places?
a: They cling to animal fur with hooks
They are carried far by the wind
They are thrown out of the fruit
105708.e: Burrs have small hooks. With them they get caught in fur or feathers and fall off somewhere later. They were the model for Velcro.
105708.m: Burrs travel on the outside of animals’ fur.

105709.q: How do birds take the seeds of many berries to new places?
a: They are eaten and passed out in droppings
They are built into the nest
They are blown by the beating wings
105709.e: Birds eat the flesh, and the hard seeds pass through the gut undamaged. With the droppings they land in a new place, complete with fertiliser.
105709.m: Birds sow berry seeds with their droppings.

105710.q: Which bird hides lots of acorns in autumn and so helps oaks to spread?
105710.e: The jay buries acorns as a winter store. It does not find many of them again, and young oaks can grow from them.
105710.m: The jay’s forgotten stores grow into new oaks.

105711.q: Which animals carry off seeds with a nutritious attachment called an elaiosome?
105711.e: The elaiosome is an attachment on the seed that is rich in fat and protein. Ants carry the seed into their nest, eat the attachment and leave the seed.
105711.m: Ants spread seeds that have a treat attached.

105712.q: How do the seeds of mistletoe get onto other tree branches?
a: The wind carries them with wings
They jump out of the fruit
105712.e: Mistletoe berries contain a very sticky slime. Birds pass the seeds out or wipe them off on a branch, where they stick and germinate.
105712.m: Mistletoe gets birds to take its sticky seeds onto branches.

105713.q: Why are many ripe berries a striking red or black colour?
105713.e: Birds see colours well and recognise ripe berries by their colour. Unripe fruits are often green and inconspicuous.
105713.m: Bright berry colours are a signal for birds.

105714.q: Which mammal spreads hazelnuts and beechnuts by burying supplies in the ground?
105714.e: Squirrels make lots of hiding places in autumn. Whatever they do not find again in winter can germinate in spring.
105714.m: Squirrels plant new trees without meaning to.

105715.q: How are fruits that can float spread?
105715.e: Floating fruits are carried away by streams, rivers or ocean currents. Experts call this hydrochory, from the Greek word ‘hydor’ for water.
105715.m: Fruits that float are spread by water.

105716.q: Which fruit can drift in the sea for weeks and germinate on faraway coasts?
105716.e: The coconut has a thick, fibrous, air-filled husk. So it floats and can drift across the sea for months before germinating on a beach.
105716.m: Coconuts travel across the sea by floating.

105717.q: Which tree on the banks of streams has small fruits that can float?
105717.e: The little nuts of the black alder contain air-filled tissue and float on the water. In this way the alder settles new places along the bank.
105717.m: The alder sends its fruits floating down the stream.

105718.q: What helps many fruits and seeds to float on water?
105718.e: Air-filled spaces make a fruit lighter than water. A waxy surface also stops it from soaking up water.
105718.m: Air in the tissue makes seeds able to float.

105719.q: In mangroves the seeds already germinate on the parent plant. How are the seedlings spread?
a: They fall into the water and drift away
105719.e: The rod-shaped seedlings of mangroves come away from the tree and drift in the seawater. When they reach shallow mud, they quickly take root.
105719.m: Mangroves send ready-made seedlings on a journey.

105720.q: In which direction do streams and rivers mainly spread seeds?
105720.e: Flowing water carries everything down the valley with the current. That is why you often find riverbank plants along a whole river.
105720.m: Rivers carry seeds downstream with the current.

105721.q: What does a seed need to survive a long journey in seawater?
105721.e: Salt water would damage the seedling. A tight, hard shell protects the seed until it is washed ashore.
105721.m: A tight shell protects sea-going seeds from salt water.

105722.q: Some plants use the rain to spread their seeds. How does that work?
a: Raindrops splash the seeds out of the fruit
Raindrops stick the seeds to birds
Rain makes the seeds germinate at once
Rain dissolves the seeds in the soil
105722.e: In some plants the fruit works like a cup or a seesaw. When a raindrop hits it, the seeds splash out.
105722.m: Some plants use the force of raindrops.

105723.q: What does self-dispersal mean in plants?
a: The plant spreads its seeds without wind, water or animals
The plant keeps growing without seeds
The plant lets birds eat its seeds
The plant is sown by people
105723.e: Self-dispersing plants fling their seeds away or simply let them drop. They need no help from wind, water or animals.
105723.m: In self-dispersal the plant spreads its seeds itself.

105724.q: Which plant has the nickname ‘touch-me-not’ because its fruits burst open when touched?
105724.e: The ripe capsules of balsam are under tension. Even a light touch makes them roll up and fling the seeds away.
105724.m: Balsam flings its seeds away when touched.

105725.q: What causes the tension in the capsules of balsam?
a: warmth from the sun in the seed
105725.e: The cells of the fruit wall are tightly filled with water. This inner pressure builds up a tension that is suddenly released when the capsule is touched.
105725.m: Water pressure in the cells tightens the balsam capsule.

105726.q: Which plant squirts its seeds out of the fruit together with juice when ripe?
105726.e: In the squirting cucumber a high pressure builds up in the fruit. When it comes off the stalk, a jet of juice and seeds shoots out.
105726.m: The squirting cucumber shoots out its seeds in a jet of juice.

105727.q: How does broom fling its seeds away?
a: The drying halves of the pod twist
105727.e: As the pod walls dry out, they shrink unevenly. Suddenly the pod splits open, the halves twist and fling the seeds away.
105727.m: Broom pods burst open as they dry and fling out seeds.

105728.q: Which plant is named after the beak-like shape of its fruit and flings its seeds away?
105728.e: The fruit of the cranesbill looks like a long bird’s beak. When ripe, the parts roll up with a jerk and catapult the seeds.

105729.q: How do the heavy fruits of the horse chestnut reach the ground without outside help?
a: They fall because of their weight
They are carried far by the wind
They float away on the water
105729.e: Heavy fruits simply fall to the ground because of gravity. So they usually land under or near the parent plant.
105729.m: Heavy fruits fall to the ground because of their weight.

105730.q: What is usually the disadvantage of self-dispersal compared with wind dispersal?
a: The seeds land near the parent plant
105730.e: Flinging or falling usually takes seeds only a few metres. The young plants then compete with the parent plant for light and water.
105730.m: Self-dispersing plants usually stay near the parent plant.

105731.q: What does it mean when a seed is dormant?
a: It does not germinate for now, even though it is damp and warm
105731.e: While dormant, the seed waits until certain conditions are met, for example until a winter has passed. Only then does it germinate.
105731.m: A dormant seed waits before germinating.

105732.q: What is the advantage of seed dormancy for plants in Switzerland?
a: It stops them germinating just before winter
105732.e: If a seed germinated in a warm autumn, the young seedling could freeze in winter. Dormancy moves germination to the spring.
105732.m: Seed dormancy protects seedlings from winter.

105733.q: What do many seeds of native trees need before they germinate?
105733.e: Many seeds only germinate after a long cold period. Gardeners copy the winter by keeping the seeds damp in the fridge.
105733.m: Many seeds need cold before they germinate.

105734.q: Why do people lightly scratch some very hard seeds before sowing them?
a: So that water can get in
So that birds do not eat them
105734.e: Some seed coats are so hard that no water can get in. Scratching lets the seed take in water, swell and germinate.
105734.m: Hard seed coats can be scratched so that they germinate.

105736.q: In 2005 a young plant grew from a seed about 2000 years old from Israel. Which plant?
105736.e: The seed came from excavations at the fortress of Masada. The date palm that grew from it was nicknamed ‘Methuselah’.
105736.m: Some seeds can still germinate after hundreds of years.

105737.q: How is seed stored in the huge seed vault on Svalbard?
105737.e: In the Svalbard Global Seed Vault, seed samples from all over the world are kept in cold rooms far below zero degrees. Cold and dryness greatly slow down the ageing of the seeds.
105737.m: Cold keeps seeds able to germinate for a long time.

105738.q: What do you call the store of dormant seeds that can still germinate, lying in the soil?
105738.e: There are often thousands of seeds in the soil that rest for years. When the soil is dug up, some suddenly germinate, for example poppies on freshly dug earth.
105738.m: A seed bank in the soil waits for its chance.

105739.e: A large, very hard capsule grows on the Brazil nut tree. Inside, many seeds lie tightly packed, and these are sold as Brazil nuts.
105739.m: Brazil nuts are seeds and not true nuts.

105740.q: In what weather do spruce cones open and release their winged seeds?
105740.e: When the cone scales dry out, they spread apart. The winged seeds fly especially well in dry air; when it is wet the cone closes again.
105740.m: Spruce cones open when it is dry.

105832.q: What is the tube-shaped pocket in the skin that a hair sits in called?
105832.e: The hair follicle wraps around the hair root like a small tube. In it, the hair is made and anchored.
105832.m: Every hair sits in a hair follicle.

105833.q: Which small muscle on the hair follicle makes the hair stand up when you are cold?
105833.e: A tiny muscle is attached to the hair follicle. When it contracts, the hair stands up and you get goose bumps.
105833.m: The hair erector muscle makes hairs stand up in the cold.

105834.q: Which cells in the hair follicle make sure a new hair can grow after one falls out?
105834.e: There are stem cells in the upper part of the hair follicle. They can divide again and again and build a new hair root.
105834.m: Stem cells in the hair follicle make new hair growth possible.

105835.q: What are the thick hairs on a cat’s muzzle called, whose follicles are surrounded by especially many nerves?
105835.e: Whiskers, also called vibrissae, are touch hairs. Their follicles have lots of nerves, so the cat can feel the slightest air movements and obstacles in the dark.

105836.q: What are the fine, short, pale little hairs called that grow on the cheeks and arms, for example?
105836.e: Vellus hairs are thin, short and hardly coloured, and they cover large parts of the skin. Hair on the head and eyebrows, by contrast, is thicker and strongly coloured.
105836.m: The fine fuzz on the skin is made of thin, pale little hairs.

105837.q: Do unborn babies in the womb already have hair?
a: Yes, a fine fuzz that usually falls out before birth
No, hair only grows after birth
Yes, thick hair on the head that never falls out
105837.e: Even an unborn baby grows a very fine fuzz all over its body. It is called lanugo and usually falls out before birth.
105837.m: Unborn babies have a fine fuzz of hair.

105838.q: Why can you feel even a very light touch on a single hair?
a: There are nerve endings around the hair follicle
The tip of the hair is a sense organ
The hair conducts electricity to the brain
105838.e: A fine network of nerve endings lies around every hair follicle. When the hair moves, the movement is detected at the root and reported to the brain.
105838.m: Hairs work like little feelers because their follicles are surrounded by nerves.

105839.q: What is an inflammation of the hair follicle, usually caused by bacteria, called?
105839.e: In folliculitis, hair follicles become inflamed, often because of bacteria. Small red bumps or tiny spots of pus appear around a hair.
105839.m: Folliculitis is an inflammation of hair follicles.

105840.q: Which property of keratin means hair does not dissolve when you wash it?
a: It does not dissolve in water
105840.e: Keratin is a fibrous protein that does not dissolve in water. It can soak up a little water and swell, but it stays stable.
105840.m: Keratin does not dissolve in water.

105841.q: Which group of substances does keratin belong to?
105841.e: Keratin is a protein made of long chains of amino acids. These chains are twisted into very strong fibres.
105841.m: Keratin is an especially strong protein.

105842.q: Which parts of animals are also mainly made of keratin?
a: The shells of beetles and crabs
105842.e: Hooves, claws, feathers, reptile scales and the outer covering of horns are made of keratin. Snail shells are made of lime, beetle shells of chitin.
105842.m: Hooves, claws and feathers are made of keratin, like our hair.

105843.q: Which chemical element in keratin is responsible for burnt hair smelling so unpleasant?
105843.e: Keratin contains many building blocks with sulphur. When it burns, sulphur compounds form that smell strong and unpleasant.
105843.m: The sulphur in keratin makes burnt hair stink.

105844.q: Which bonds in keratin are broken during a perm and joined again in a new shape?
105844.e: Sulphur bridges hold the keratin chains in their shape. A perm breaks them chemically, the hair is wound round curlers and the bridges are joined again in the new shape.
105844.m: A perm changes the sulphur bridges in keratin.

105845.q: Which cells of the epidermis make keratin?
105845.e: Keratinocytes are the most common cells in the epidermis. They make keratin and slowly move up to the surface as they do so.
105845.m: Keratinocytes are the cells that make keratin.

105846.q: Which layer of the skin is made of dead cells full of keratin?
105846.e: The horny layer is the outermost layer of the epidermis. Its dead, keratin-rich cells protect the body against water loss and germs.
105846.m: The horny layer protects the skin with dead keratin cells.

105847.q: What is the process called in which cells fill up with keratin and die?
105847.e: In keratinisation, cells fill with keratin, lose their nucleus and die. This is how hair, nails and the horny layer of the skin are formed.
105847.m: In keratinisation, living cells turn into firm horn.

a: The scales of the outermost layer of hair lie flat
105848.e: The outermost layer of a hair is made of keratin scales like roof tiles. When they lie flat, the hair reflects the light and shines.
105848.m: Flat hair scales make hair shine.

105849.q: What is the thickened lower end of the hair root called?
105849.e: The hair bulb is the onion-shaped swelling at the end of the hair root. There, the cells that the hair grows from divide.
105849.m: The hair bulb is at the lower end of the hair root.

105850.q: What does the hair papilla bring to the growing cells of the hair root?
105850.e: The hair papilla reaches up into the hair bulb from below and contains tiny blood vessels. Through it, the hair root gets oxygen and nutrients.
105850.m: The hair papilla supplies the hair root with blood.

105851.q: Which part of a hair is made of living cells?
105851.e: Living cells only divide in the hair root. As soon as they are pushed upwards, they harden and die, which is why having your hair cut does not hurt.
105851.m: Only the root of a hair is alive.

105852.q: What is the part of the hair that sticks out of the skin and can be seen called?
105852.e: The hair shaft is the visible hair above the skin. The hair root, on the other hand, is hidden in the hair follicle.
105852.m: The visible part of a hair is called the hair shaft.

105853.q: Where are the pigments made that give hair its colour?
a: In pigment cells in the hair root
105853.e: Pigment cells called melanocytes sit in the hair bulb. They pass the pigment on to the new hair cells as they form.
105853.m: Hair colour is made down in the hair root.

105854.q: Why can the police get DNA more easily from a hair pulled out with its root than from a cut hair?
a: The root contains cells with a nucleus
The root is longer than the shaft
105854.e: Cells with a nucleus, which holds the genetic information, are attached to the hair root. In the hardened hair shaft, hardly any of this is left.
105854.m: For a DNA trace, the hair root is more valuable than the shaft.

105855.q: What usually happens if you pull out a hair but the hair follicle stays undamaged?
a: A hair never grows there again
