106121.m: The physalis grows in a case like a lantern.

106122.q: What is the part called in which an acorn sits as if in a cup?
106122.e: The cup is typical of the beech family. In the oak it only covers the bottom of the nut.
106122.m: The acorn sits in a cup.

106123.q: Why do only a few plants grow on the ground in a dense beech wood in summer?
a: The dense leafy roof lets hardly any light through
Beeches release poison into the air
The ground there is always frozen
106123.e: Beeches form a very dense canopy that lets little light reach the ground. That is why many woodland plants flower before the leaves come out.
106123.m: In a beech wood it is very shady on the ground in summer.

106124.q: Which wood are wine barrels (barriques) traditionally made from?
106124.e: Oak is dense, durable and gives flavours to the wine. That is why wine has been stored in oak barrels for centuries.
106124.m: Wine barrels are made from oak.

106125.q: Which tree does NOT belong to the beech family?
106125.e: The horse chestnut belongs to the soapberry family. Despite having similar fruits, it is not closely related to the sweet chestnut.
106125.m: The horse chestnut does not belong to the beech family.

106126.q: In which canton have chestnut groves (selve) shaped the landscape for centuries?
106126.e: The fruits of the sweet chestnut used to be a staple food in southern Switzerland. They were called the ‘bread of the poor’.
106126.m: Sweet chestnuts shape the landscape in Ticino.

106127.q: Which raw material does the cork oak from the Mediterranean provide?
106127.e: The thick bark of the cork oak is peeled off about every nine years without cutting the tree down. It is used, for example, to make bottle corks.
106127.m: Cork is the bark of the cork oak.

106128.q: What is a ‘mast year’ for beeches and oaks?
a: A year with especially many fruits
A year with lots of storm damage
106128.e: In mast years beeches and oaks produce huge numbers of fruits. In the past, pigs were driven into these woods to fatten up.
106128.m: In a mast year beeches and oaks produce a great many fruits.

106129.q: How many beechnuts usually sit together in one prickly beech cup?
106129.e: The woody cup with soft prickles opens in autumn with four flaps. Inside there are usually two three-sided beechnuts.
106129.m: A beech cup usually holds two beechnuts.

106224.q: What is the part of a tooth that sticks out of the gum and can be seen called?
106224.e: The crown is the part you see in your mouth and chew with. The root and the socket are hidden in the jawbone.
106224.m: The crown is the visible part of a tooth.

106225.q: Which layer covers the crown of a tooth on the outside?
106225.e: The crown is covered by a hard, shiny layer of enamel. It protects the more sensitive inside of the tooth.
106225.m: Enamel protects the crown like armour.

106226.q: What is the hardest substance in the human body?
106226.e: Tooth enamel is made almost entirely of minerals and is harder than any bone. That is why it stands up to chewing for decades.
106226.m: Tooth enamel is harder than any bone in the body.

106227.q: Which mineral is an important building block of tooth enamel?
106227.e: Tooth enamel is made almost entirely of minerals. The most important building block is calcium together with phosphate.
106227.m: Tooth enamel contains lots of calcium.

106228.q: Why can the body not rebuild lost tooth enamel itself?
a: Finished enamel contains no living cells
Enamel only grows back during sleep
Saliva dissolves new enamel straight away
Enamel only forms again during a fever
106228.e: The cells that build the enamel die as soon as the tooth has come through. That is why a hole in the enamel has to be filled by the dentist.
106228.m: Lost tooth enamel does not grow back.

106229.q: What are the fine grooves on the chewing surface of the back teeth, where decay easily starts, called?
106229.e: Fissures are narrow grooves between the bumps of the back teeth. Food scraps and bacteria easily get stuck there.
106229.m: Decay starts especially easily in the fissures of the back teeth.

106230.q: What are the raised points on the chewing surface of a back tooth called?
106230.e: Back teeth have a wide chewing surface with several cusps. They grind food as if between two millstones.
106230.m: The cusps of the back teeth grind food.

106231.q: What does the dentist do when sealing fissures?
a: She fills the grooves of the chewing surface with plastic
She pulls out a milk tooth
She glues a wire onto the teeth
106231.e: In sealing, the deep grooves of the back teeth are closed with runny plastic. Then bacteria can no longer settle there.
106231.m: Fissure sealing protects the chewing surfaces from decay.

106232.q: What is an artificial cap placed over a badly damaged tooth called?
106232.e: If not enough healthy tooth is left, it is capped with an artificial crown. A bridge, on the other hand, spans a gap between teeth.
106232.m: An artificial crown protects a badly damaged tooth.

106233.q: Which part of the tooth sits in the jawbone and holds the tooth in place?
106233.e: The root sits out of sight in the jawbone. It anchors the tooth so that it does not wobble when you chew.
106233.m: The root anchors the tooth in the jaw.

106234.q: Which hard layer covers the outside of the root of a tooth?
106234.e: The root is not covered with enamel but with a thin, bone-like layer called cementum. The fibres that hold the tooth are anchored in it.
106234.m: The root of a tooth is covered with cementum.

106235.q: What is the hollow in the jawbone that a tooth root sits in called?
106235.e: Each tooth root sits in its own socket, which experts call an alveolus. The socket is part of the jawbone.
106235.m: Each tooth root sits in its own socket.

106236.q: How is a tooth fixed in its socket?
a: With many fine fibres of the root lining
Only by the pressure of the gum
With a kind of glue made of saliva
106236.e: Between the root and the bone lies a lining with thousands of collagen fibres. They cushion the pressure of chewing, which is why a healthy tooth can move just a tiny bit.
106236.m: Fine fibres hold the tooth springily in the jawbone.

106237.q: Why do large back teeth have several roots?
a: They have to withstand strong chewing pressure
So that they fall out more easily
106237.e: You grind food with your back teeth. Several roots spread the strong chewing pressure onto the jawbone.
106237.m: Several roots hold back teeth firmly when you chew.

106238.q: How do nerves and blood vessels get inside a tooth?
a: Through a small opening at the tip of the root
Through the enamel of the crown
Through the gaps between the teeth
106238.e: At the tip of each root there is a tiny opening. There, nerves and blood vessels enter the root canal.
106238.m: Nerves and blood vessels reach the tooth through the tip of the root.

106239.q: Which metal is an artificial tooth root, a dental implant, usually made of?
106239.e: Most dental implants are made of titanium. It is very well tolerated and grows firmly together with the jawbone.
106239.m: Dental implants are usually made of well-tolerated titanium.

106240.q: Why does a milk tooth that has fallen out have almost no root left?
a: Its root was broken down beforehand
Milk teeth never grow with a root
The root stays stuck in the jaw
The root is worn away by chewing
106240.e: When the permanent tooth moves up, the body gradually breaks down the root of the milk tooth. In the end only a little tissue holds the milk tooth, and it wobbles.
106240.m: Before the teeth change, the root of the milk tooth is broken down.

106241.q: Where is the neck of a tooth?
a: Where the crown meets the root
At the tip of the root
In the middle of the chewing surface
106241.e: The neck of the tooth is the narrow area between the crown and the root. In healthy teeth, it lies at the edge of the gum.
106241.m: The neck of the tooth joins the crown and the root.

106242.q: Which two hard substances meet on the outside at the neck of a tooth?
106242.e: The crown is covered with enamel, the root with cementum. The border between the two runs exactly at the neck of the tooth.
106242.m: At the neck of the tooth, the enamel ends and the cementum begins.

106243.q: Why are exposed tooth necks often sensitive to pain?
a: Because unprotected dentine is exposed there
Because especially thick enamel lies there
106243.e: At the neck of the tooth there is no protective enamel. If it is exposed, fine channels in the dentine pass stimuli straight to the nerve.
106243.m: Exposed tooth necks are sensitive because they have no enamel.

106244.q: Which stimulus most often makes sensitive tooth necks hurt?
a: Cold, for example when eating ice cream
Breathing in deeply through the nose
106244.e: Cold, but also sweet or sour things, changes the fluid in the channels of the dentine. This irritates the nerve and causes a short, sharp pain.
106244.m: Sensitive tooth necks react especially strongly to cold.

106245.q: What can cause tooth necks to become exposed?
a: Scrubbing too hard with a hard toothbrush
106245.e: If you scrub with a lot of pressure and a hard brush, you can push the gum back. Gum disease (periodontitis) also makes the gum shrink.
106245.m: Gentle brushing protects the gums and the tooth necks.

106246.q: Why does decay start more easily on an exposed tooth neck than on the crown?
a: Because cementum and dentine are softer than enamel
Because the tooth neck keeps growing back
106246.e: Cementum and dentine contain fewer minerals than tooth enamel. That is why acids from bacteria attack them faster.
106246.m: An exposed tooth neck is especially prone to decay.

106247.q: How do many toothpastes for sensitive teeth help?
a: They seal the fine channels in the dentine
106247.e: Special ingredients settle in the open channels of the dentine and seal them. Stimuli such as cold then reach the nerve less strongly.
106247.m: Toothpaste for sensitive teeth seals open channels in the dentine.

106248.q: How should you brush so that the tooth necks are not damaged?
a: Scrubbing sideways with a lot of pressure
106248.e: If you scrub sideways with a lot of pressure, you can rub notches into the tooth at the neck. Brushing gently with a soft brush protects teeth and gums.
106248.m: Gentle brushing protects the tooth necks.

106249.q: What is the hard substance called that lies under the enamel and makes up most of the tooth?
106249.e: Dentine makes up the main part of the tooth. In the crown it lies under the enamel, in the root under the cementum.
106249.m: Dentine makes up most of a tooth.

106251.q: How hard is dentine compared with tooth enamel and bone?
a: Softer than enamel but harder than bone
106251.e: Dentine contains about 70 per cent minerals, which is less than enamel but more than bone. In return, it is a little more elastic than enamel.
106251.m: In hardness, dentine lies between enamel and bone.

106252.q: What runs through dentine in large numbers?
106252.e: Dentine is crossed by countless tiny channels that reach the pulp. They contain extensions of the cells that make the dentine.
106252.m: Countless fine channels run through dentine.

106253.q: Why do teeth with exposed dentine often hurt when you eat something cold?
a: Fine channels in the dentine pass the stimulus to the tooth nerve
106253.e: Dentine is crossed by tiny channels that reach the pulp. Without the protective enamel, cold and sweet things quickly reach the nerve.

106254.e: Dentine is yellowish. Because enamel is see-through, the dentine helps give the tooth its shade.
106254.m: The yellowish dentine shows through the enamel.

106255.q: What is ivory, the material of elephants’ tusks, made of?
106255.e: Elephants’ tusks are greatly lengthened teeth. Their ivory is mainly made of dentine.
106255.m: Ivory is the dentine of elephant tusks.

106256.q: What happens to the space for the pulp over a lifetime?
a: It gets smaller because new dentine forms
It gets bigger because dentine disappears
It always stays exactly the same size
106256.e: Throughout life, the odontoblasts slowly make more dentine towards the inside. This makes the pulp chamber narrower with age.
106256.m: With age, new dentine makes the pulp chamber narrower.

106257.q: What is the soft tissue inside a tooth called?
106257.e: Inside every tooth lies the dental pulp, a soft tissue. It fills the pulp chamber in the crown and the root canals.
106257.m: The soft dental pulp lies inside the tooth.

106259.q: What does the dental pulp contain?
106259.e: The pulp is made of connective tissue with nerves and blood vessels. It supplies the tooth and reports stimuli such as cold or pain.
106259.m: Through the pulp, nerves and blood vessels keep the tooth alive.

106260.q: What do you often feel when the pulp is inflamed?
a: A rushing sound in the ears
106260.e: The pulp contains nerves. When it is inflamed, severe, throbbing toothache often follows.
106260.m: An inflamed pulp causes severe toothache.

106261.q: In what order does deep decay get into a tooth from the outside?
106261.e: Decay starts in the outer enamel and eats its way into the dentine. If it reaches the pulp, the pulp becomes inflamed.
106261.m: Decay eats its way from the enamel through the dentine to the pulp.

106262.q: What is the part of the pulp chamber that runs through the root of the tooth called?
106262.e: In each root, the pulp chamber continues as a narrow root canal. Nerves and vessels run through it to the tip of the root.
106262.m: Nerves and vessels run through the root canal into the root.

106263.q: What does the dentist remove during root canal treatment?
a: The whole tooth with its root
106263.e: In root canal treatment, the diseased pulp is removed from the root canals. Then the canals are cleaned and tightly filled, so the tooth is saved.
106263.m: Root canal treatment saves the tooth by removing the diseased pulp.

106264.q: How can you often recognise a tooth whose pulp has died?
106264.e: If the pulp dies, for example after an accident, waste substances build up in the dentine. The tooth then looks grey or brownish.
106264.m: A dead tooth often turns dark.

106265.q: What is the best way to clean the gaps between the teeth at the edge of the gum?
106265.e: A toothbrush hardly reaches the gaps. Dental floss removes plaque there and so protects the gums.
106265.m: Dental floss cleans the gaps between the teeth.

106266.q: What do healthy gums look like?
106266.e: Healthy gums are pale pink and firm and fit tightly around the tooth. Redness and swelling are signs of inflammation.
106266.m: Healthy gums are pale pink and firm.

106267.q: What helps most against inflamed gums?
a: Brushing thoroughly and using dental floss
106267.e: Inflamed gums are usually caused by plaque at the edge of the gum. If it is removed regularly, the gums usually heal again.
106267.m: Good tooth care helps against inflamed gums.

106268.q: What is a typical sign of inflamed gums?
a: Bleeding gums when brushing your teeth
106268.e: Inflamed gums are red, swollen and bleed easily, for example when brushing. Healthy gums do not normally bleed when you do this.
106268.m: Bleeding gums are often a sign of inflammation.

106269.q: What is the most common cause of inflamed gums?
a: A layer of bacteria at the edge of the gum
106269.e: If plaque at the edge of the gum is not removed thoroughly, the gum reacts with inflammation. Good oral hygiene prevents this.
106269.m: Plaque at the edge of the gum causes inflamed gums.

106270.q: Where does plaque get stuck especially easily?
a: In the gaps between the teeth
On the tip of the tongue
On the front of the front teeth
106270.e: The toothbrush finds it hard to reach between the teeth. That is why plaque easily builds up there and irritates the gums.
106270.m: Plaque easily gets stuck between the teeth.

106271.q: Can inflamed gums heal completely again?
a: Yes, usually with good oral hygiene
Only by pulling out the teeth
106271.e: Gum inflammation on its own can be reversed. If the plaque is removed regularly, the gums usually become healthy again within a few days to weeks.
106271.m: Gingivitis usually heals completely with good tooth care.

106272.q: What is the narrow groove between the tooth and the edge of the gum called?
106272.e: Between the tooth and the edge of the gum there is a shallow groove. With healthy gums, it is only a few millimetres deep.
106272.m: A narrow gum groove lies between the tooth and the gum.

a: An inflammation of the tissues that hold the teeth
An inflammation of the jaw joint
A hole in the tooth enamel
Teeth that are out of line
106273.e: In periodontitis, the tissues that hold the tooth in the jaw become inflamed. In everyday language it is often simply called gum disease.
106273.m: Periodontitis attacks what holds the teeth in place.

106274.q: What makes periodontitis different from simple gum inflammation?
a: It also breaks down the jawbone
It only affects the tooth enamel
106274.e: Gingivitis only affects the gums. In periodontitis, the fibres that hold the tooth and the jawbone are broken down as well, and these do not grow back by themselves.
106274.m: In periodontitis, jawbone is lost too.

106275.q: Which warning sign can point to inflammation of the gums?
a: Bleeding gums when brushing your teeth
106275.e: Healthy gums are firm and do not bleed. If they bleed when you brush, they are often inflamed, and this can turn into periodontitis.
106275.m: Bleeding gums are a warning sign.

106276.e: Bacteria from plaque on and below the edge of the gum trigger the inflammation. The body’s defence reaction also destroys tissue in the process.
106276.m: Bacteria in plaque are the main cause of periodontitis.

106277.q: What can happen if periodontitis is not treated?
a: The teeth become loose and fall out
The teeth become longer and stronger
106277.e: As more and more bone is broken down, the teeth lose their hold. In adults, periodontitis is a common cause of losing teeth.
106277.m: Untreated periodontitis can lead to losing teeth.

106278.q: Which habit clearly increases the risk of periodontitis?
106278.e: Smoking reduces the blood supply to the gums and weakens the body’s defences. Smokers get periodontitis much more often.
106278.m: Smoking harms the gums and encourages periodontitis.

106279.q: What does the dentist measure with a fine probe to detect periodontitis?
a: The depth of the gum pockets
106279.e: In periodontitis, the gum comes away from the tooth and deep pockets form. Their depth is measured in millimetres with a probe.
106279.m: Deep gum pockets are a sign of periodontitis.

106280.q: With which general illness is the risk of periodontitis higher?
106280.e: People with diabetes mellitus get periodontitis more often and more severely. In turn, periodontitis can make blood sugar harder to control.
106280.m: Diabetes and periodontitis affect each other.

106281.q: What is the branch of dentistry called that treats crooked teeth with braces?
106281.e: Orthodontics corrects crooked teeth and bites that do not meet properly. The specialists are called orthodontists.
106281.m: Orthodontists straighten crooked teeth with braces.

106282.q: In fixed braces, what connects the brackets to each other?
106282.e: A springy archwire runs through all the brackets. It applies gentle pressure and slowly moves the teeth into the desired position.
106282.m: The archwire of the brace slowly pushes the teeth into place.

106283.q: What are the clear plastic trays called that can straighten teeth without brackets?
106283.e: Aligners are almost invisible trays that are replaced by new ones every few weeks. Each tray moves the teeth a little further.
106283.m: Aligners are clear trays that move teeth step by step.

106284.q: What is a retainer for after treatment with a brace?
a: It holds the teeth in their new position
106284.e: After treatment, teeth often want to move back to where they were. A retainer, such as a thin wire behind the teeth, prevents this.
106284.m: A retainer keeps the result of the brace.

106285.q: Why can teeth be moved with a brace at all?
a: The jawbone breaks down on the pressure side and builds up on the pulling side
The teeth become as soft as rubber
The roots come away from the tooth
The wire makes the jaw grow faster
106285.e: Constant light pressure means bone in front of the tooth is broken down and new bone forms behind it. So the tooth slowly travels through the bone.
106285.m: Teeth move because the jawbone reshapes itself under pressure.

106286.q: Which kind of brace can you take out of your mouth yourself?
106286.e: A removable brace is made of a plastic plate with wires and is taken out for eating. But it only works if you wear it for long enough.
106286.m: A removable brace only works if you wear it regularly.

106287.q: Why is thorough brushing especially important with fixed braces?
a: Plaque easily gets stuck on the brackets
Otherwise the wire rusts straight away
Otherwise the teeth grow too fast
106287.e: Food scraps and bacteria collect around the brackets and wire. Without thorough care, white decay spots and inflamed gums are a risk.
106287.m: Fixed braces need especially thorough tooth care.

106288.q: Which tooth is the wisdom tooth?
106288.e: The wisdom tooth is the very back tooth in each row. Experts call it the third molar.
106288.m: The wisdom tooth is the last large back tooth.

106289.q: How many wisdom teeth does a complete set of permanent teeth have?
106289.e: A complete set of permanent teeth has 32 teeth. In each of the four quarters of the jaw, there is a wisdom tooth at the back.
106289.m: A complete set of teeth has four wisdom teeth.

106290.q: When do wisdom teeth usually come through?
a: In the late teens or early adulthood
106290.e: Wisdom teeth are the last teeth to appear, often between about 16 and 25. In some people they never come through.
106290.m: Wisdom teeth come last, often only in early adulthood.

106291.q: Where does the wisdom tooth get its name from?
a: It only comes when you are older and supposedly wiser
It was discovered by a scholar called Wisdom
It sits right under the brain
106291.e: Because the tooth appears late, when you are already grown up, it was called the wisdom tooth. It has nothing to do with cleverness.
106291.m: The wisdom tooth is called that because it comes through late.

106292.q: Why do wisdom teeth often have to be removed?
a: Because there is too little room for them in the jaw
106292.e: Often there is not enough room in the jaw. The teeth then stay stuck at an angle in the bone, press on neighbouring teeth or become inflamed.
106292.m: There is often not enough room in the jaw for wisdom teeth.

106293.q: Do all people have wisdom teeth forming?
a: No, some people are missing some or all of them
Yes, every single person has all four
106293.e: In many people, one or more wisdom teeth never form at all. This is harmless.

106294.q: What is a wisdom tooth called that lies at an angle in the jaw and cannot come through properly?
106294.e: If there is no room, the wisdom tooth often tilts and stays wholly or partly stuck in the bone. This is called an impacted tooth.
106294.m: An impacted wisdom tooth stays stuck at an angle in the jaw.

106295.q: How many teeth does a complete set of permanent teeth with wisdom teeth have?
106295.e: The permanent set has 32 teeth, four of them wisdom teeth. The set of milk teeth has only 20 teeth.
106295.m: A complete set of permanent teeth has 32 teeth.

a: It hardens tooth enamel and protects against decay
It makes the gums grow back
106296.e: Fluoride makes tooth enamel more resistant to acids. This makes it one of the most important protective substances against decay.
106296.m: Fluoride in toothpaste protects the teeth from decay.

106297.q: How does fluoride act on early, still small spots of decay?
a: It helps minerals to be stored again
It eats the bacteria up straight away
It fills the hole with plastic
106297.e: Fluoride encourages remineralisation, which means calcium and phosphate are stored in the enamel again. In this way, early loss of minerals can heal.
106297.m: Fluoride helps enamel to store lost minerals again.

106298.q: Which food is widely enriched with fluoride in Switzerland?
106298.e: Switzerland has had fluoridated table salt for decades. It is used at home and by many bakeries and restaurants.
106298.m: In Switzerland, table salt is often enriched with fluoride.

106299.q: How often a day should you brush your teeth with fluoride toothpaste?
106299.e: Dentists recommend brushing with fluoride toothpaste at least twice a day, ideally in the morning and evening.
106299.m: Brushing twice a day protects the teeth.

106300.q: What can too much fluoride cause in children while their teeth are developing?
a: White spots in the tooth enamel
106300.e: If too much fluoride is taken in over a long time while the teeth are forming, dental fluorosis can develop. It usually shows as white spots or streaks.
106300.m: Too much fluoride can cause white spots on children’s teeth.

106301.q: Which chemical element does fluoride come from?
106301.e: Fluorides are compounds of the element fluorine. Fluorine itself is a very reactive, poisonous gas, but fluorides in small amounts protect the teeth.
106301.m: Fluorides are compounds of the element fluorine.

106302.q: What is recommended after brushing your teeth so that the fluoride works better?
a: Just spit out the foam, do not rinse hard
Drink a glass of orange juice straight away
Rinse your teeth with hot water
106302.e: If you rinse hard with water after brushing, you also rinse away the fluoride. Just spitting out leaves more of it working on your teeth.
106302.m: Spitting out instead of rinsing after brushing lets the fluoride work for longer.

106303.q: Which fluoride treatment does the dentist put directly on the teeth?
106303.e: Fluoride varnish is painted onto the teeth at the dentist’s. It sticks for a few hours and releases a lot of fluoride into the enamel.
106303.m: Fluoride varnish is painted onto the teeth at the dentist’s.

106304.q: Apart from hardening the enamel, what other protective effect does fluoride have?
a: It slows down the production of acid by bacteria
It kills all the viruses in the mouth
106304.e: Fluoride interferes with the metabolism of decay bacteria. As a result, they make less acid from sugar.
106304.m: Fluoride slows down acid production by decay bacteria.

106305.q: What is plaque on the teeth?
a: A hard layer of tooth enamel
106305.e: Plaque is a sticky film of bacteria, the substances they produce and food scraps. It forms again every day.
106305.m: Plaque is a soft layer of bacteria on the teeth.

106306.q: How does plaque lead to tooth decay?
a: Bacteria make acids from sugar that remove minerals from the enamel
Plaque sucks water out of the tooth
Plaque grows into the tooth like a root
106306.e: The bacteria in plaque use sugar and give off acids as they do so. These dissolve minerals out of the enamel until a hole forms.
106306.m: Acids from plaque dissolve tooth enamel.

106307.q: What forms if plaque is not removed for a long time and hardens?
106307.e: Minerals from saliva build up in the plaque. This makes it hard, and then it can only be removed at the dentist’s.

106308.q: How can you make plaque on the teeth visible?
106308.e: Disclosing tablets or solutions colour the plaque red or blue. This shows exactly where you have not yet brushed thoroughly.
106308.m: Disclosing tablets show where plaque is still sitting.

106309.q: Why is brushing your teeth before going to sleep especially important?
a: During sleep little saliva flows to buffer acids
Teeth grow at night and need room
Enamel becomes as soft as rubber during sleep
The mouth makes more sugar at night
106309.e: During sleep the body makes only a little saliva. Acids from plaque can then work on the teeth undisturbed for a long time.
106309.m: Plaque should be removed thoroughly before going to sleep.

106310.q: In biology, what is plaque described as?
106310.e: Plaque is a biofilm, a community of microorganisms that stick to a surface in a slimy layer. Biofilms like this are also found on stones in a stream.
106310.m: Plaque is a biofilm made of many bacteria.

106311.q: Why is snacking often throughout the day especially bad for your teeth?
a: Every time you eat sugar, a new acid attack starts
Sugar makes saliva sweet and sticky like glue
106311.e: After each time you eat sugar, the bacteria produce acid for a while. If you snack all the time, the saliva has no time to neutralise the acid.
106311.m: Snacking less often gives your teeth a rest from acid attacks.

106312.q: How does saliva protect the teeth from the acids in plaque?
a: It neutralises acids and supplies minerals
106312.e: Saliva buffers acids and contains calcium and phosphate. With these it can partly repair damaged enamel.
106312.m: Saliva neutralises acids and so protects tooth enamel.

106313.q: Which drink is best for your teeth?
106313.e: Squash, fruit juice and iced tea contain lots of sugar. The bacteria in plaque turn it into acid, which harms the teeth. Water has no sugar.
106313.m: Water is the most tooth-friendly drink for quenching thirst.

106314.e: If plaque stays on the teeth for a longer time, minerals build up in it and it hardens. This creates firm tartar.

106315.q: Where do the minerals that harden plaque into tartar come from?
a: From the blood in the gums
106315.e: Saliva contains dissolved calcium and phosphate. These substances settle in the plaque and make it hard.
106315.m: Minerals from saliva turn plaque into tartar.

106316.q: Where does tartar form especially often?
a: On the inside of the lower front teeth
On the chewing surface of the wisdom teeth
On the tip of the tongue
On the outside of the lower canines
106316.e: Large salivary glands open under the tongue. That is why especially a lot of tartar builds up on the inside of the lower front teeth.
106316.m: Especially a lot of tartar forms behind the lower front teeth.

106317.q: Can you remove hard tartar yourself with a toothbrush?
a: No, a professional has to do it at the practice
Yes, with lots of dental floss
106317.e: Tartar sticks so firmly that a brush and floss are not enough. It is removed with special instruments at the dental practice.
106317.m: Only a professional at the practice can remove tartar.

106318.q: In Switzerland, which professional often removes tartar during regular teeth cleaning?
106318.e: Dental hygienists specialise in professional teeth cleaning. They remove tartar and plaque and give advice on oral hygiene.
106318.m: The dental hygienist removes tartar during teeth cleaning.

106319.q: Which device is often used to remove tartar?
106319.e: An ultrasonic device makes a fine tip vibrate very quickly. The vibrations loosen the hard deposit without damaging the tooth.
106319.m: An ultrasonic device shakes tartar off the teeth.

106320.q: Why is tartar harmful even though it does not make a hole in the tooth itself?
a: New plaque sticks especially well to its rough surface
It is so heavy that the teeth break
It sends electrical signals to the nerve
106320.e: Tartar is rough and porous. New plaque keeps settling on it and inflames the gums.
106320.m: Tartar encourages inflamed gums because new plaque sticks to it.

106321.q: Why does tartar often turn dark in smokers or tea drinkers?
a: Colourings settle in its porous surface
It rusts because of the oxygen
It burns because of the heat
It takes on the colour of the gums
106321.e: The rough, porous surface of tartar soaks up colourings from tobacco, tea or coffee. This turns it yellowish to brown.
106321.m: Tartar soaks up colourings from tea, coffee and tobacco.

106322.q: How does tartar below the edge of the gum usually differ from tartar above it?
a: It is darker and sticks more firmly
106322.e: Tartar under the gum takes up blood pigments and therefore looks dark. It is very hard, sits firmly on the root and encourages periodontitis.
106322.m: Tartar under the gum is dark and especially stubborn.

106323.q: Which kind of friction stops an object at rest from starting to slide?
106323.e: As long as two surfaces do not move against each other, static friction acts. It holds a box in place on a slightly sloping ramp, for example.
106323.m: Static friction keeps objects at rest where they are.

106324.q: Why does it take more force to get a heavy crate moving than to keep pushing it afterwards?
a: Static friction is greater than sliding friction
The crate gets lighter as you push
Sliding friction is greater than static friction
The floor gets smoother as you push
106324.e: For the same materials, the maximum static friction is greater than the sliding friction. Once the crate has started to slide, less force is enough.
106324.m: Getting something moving takes more force than keeping it going.

106325.q: A crate presses on the floor with 200 N, and the coefficient of static friction is 0.5. How big is the maximum static friction?
106325.e: The maximum static friction is the coefficient of static friction times the normal force. So 0.5 times 200 N equals 100 N.
106325.m: Static friction is the coefficient of static friction times the normal force.

106326.q: A crate with a mass of 50 kg stands on the floor, and the coefficient of static friction is 0.6. What is the minimum force you must pull with to make it slide (g equals 10 N/kg)?
106326.e: The normal force is 50 kg times 10 N/kg, which equals 500 N. The maximum static friction is 0.6 times 500 N, which equals 300 N; only above that does the crate slide.
106326.m: An object only starts to slide when the pull exceeds the maximum static friction.

106327.q: What unit does the coefficient of static friction have?
106327.e: The coefficient of static friction is the ratio of two forces: friction divided by normal force. The newtons cancel out.
106327.m: Coefficients of friction are pure numbers without a unit.

106328.q: Which kind of friction do you need when walking so that your foot does not slip as you push off?
106328.e: As you push off, your shoe rests on the ground for a moment. Static friction then passes on the force; on black ice it is missing and you slip.
106328.m: Without static friction between shoe and ground we could not walk.

106329.q: Which kind of friction passes the driving force of a rolling car tyre onto the road?
106329.e: The part of the tyre that is touching the road is briefly at rest relative to the surface. So static friction acts there, as long as the wheel does not spin.
106329.m: A rolling tyre grips the road and so passes on the force.

106330.q: What does the maximum static friction between two solid objects hardly depend on?
a: The size of the contact area
106330.e: Static friction depends mainly on the pressing force and the materials. According to the simple law of friction, it makes hardly any difference whether a brick lies flat or on its side.
106330.m: Static friction hardly depends on the size of the contact area.

106331.q: A book lies on a board that is slowly tilted more and more steeply. What happens?
a: At a certain angle the book starts to slide
The book stays put at any angle
The book slides at the slightest tilt
106331.e: The steeper the board, the bigger the downhill force. When it exceeds the maximum static friction, the book starts to slide.
106331.m: On a steep surface static friction is eventually not enough.

106332.q: Which kind of friction acts when a sledge slides over snow?
106332.e: When two surfaces slide over each other, sliding friction acts. It slows the sliding object down.
106332.m: Sliding friction slows objects that slide over a surface.

106333.q: How do you calculate sliding friction?
a: Coefficient of sliding friction times normal force
106333.e: Sliding friction is proportional to the force pressing the surfaces together. The factor is the coefficient of sliding friction for the pair of materials.
106333.m: Sliding friction is the coefficient of sliding friction times the normal force.

106334.q: A wooden crate presses on the floor with 400 N, and the coefficient of sliding friction is 0.3. How big is the sliding friction?
106334.e: The sliding friction is 0.3 times 400 N. That gives 120 N.
106334.m: The bigger the normal force, the bigger the sliding friction.

106335.q: A crate is pulled steadily across the floor with 50 N, and its normal force is 250 N. What is the coefficient of sliding friction?
106335.e: The coefficient of sliding friction is friction divided by normal force. So 50 N divided by 250 N equals 0.2.
106335.m: The coefficient of sliding friction is friction divided by normal force.

106336.q: You pull a wardrobe across the floor at constant speed and need 80 N to do so. How big is the sliding friction?
106336.e: If an object moves at constant speed, the resultant force is zero. So friction is exactly as big as the pulling force, just in the opposite direction.
106336.m: In steady motion the pulling force equals the friction.

106337.q: Which pair of materials has the smallest coefficient of sliding friction?
106337.e: Steel runners slide especially easily on ice; the coefficient of sliding friction is very small. Rubber on asphalt, on the other hand, has a large coefficient.
106337.m: Steel on ice slides with especially little friction.

106338.q: Why does an ice hockey puck slide much further on ice than on asphalt?
a: Sliding friction is much smaller on ice
The puck is lighter on ice
There is no friction on asphalt
The wind carries the puck on ice
106338.e: Hard rubber on ice has a very small coefficient of sliding friction, on rough asphalt a large one. That is why the puck is slowed down quickly on asphalt.
106338.m: The smaller the sliding friction, the further an object slides.

106339.q: How does sliding friction change if you double the normal force?
106339.e: Sliding friction is proportional to the normal force. So twice the normal force means twice the friction.
106339.m: Twice the pressing force gives twice the sliding friction.

106340.q: What mainly causes friction between two surfaces?
a: Tiny bumps that catch on each other
106340.e: Even surfaces that look smooth are rough under the microscope. The bumps catch on each other, and the particles of the surfaces also attract each other.
106340.m: Friction arises because tiny bumps on the surfaces catch on each other.

106341.q: Why are heavy loads much easier to move on wheels than by dragging them?
a: Rolling friction is much smaller than sliding friction
Rolling friction is greater than sliding friction
106341.e: When rolling, the surfaces do not slide over each other. Rolling friction is therefore usually much smaller than sliding friction.
106341.m: Wheels replace large sliding friction with small rolling friction.

a: The deformation of the wheel and the surface
The spokes catching on each other
106342.e: The wheel and the surface are pressed in slightly where they touch. This constant deformation costs energy and slows the wheel down.
106342.m: Rolling friction comes from the deformation of the wheel and the surface.

106343.q: Why is a bike with badly inflated tyres harder to ride?
a: The air in the tyre gets heavier
The chain comes off more often
106343.e: A soft tyre is squashed and flexed more as it rolls. This increases rolling friction, so you have to pedal harder.

106344.q: Why does a train on steel rails need especially little energy per tonne of load?
a: Steel wheels on steel rails have very low rolling friction
106344.e: Hard steel wheels and steel rails hardly deform. That is why rolling friction is much smaller than with rubber tyres on asphalt.
106344.m: Steel on steel rolls with very low rolling friction.

106346.q: Why is cycling on soft sand much harder work than on asphalt?
a: The sand gives way and deforms a lot
There is no gravity on sand
106346.e: The wheel sinks into the sand and constantly has to push a small hollow ahead of it. The strong deformation of the surface increases the rolling friction.
106346.m: A soft surface increases rolling friction.

106347.q: For the same load, how is rolling friction related to the size of the wheel?
a: Only wheels over a metre roll
106347.e: A big wheel sinks in less and rolls over bumps more easily. That is why big wheels, for example on off-road pushchairs, roll more easily.
106347.m: Big wheels roll more easily over the ground.

106348.q: What is the force that slows down a rolling wheel often also called?
106348.e: The braking effect when rolling is called rolling friction or rolling resistance. Tyre tests measure rolling resistance because it affects fuel consumption.
106348.m: Rolling friction is also called rolling resistance.

106349.q: Where on a bike do you find ball bearings?
106349.e: There are bearings in the wheel hubs, the bottom bracket and the headset. They make the wheels, cranks and handlebars turn easily.
106349.m: Ball bearings in the hubs let bike wheels turn easily.

106350.q: Which part of a ball bearing keeps the balls apart?
106350.e: The balls run between the inner and outer rings. A cage keeps them evenly spaced so they do not touch each other.
106350.m: The cage keeps the balls in the bearing apart.

106351.q: Between which two parts do the balls of a ball bearing roll?
a: Between the inner ring and the outer ring
Between the tyre and the road
Between the chain and the gear
Between the axle and the spoke
106351.e: The inner ring sits on the axle and the outer ring in the housing. The balls roll between them in grooves called raceways.
106351.m: In a ball bearing the balls roll between the inner and outer rings.

106352.q: Why does a wheel with a ball bearing turn more easily than one without?
a: The balls roll instead of rubbing
The balls make the wheel heavier
106352.e: In a ball bearing small balls roll between two rings. Rolling creates much less friction than sliding, so the wheel turns easily.
106352.m: In a ball bearing, rolling replaces rubbing.

106353.q: In which piece of sports equipment is there a ball bearing in every wheel?
106353.e: Each wheel of an inline skate or skateboard runs on two small ball bearings. That lets you roll a long way with little force.
106353.m: Ball bearings in the wheels make inline skates fast.

106354.q: What are the balls of an ordinary ball bearing usually made of?
106354.e: The balls have to withstand large forces and hardly deform. That is why they are usually made of very hard steel.
106354.m: The balls in a ball bearing are usually made of hard steel.

106355.q: Why are ball bearings lubricated too?
a: To make friction and wear even smaller
106355.e: Even in ball bearings there is some friction between the balls, cage and rings. Grease or oil reduces it and protects the parts from rust.
106355.m: Grease makes ball bearings run longer and more easily.

106356.q: What is a lubricant between two machine parts for?
106356.e: Lubricants such as oil or grease reduce friction between moving parts. As a result the parts wear less.

106357.q: How does oil reduce the friction between two metal parts?
a: It separates the surfaces with a thin film
It cools the parts to zero degrees
106357.e: A thin film of oil keeps the metal surfaces apart. Instead of the rough surfaces, layers of liquid then slide over each other.
106357.m: A film of oil keeps moving parts apart.

106358.q: Which substance is used as a solid lubricant?
106358.e: Graphite is made of layers of carbon that slide easily over each other. It is used, for example, as a powder for locks.
106358.m: Graphite is a solid lubricant made of sliding layers.

106359.q: What job does engine oil do besides lubricating?
106359.e: Engine oil reduces friction in the engine and at the same time carries heat away from hot parts. It also protects against corrosion.
106359.m: Engine oil lubricates and cools the engine.

106360.q: Why should you oil a bike chain regularly?
a: So that it runs smoothly and does not rust
106360.e: A thin film of oil reduces the friction in the chain links. At the same time it protects the chain from rust.
106360.m: An oiled bike chain runs smoothly and does not rust.

106361.q: What is the thickness or runniness of an oil called in technical language?
106361.e: Viscosity tells you how thick and slow-flowing a substance is. Honey has a high viscosity, water a low one.
106361.m: Viscosity describes how thick an oil is.

106362.q: Why is grease rather than oil used in places where the lubricant should not run away?
a: Grease is thick and stays in place
106362.e: Lubricating grease is a paste that hardly flows. So it stays in bearings and joints for a long time.
106362.m: Grease stays where you put it.

106363.q: Which fluid lubricates the joints in the human body?
106363.e: Synovial fluid acts like a natural lubricant between the cartilage surfaces. This lets the joints move almost without friction.
106363.m: Synovial fluid is the natural lubricant of the joints.

106364.q: Why do winter tyres grip better than summer tyres in the cold?
a: Their rubber compound stays soft even in the cold
They are filled with warmer air
They are heavier than summer tyres
They have no tread at all
106364.e: Summer tyres go hard in the cold and grip less well. The compound of winter tyres stays soft and grips better on a cold road.
106364.m: Winter tyres stay soft in the cold and grip better.

106365.q: What are the many fine cuts in the tread of a winter tyre, called sipes, for?
106365.e: The sipes open as the tyre rolls and grip snow and slush like little edges. Snow in the tread also sticks well to the snow on the road.
106365.m: The sipes of winter tyres dig into the snow.

106366.q: Which symbol marks genuine winter tyres that have been tested for snow?
a: A snowflake in front of a mountain
106366.e: The alpine symbol shows a snowflake in front of a mountain with three peaks. It only appears on tyres that have passed a test on snow.
106366.m: The mountain symbol with a snowflake marks tested winter tyres.

106367.q: Is there a general legal requirement for winter tyres in Switzerland (as of 2025)?
a: No, but the car must be equipped to suit the conditions
Yes, but only in the mountain cantons
106367.e: The law does not require winter tyres. But anyone who causes an accident or holds up traffic with unsuitable tyres can be fined and shares the liability.
106367.m: In Switzerland a car must be fit for winter in winter, even without a winter tyre requirement.

106368.q: Which rule of thumb is often given for the period when you should use winter tyres?
a: From O to O, so October to Easter (Ostern)
From J to J, so January to July
From M to M, so March to May
From A to A, so April to August
106368.e: The well-known German rule of thumb is “von O bis O”. It means you should drive on winter tyres roughly from October to Easter.
106368.m: Winter tyres belong on the car roughly from October to Easter.

106369.q: Why must a car tyre have enough tread?
a: So that it grips well on a wet road
So that it rolls more quietly
106369.e: The grooves in the tread channel water away from under the tyre. If the tread is worn, the car can start to slide on a wet road. By law at least 1.6 mm is required.
106369.m: Good tread keeps the car safe on a wet road.

106370.q: What happens if the tread of a winter tyre is badly worn?
a: It grips much worse on snow
It automatically becomes a summer tyre
106370.e: A winter tyre needs deep grooves and sipes to dig into the snow. Experts therefore recommend at least about 4 mm of tread.
106370.m: Worn winter tyres grip badly on snow.

106371.q: According to a common rule of thumb, below what temperature do winter tyres have the advantage?
106371.e: Below around 7 degrees Celsius, winter tyres usually give better grip and shorter braking distances in tests. This is true even on dry roads without snow.
106371.m: Even below about 7 degrees, winter tyres give more safety.

a: The tyre rides up on a film of water
The tyre bursts because of the wet
The car is washed by the rain
106372.e: During aquaplaning a wedge of water forms between the tyre and the road. The tyre loses contact with the road surface and slides on the water.
106372.m: During aquaplaning the tyre loses contact with the road.

a: The tread cannot push the water away fast enough
The tyre has too much tread
106373.e: The tread channels water sideways and backwards. If more water arrives than it can carry away, a wedge of water pushes under the tyre.
106373.m: Aquaplaning happens when the tyre tread can no longer channel the water away.

106374.q: How is the risk of aquaplaning related to speed?
a: It does not depend on speed
It only exists when standing still
106374.e: The faster a car goes, the less time the tread has to push the water away. Driving more slowly is therefore the most important protection.
106374.m: In the wet, driving slowly protects against aquaplaning.

106375.q: Which tyres increase the risk of aquaplaning?
106375.e: The less tread a tyre has, the less water it can channel away. Worn tyres therefore ride up on the water much sooner.

106376.q: What should you do if the car starts aquaplaning?
a: Take your foot off the accelerator and keep the steering wheel straight
106376.e: As the car slows down, the tyres get contact with the road again. Steering or braking hard can then make the car skid.
106376.m: When aquaplaning, calmly ease off the accelerator and steer straight.

106377.q: Why does the car hardly respond to steering during aquaplaning?
a: There is hardly any friction left between tyre and road
106377.e: Steering only works if the tyres pass forces onto the road through static friction. On the film of water this grip is almost completely missing.
106377.m: Without static friction a car cannot be steered.

106378.q: Where on roads does a lot of water collect that can lead to aquaplaning?
106378.e: Ruts are dips that many heavy vehicles have pressed into the road surface. Rainwater stays in them.
106378.m: A dangerous amount of water can collect in ruts.

106379.q: What is often a sign that aquaplaning is starting?
a: The steering suddenly feels very light
106379.e: When the front wheels ride up on the water, you need almost no force to steer. Often the engine revs briefly rise too because the wheels spin.
106379.m: Suddenly light steering warns of aquaplaning.

106380.q: What does an anti-lock braking system, ABS for short, prevent in an emergency stop?
106380.e: The ABS briefly releases the brake on a wheel as soon as it is about to lock. This keeps the wheels turning while braking.
106380.m: ABS stops the wheels locking when braking.

106381.q: Why is it important that the wheels do not lock when braking?
a: Rolling wheels can still be steered
Locked wheels make the car faster
106381.e: A locked wheel slides and cannot pass on any sideways forces. With ABS you can steer round an obstacle even during an emergency stop.
106381.m: Thanks to ABS a car can still be steered in an emergency stop.

106382.q: Which driver assistance system uses the ABS sensors and stops the car skidding in bends?
106382.e: The electronic stability programme ESP is built on ABS. If the car threatens to break away, it brakes individual wheels in a targeted way.
106382.m: ESP helps against skidding and uses the ABS sensors to do so.

106383.q: How does the ABS detect that a wheel is about to lock?
a: With sensors that measure wheel speed
With a camera in the boot
From the sound of the engine
From the temperature of the seats
106383.e: On each wheel a speed sensor measures how fast it is turning. If one wheel suddenly slows down much more than the others, the ABS steps in.
106383.m: Wheel speed sensors tell the ABS when a wheel is locking.

106384.q: What can you often feel in the brake pedal when the ABS is working?
a: The pedal jumping up and staying there
106384.e: The ABS releases and applies the brake many times a second. You feel this as juddering in the pedal, but you should keep braking hard.
106384.m: If the brake pedal judders, the ABS is working and you keep braking.

106385.q: How common is ABS in new cars today?
a: It is only found in racing cars
It is only found in lorries
106385.e: ABS came onto the market at the end of the 1970s. Today practically all new cars have ABS fitted.
106385.m: ABS is standard in new cars today.

106386.q: Why is ABS especially helpful on a motorbike?
a: A locked front wheel easily leads to a fall
106386.e: If a motorbike's front wheel locks, the bike loses its stability and falls over. ABS prevents this and often shortens the braking distance.
106386.m: ABS protects motorcyclists from falling when braking.

106387.q: On which surface can the braking distance with ABS be longer than without?
a: On loose gravel or fresh snow
106387.e: On a loose surface a locked wheel pushes a braking wedge of material ahead of it. ABS prevents this wedge, but in return the car stays steerable.
106387.m: On loose surfaces ABS does not always brake shorter, but it keeps you steerable.

106388.q: Why do curlers sweep the ice in front of the stone?
a: The ice is warmed slightly and the stone slides further
They remove snow falling from the sky
106388.e: Sweeping warms the ice surface slightly, and a thin film of water reduces the friction. The stone then slides further and runs straighter.
106388.m: Sweeping reduces friction and lets the curling stone slide further.

106389.q: Why are fine drops of water sprayed onto the ice before curling and left to freeze?
a: The stone rests on only a few points and slides better
106389.e: The frozen droplets are called pebbles. The stone only touches their tips, so the friction is small.
106389.m: Frozen droplets help the curling stone slide better.

106390.q: Roughly how heavy is a curling stone?
106390.e: A curling stone may weigh at most just under 20 kg. Despite this weight it slides dozens of metres thanks to low friction.
106390.m: A curling stone weighs about 20 kilograms.

106391.q: What rock are curling stones made from?
106391.e: Curling stones are made of especially dense, hard granite. Many come from the Scottish island of Ailsa Craig.
106391.m: Curling stones are made of hard granite.

106392.q: What happens when a curling stone is released with a slight spin?
106392.e: A spinning stone drifts sideways on its way and follows a curve. The sport takes its name from this movement: to curl means to bend.
106392.m: A spinning curling stone travels in a curve.

106393.q: What part of a curling stone touches the ice?
a: A narrow ring on the underside
106393.e: The underside of the stone is slightly hollowed. It rests only on a narrow running ring, which keeps the friction small.
106393.m: A curling stone touches the ice only with a narrow ring.

106394.q: Which country does the sport of curling come from?
106394.e: Curling was played on frozen lakes in Scotland centuries ago. Later it spread to Canada and the Alpine countries.
106394.m: Curling has its origins in Scotland.

106395.q: How do curlers influence the path of the stone after it has been released?
a: With brooms they use to sweep the ice
With sticks they use to push the stone
106395.e: After release nobody may touch the stone. But sweeping with the broom makes it slide further and straighter.
106395.m: In curling you guide the stone with the broom.

106396.q: Why is glide wax put on the base of skis?
a: So that the skis glide better
So that the skis brake better
So that the skis get heavier
106396.e: Glide wax reduces sliding friction between ski and snow. It also protects the base from drying out.

106397.q: Which wax stops the ski slipping back when you push off in classic cross-country skiing?
106397.e: Grip wax is put on under the binding. When you push off it sticks briefly to the snow, yet when gliding it still lets the ski run forwards.
106397.m: In classic cross-country skiing, grip wax gives you hold when pushing off.

106398.q: Why is ski wax chosen to match the snow temperature?
a: Cold and warm snow rub differently against the base
Otherwise the wax melts away completely at once
The colour of the wax must match the snow
Only then does the ski stay dry
106398.e: Cold snow has sharp, hard crystals, and wet snow forms more water. For cold snow you use harder wax, for warm snow softer wax.
106398.m: Good ski wax matches the temperature of the snow.

106399.q: Which ski waxes have been banned in international ski racing since the 2023/24 season?
106399.e: Fluorine waxes contain fluorine compounds that break down very slowly and harm the environment and health. The International Ski Federation has therefore banned them in racing.
106399.m: Ski waxes containing fluorine are banned in racing.

106400.q: How is glide wax often applied to a ski?
a: Ironed in with a hot waxing iron
Painted on cold with a brush and washed off at once
Diluted with water and poured on
106400.e: The wax is melted with an iron and worked into the base. After it cools, the excess is scraped off and the base is brushed out.
106400.m: Glide wax is ironed hot into the ski base.

106401.q: What is the base on the underside of a ski usually made of?
106401.e: Ski bases are usually made of a special plastic. It glides well on snow and can absorb wax.
106401.m: Ski bases are made of plastic that absorbs wax.

106402.q: Why are fine grooves, a structure, ground into the ski base?
a: So that no suction effect forms in wet snow
So that the ski brakes in the cold
So that the ski is easier to carry
So that the wax does not stick
106402.e: In wet snow a film of water can literally suck the ski down. The grooves channel the water away and reduce this effect.
106402.m: Grooves in the ski base stop suction on wet snow.

106403.q: What do some cross-country skis use instead of grip wax to get a hold when pushing off?
a: Fish scales or skins under the binding
106403.e: Fish scales in the base or fitted skins grip the snow when pushing off. When gliding forwards they lie flat.
106403.m: Fish scales or skins replace grip wax in cross-country skiing.

106404.q: What does a freshly waxed ski do when gliding compared with an unwaxed one?
a: Less sliding friction and higher speed
More sliding friction and more grip
106404.e: The wax fills the fine pores of the base and makes it smoother. This lowers friction, and you glide faster on the same slope.
106404.m: A well-waxed ski glides faster than a dry one.

106405.q: Why do sparks fly when you grind steel on a fast-spinning grinding wheel?
a: Frictional heat makes tiny metal particles glow
The grinding wheel contains firework powder
The spinning sets the air alight
106405.e: The grinding wheel tears off small steel shavings and heats them strongly through friction. The glowing particles fly off as sparks and partly burn in the air.
106405.m: Grinding creates so much frictional heat that metal shavings glow.

106406.q: What makes a match catch fire?
a: Frictional heat on the striking surface
An electric spark from a battery
106406.e: Striking it on the striking surface creates so much heat that the chemicals in the head start to burn. Safety matches only light on the striking surface of the box.
106406.m: Frictional heat lights the head of a match.

106407.q: How could people in the Stone Age make fire using friction?
a: By spinning a wooden stick quickly in a wooden board
By rubbing two pieces of ice together
106407.e: With a fire drill you spin a wooden stick quickly in a hollow. The frictional heat makes fine wood dust glow.
106407.m: Frictional heat can make wood glow.

106408.q: Why do a car's brake discs get very hot after a long descent from a mountain pass?
a: The brakes turn kinetic energy into heat
The air gets warmer going downhill
106408.e: When braking, the brake pads rub against the discs. The car's kinetic energy is turned into heat, and the discs can become glowing hot.
106408.m: Brakes turn the energy of motion into heat.

106409.q: Why should you drive in a low gear on long descents from Swiss mountain passes?
a: So that the brakes do not overheat
So that the tank fills up
So that the tyres get colder
So that the car goes faster
106409.e: In a low gear the engine helps to brake. So the brakes have to absorb less frictional heat and do not lose their effect.
106409.m: Going downhill in a low gear spares the brakes.

106410.q: Why do skis glide so well on snow in the first place?
a: Frictional heat creates a thin film of water
106410.e: Gliding creates a little heat through friction. It melts a wafer-thin layer of snow, and the ski glides more easily on this film of water.
106410.m: A wafer-thin film of water lets skis glide on snow.

106411.q: Why can you get burnt if a rope slides quickly through your hands?
a: The friction creates a lot of heat on the skin
The rope is soaked in acid
The rope is always electrically charged
The skin freezes onto the rope
106411.e: The fast-sliding rope rubs hard against the skin. The frictional heat produced can injure the skin like a burn.
106411.m: A fast-sliding rope can burn the skin through frictional heat.

106412.q: Why does a drill bit get hot when drilling into metal?
a: Because of friction between the bit and the metal
Because of the current in the cable
Because the air in the hole is burning
106412.e: When drilling, the cutting edge rubs hard against the workpiece. The frictional heat can be so great that you have to cool it with cutting oil or coolant.
106412.m: Drilling produces a lot of heat through friction.

106413.q: What happens to the kinetic energy of a sledge that comes to a stop through friction?
a: It is stored in the snow as electricity
106413.e: Energy is never lost, it is only changed. Friction turns the kinetic energy into heat in the runners and the snow.
106413.m: Friction turns kinetic energy into heat; it does not vanish.

106414.q: What are snow chains on a car for?
a: They improve grip on snow and ice
They protect the tyres from stones
106414.e: With chains the wheels can pass much bigger driving and braking forces onto snow and ice. That is why they are often essential on snowy mountain roads.
106414.m: Snow chains give tyres grip on snow and ice.

106415.q: In Switzerland, what does a round blue sign showing a tyre with a chain round it mean?
a: Snow chains are for sale here
106415.e: Round blue signs give an instruction. From this sign onwards you may only continue with snow chains fitted.
106415.m: The blue snow chain sign makes snow chains compulsory.

106416.q: On which wheels do you fit snow chains?
a: Only ever on the spare wheel
Only on the wheels that are not driven
106416.e: The chains are mainly meant to get the driving force onto the road. That is why they belong on the driven wheels.
106416.m: Snow chains belong on the driving wheels.

106417.q: Why should you take snow chains off on a road clear of snow?
a: They damage the road and tyres, and the car slides more easily
They make the car too light
Otherwise they freeze onto the tyre
106417.e: On dry asphalt the chain links do not grip but hammer on the surface. This damages the road, chains and tyres, and braking can get worse.
106417.m: Take snow chains off on a road clear of snow.

106418.q: How do snow chains improve friction on ice?
a: The chain links press into the ice and interlock
They melt the ice with electricity
They scatter salt on the road
They lift the car off the ice
106418.e: The hard chain links press into the surface of the ice and snow. This creates an interlocking grip that passes on much more force than smooth rubber.
106418.m: Snow chains interlock with snow and ice.

106419.q: When is the best time to practise fitting snow chains?
a: At home, before you drive into the mountains
Not until a snowstorm on the pass
Never, you fit them while driving
Only in summer on the motorway
106419.e: In snow and cold, fitting unfamiliar chains is hard work. If you have practised beforehand, you are quicker and safer when it really matters.
106419.m: It is best to try fitting snow chains at home first.

106420.q: What are so-called snow socks for car tyres?
a: Fabric covers that improve grip as a light alternative to chains
106420.e: Snow socks are fabric covers pulled over the tyres. The fabric soaks up moisture and so improves grip on snow.
106420.m: Fabric snow socks are a light alternative to snow chains.

106421.q: Are good winter tyres enough on a road with the sign “snow chains compulsory”?
a: No, you still need snow chains
Yes, if they are less than a year old
Yes, but only during the day
106421.e: The sign applies whatever tyres you have. Even cars with good winter tyres must fit snow chains there.
106421.m: Where snow chains are compulsory, winter tyres alone are not enough.

106422.q: In ecology, what is meant by an altitude zone?
a: A height range with typical plant life
A measuring stick for snow depth
106422.e: As altitude increases, temperature and climate change. That is why in the mountains there are zones one above the other, each with typical plants and forests.
106422.m: Each altitude zone has its own typical plant life.

106423.q: Which order is correct in the Alps from bottom to top?
a: Broadleaved forest, conifer forest, alpine pastures, rock and ice
Conifer forest, broadleaved forest, rock and ice, alpine pastures
Alpine pastures, broadleaved forest, conifer forest, rock and ice
Rock and ice, alpine pastures, conifer forest, broadleaved forest
106423.e: Down in the warm hill country broadleaved forests grow, further up conifer forests. Above the tree line come alpine pastures and right at the top rock, snow and ice.
106423.m: From bottom to top: broadleaved forest, conifer forest, alpine pastures, rock and ice.

106424.q: Why are there altitude zones in the mountains at all?
a: Because it gets cooler with height
Because the air is damper higher up
Because more animals live higher up
Because the sun shines more weakly higher up
106424.e: With every metre of height the average temperature drops, and the growing season gets shorter. That is why only plants that cope well with cold can grow higher up.
106424.m: The drop in temperature with height is the main reason for altitude zones.

106426.q: What is typical of the highest altitude zone in the Alps?
106426.e: Right at the top the snow often stays all year round. Experts call this zone the nival zone, from the Latin word for snow. Only a few plants survive there.
106426.m: Snow and ice rule the highest altitude zone.

106427.q: Why are the altitude zones on south-facing slopes usually higher than on north-facing slopes?
a: South-facing slopes get more sun and warmth
There is no wind on north-facing slopes
106427.e: In Switzerland south-facing slopes face the sun more and are therefore warmer. Plants find good conditions there even at greater heights.
106427.m: On the sunny side the altitude zones reach further up.

106428.q: What happens to the growing season the higher you climb in the mountains?
106428.e: The growing season is the time of year when plants can grow. High up, spring starts later and winter earlier.
106428.m: The higher you go, the shorter the growing season for plants.

106429.q: What is the height line called above which the snow no longer melts away completely, even in summer?
106429.e: Above this line more snow falls in a year than can melt in summer. Firn and glaciers can form there.
106429.m: Above the snow line the snow stays all year round.

106430.q: People talk about the ‘aspect’ of a slope. What does that mean?
a: How many trees grow on it
106430.e: Whether a slope faces south or north decides how much sun it gets. This strongly affects temperature, snow cover and plant life.
106430.m: The aspect of a slope affects its plant life.

106431.e: The word comes from the Latin ‘collis’ for hill. The colline zone is the lowest and warmest altitude zone.
106431.m: The colline zone is the zone of the hill country.

106432.q: Where is the colline zone compared with the other altitude zones?
a: Right at the bottom, in the lowest areas
Right at the top by the glaciers
In the middle of the high mountains
106432.e: The colline zone is the lowest altitude zone. On the northern side of the Alps it reaches up to about 600 metres above sea level.
106432.m: The colline zone is the lowest altitude zone.

106433.q: Which crop is typical of sunny slopes in the colline zone in Switzerland?
106433.e: The vine needs a lot of warmth and a long summer. That is why vineyards such as those in Lavaux or Valais lie mainly in low, sunny places.
106433.m: Vineyards show typical places of the colline zone.

106434.q: Which kind of tree shapes many dry, warm forests of the colline zone?
106434.e: In warm, dry places such as Valais or the southern foot of the Jura, oak forests grow, for example with the downy oak. They cope well with heat and drought.
106434.m: Oaks love the warm places of the colline zone.

106435.q: Which type of tree naturally shapes the forests of the colline zone?
106435.e: At low altitudes the summers are long and warm, which suits broadleaved trees such as oak, lime and maple. Conifers are naturally rare there.
106435.m: Broadleaved forests naturally dominate the colline zone.

106436.q: Why is only a little natural forest left in the colline zone today?
a: People use it heavily for towns and farming
The ground there is too rocky
106436.e: The warm, flat areas are good for living in and for fields, fruit growing and vineyards. That is why a lot of forest was cleared there early on.
106436.m: The colline zone is strongly shaped by people.

106437.q: Where is the lowest point in Switzerland, a place in the colline zone?
106437.e: Lake Maggiore lies at about 193 metres above sea level, which makes it the lowest point in Switzerland. Even palms and camellias grow there.
106437.m: The lowest point in Switzerland is at Lake Maggiore.

106438.q: Which altitude zone comes directly above the colline zone in the mountains?
106438.e: Above the warm hill country comes the montane zone with mountain forests. After that come the subalpine, the alpine and, at the very top, the nival zone.
106438.m: The montane zone lies above the colline zone.

106439.q: What is the climate like in the colline zone compared with higher places?
a: Warmer, with a longer growing season
Exactly the same as in the high mountains
106439.e: At low altitudes the summers are long and warm and the winters mild. That is why broadleaved forests, fruit trees and vines grow well here.
106439.m: The colline zone is the warmest altitude zone.

106440.q: Where does the term ‘montane’ come from?
a: From the Latin word for mountain
From the Latin word for water
From the Greek word for forest
From the French word for meadow
106440.e: The Latin ‘mons, montis’ means mountain. The montane zone is the mountain forest zone above the hill country.
106440.m: The montane zone is the zone of mountain forests.

106441.q: Roughly what height range does the montane zone cover on the northern side of the Alps?
106441.e: The montane zone follows on from the colline zone. Depending on the region it reaches up to about 1400 metres, and a bit higher in the Central Alps because of the warmer climate.
106441.m: On the northern side of the Alps the montane zone starts at about 600 metres.

106442.q: Which two tree species shape many natural forests of the montane zone in the Alpine foothills?
106442.e: In the damp, fairly cool montane zone, beech and silver fir grow especially well together. Higher up, the spruce joins them.
106442.m: Beech and fir are the typical trees of the montane zone.

106443.q: What kind of farming is typical in the montane zone?
a: Meadows and pastures with dairy farming
106443.e: At this height it is too cool and wet for many field crops. But grass grows well, so mainly cows are kept there.
106443.m: Meadows, pastures and dairy farming dominate the montane zone.

106444.q: What are the typical pastures in the Jura called, where trees stand loosely scattered?
106444.e: Wooded pastures, in French ‘pâturages boisés’, combine forest and pasture on the same land. They shape the landscape of the Jura in the montane zone.
106444.m: Wooded pastures in the Jura are pastures with scattered trees.

106445.q: Which altitude zone covers most of the slopes in the Swiss Alpine foothills and the Jura?
106445.e: Many foothills, such as in the Emmental or Toggenburg, and the Jura heights lie between about 600 and 1400 metres. That matches the mountain forest zone.
106445.m: The Alpine foothills and the Jura lie mostly in the montane zone.

106446.q: Which tree species often joins beech and fir in the upper montane zone?
106446.e: The higher and cooler it gets, the better the spruce can compete. In the upper montane zone it often forms mixed forests with fir and beech.
106446.m: Further up in the montane zone the spruce joins in.

106447.q: Which statement about the climate of the montane zone is true?
a: It is cooler and wetter than on the Swiss Plateau
It is warmer and drier than on the Swiss Plateau
There is snow there all year round
106447.e: As altitude increases, temperatures drop, and clouds drop more rain on the mountains. That is why the montane zone is cooler and wetter.
106447.m: The montane zone is cooler and damper than the lowlands.

106448.q: Which altitude zone lies just below the tree line?
106448.e: The subalpine zone is the highest zone in which forest still grows. Above it comes the treeless alpine zone.
106448.m: The subalpine zone is the highest forest zone.

106449.q: What does the prefix ‘sub’ in ‘subalpine’ mean?
106449.e: ‘Sub’ is Latin and means ‘below’. So the subalpine zone lies below the alpine zone.
106449.m: Subalpine means below the alpine zone.

106450.q: Which conifer species forms most of the forests in the subalpine zone of the northern Alps?
106450.e: The spruce copes well with long, cold winters and grows even when the summer is short. That is why it shapes the subalpine forests in the northern Alps.
106450.m: Spruce dominates the subalpine zone of the northern Alps.

106451.q: Roughly how long is the growing season in the subalpine zone compared with the Swiss Plateau?
106451.e: High up, snow stays on the ground until spring, and it gets cold again in autumn. That is why trees grow only slowly there.
106451.m: In the subalpine zone trees grow slowly because of the short summers.

106452.q: Why do spruces in the subalpine zone often have narrow, pointed crowns?
a: So that snow slides off more easily
So that they produce more fruit
So that birds do not nest there
So that they lose their leaves in winter
106452.e: Heavy snow can break branches and trunks. A slim crown holds less snow and can bear the weight better.
106452.m: Slim crowns protect mountain spruces from snow damage.

106453.q: What is a grazing level between the valley and the alpine pasture called, which is used in spring and autumn?
106453.e: A Maiensäss lies between the farm in the valley and the actual alpine pasture. The cattle graze there in spring before moving further up in summer.
106453.m: On the Maiensäss the cattle graze before and after the alpine summer.

106454.q: Why do trees at the tree line often grow in small, dense groups?
a: They protect each other from snow, wind and cold
Because only then can they produce fruit
Because foresters have to plant them like that
So that cows cannot get through
106454.e: The climate in the subalpine zone is harsh. Trees in groups protect each other from snow, wind and cold.
106454.m: In the subalpine zone trees often grow in protective groups.

106455.q: Which large, rare bird of the grouse family lives in open conifer forests of the montane and subalpine zones?
106455.e: The capercaillie needs open, quiet mountain forests with lots of berry bushes on the ground. In Switzerland it has become rare and is strictly protected.
106455.m: The capercaillie is a rare inhabitant of open mountain forests.

106456.q: What is meant by the forest line?
a: The upper limit of closed forest
The edge of a forest by a lake
The boundary of a nature park
106456.e: Above the forest line the trees no longer stand close enough together to form a forest. Higher up there are only single trees.
106456.m: The forest line is the height above which no closed forest grows.

106457.q: What is the line called up to which single upright trees still grow?
106457.e: The tree line lies a little above the forest line. Between the two lines is a transition zone with scattered trees.
106457.m: The tree line lies above the forest line.

106458.q: At roughly what height is the forest line in the northern Swiss Alps?
106458.e: In the damper, cooler northern Alps the forest ends at about 1800 metres. In the Central Alps the limit is much higher.
106458.m: In the northern Alps the forest line is at about 1800 metres.

106459.q: Where in Switzerland is the forest line highest, at about 2300 m?
a: In the Central Alps such as Valais and the Engadine
106459.e: In the large, high mountain ranges of the Central Alps it is warmer and sunnier in summer. That is why the forest can climb higher there.
106459.m: In Valais and the Engadine the forest climbs especially high.

106460.q: What mainly limits tree growth at the forest line?
a: Temperatures that are too low in summer
106460.e: Trees need a minimum amount of warmth during the growing season to form new wood. As a rule of thumb, the forest line is where the warmest month reaches about 10 °C on average.
106460.m: The forest line is mainly set by a lack of summer warmth.

106461.q: What do you call the transition area at the forest line with stunted trees standing on their own?
106461.e: Here the trees struggle against cold, wind, snow and frost drought. Many grow low, crooked or only on one side.
106461.m: In the struggle zone trees only survive in harsh conditions.

106462.q: What can be seen at the forest line in many places in the Alps today?
a: The forest is slowly growing higher up
The forest is dying off completely
The forest line drops by 100 m every year
The trees are losing their needles for ever
106462.e: Warmer summers and fewer alpine pastures being farmed let young trees grow further up. This process is slow but measurable.
106462.m: With warming and less grazing, the forest is moving upwards.

106463.q: Which low conifer often forms dense, creeping thickets at the forest line?
106463.e: The dwarf mountain pine is a low-lying form of the mountain pine. Its flexible branches are pressed down by the snow but do not break.
106463.m: The dwarf mountain pine grows as crooked scrub at the forest line.

106464.q: Which type of forest would mostly grow on the Swiss Plateau without people?
106464.e: The climate and soils of the Swiss Plateau suit the beech very well. It competes so strongly there that it would push out most other tree species.
106464.m: Naturally, the Swiss Plateau would be beech forest country.

106465.q: What does the beech cope with badly?
106465.e: The beech needs well-aired soils. That is why other trees, such as alders or willows, grow in wet hollows and river floodplains.
106465.m: Beeches avoid wet soils and flood areas.

106466.q: Which Swiss forests have been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2021?
a: Stone pine forests in the Engadine
106466.e: In 2021 UNESCO added beech forests on the Bettlachstock in the canton of Solothurn and in Ticino to the World Heritage Site ‘Ancient Beech Forests of Europe’. They are regarded as especially close to nature.
106466.m: Ancient Swiss beech forests are a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

106467.q: What do you call a beech forest with tall, smooth trunks and hardly any undergrowth?
106467.e: The trunks stand like pillars in a great hall, and the canopy forms the ceiling. Little grows on the ground because of the shade.
106467.m: A dense beech forest looks like a hall of pillars.
