107922.e: Kinetic energy depends on the mass and on the square of the speed. That is why v is squared.
107922.m: Kinetic energy is calculated from the mass and the speed squared.

107923.q: How does the kinetic energy change if the speed doubles?
a: It becomes eight times as great
107923.e: The speed is squared in the formula. 2 times 2 gives 4, so the energy becomes four times as great.
107923.m: Twice the speed means four times the kinetic energy.

107924.q: A 2 kg ball rolls at 3 m/s. How great is its kinetic energy?
107924.e: You calculate ½ times 2 kg times 3 m/s squared: 0.5 times 2 times 9 gives 9 joules.
107924.m: For kinetic energy, the speed is squared first.

107925.q: A cyclist and her bike together weigh 80 kg and travel at 5 m/s. How great is her kinetic energy?
107925.e: ½ times 80 kg times 25 m²/s² gives 40 times 25, which is 1000 joules.
107925.m: Even slow bike rides already have a lot of kinetic energy.

107926.q: A bike with its rider weighs 100 kg and accelerates from standing to 4 m/s. How much kinetic energy does it gain?
107926.e: You calculate ½ times 100 kg times 16 m²/s². That gives 50 times 16, which is 800 joules.
107926.m: Anything that speeds up gains kinetic energy.

107927.q: How does the kinetic energy change if the mass is twice as great but the speed stays the same?
107927.e: The mass is not squared in the formula. Twice the mass therefore gives twice the kinetic energy.
107927.m: Kinetic energy grows in the same proportion as mass.

107928.q: Which has more kinetic energy: a 10 t lorry at 10 m/s or a 1 t car at 20 m/s?
107928.e: Lorry: ½ times 10,000 kg times 100 gives 500,000 J. Car: ½ times 1000 kg times 400 gives 200,000 J.
107928.m: Mass and speed together determine kinetic energy.

107929.q: How much kinetic energy does a football lying still on the grass have?
107929.e: Only an object that is moving has kinetic energy. At a speed of zero, it is zero too.
107929.m: An object at rest has no kinetic energy.

107930.q: How fast must a 1 kg ball fly to have 50 joules of kinetic energy?
107930.e: From ½ times 1 kg times v² equals 50 J, it follows that v² equals 100. The square root of 100 is 10, so 10 m/s.
107930.m: You can work back from kinetic energy to speed.

107931.q: What is meant by elastic energy?
107931.e: When an elastic object is stretched, squeezed or bent, it stores energy. When you let go, it releases it again.
107931.m: Deformed elastic objects store elastic energy.

107932.q: In which of these objects is elastic energy stored?
107932.e: When it is drawn, the bow is bent elastically. When it is released, the elastic energy turns into the kinetic energy of the arrow.
107932.m: A drawn bow stores elastic energy.

107933.q: Which energy conversion happens when a trampoline throws you upwards?
107933.e: When you land, the mat stretches and stores energy. As it springs back, this becomes kinetic energy that carries you upwards.
107933.m: A trampoline gives back stored elastic energy as movement.

107935.q: Which form of energy does the suspension fork of a mountain bike briefly store when the wheel rides over a root?
107935.e: With the jolt, the spring in the fork is compressed and stores energy. Afterwards, it springs back out.
107935.m: A compressed spring stores elastic energy.

107936.q: A stretched rubber band stores 2 joules and fires a paper pellet. What is the most kinetic energy the pellet can get?
107936.e: Energy cannot come from nothing. The pellet can get at most the 2 joules, and some usually turns into heat.
107936.m: Stored elastic energy limits the possible kinetic energy.

107938.q: In pole vaulting, which energy does the strongly bent pole store?
107938.e: The run-up bends the pole strongly, and it stores energy. As it straightens, it releases this energy and lifts the vaulter over the bar.
107938.m: A bent pole stores elastic energy.

a: In the movement of whole objects
In the height of an object
107939.e: In chemical reactions, bonds between atoms are broken and new ones are formed. In the process, energy is released or used.
107939.m: Chemical energy is stored in the bonds of substances.

107940.q: Which energy conversion takes place in a burning candle?
a: Chemical energy into heat and light
107940.e: The wax burns with the oxygen in the air. The chemical energy is released as heat and light.
107940.m: A candle turns chemical energy into heat and light.

107941.q: Which energy conversion takes place when a mobile phone battery is charged?
107941.e: During charging, chemical reactions take place in the battery that store energy. When it is used, they run backwards and supply electricity.
107941.m: A rechargeable battery stores electrical energy in chemical form.

107942.q: Into which forms of energy do muscles turn the chemical energy from food?
107942.e: Muscles use the energy from nutrients to move. A large part of it turns into heat, which is why we get warm when we do sport.
107942.m: Muscles turn food energy into movement and heat.

107943.q: Which energy conversion happens in photosynthesis?
107943.e: Plants use sunlight to make sugar from water and carbon dioxide. The energy is stored chemically in the sugar.
107943.m: Plants store solar energy as chemical energy.

107944.q: Which energy does a petrol engine originally use?
a: The chemical energy of the fuel
The potential energy of the road
The radiant energy of the headlights
The elastic energy of the tyres
107944.e: In the engine, petrol burns with air. The chemical energy released is turned into movement by way of heat.
107944.m: A petrol engine uses the chemical energy of the fuel.

107945.q: What is a chemical reaction called in which energy is released as heat?
107945.e: Exo means out. In an exothermic reaction, heat is given off to the surroundings, for example in burning.

107946.q: Which energy conversion takes place in a torch battery while the torch is shining?
107946.e: Chemical reactions take place in the battery that drive electrons through the circuit. This produces electrical energy.
107946.m: A battery supplies electrical energy from chemical reactions.

107947.q: A 2000-watt hair dryer runs for half an hour. How much electrical energy does it use?
107947.e: Energy is power times time: 2 kW times 0.5 h gives 1 kWh.
107947.m: Electrical energy is power times time.

107948.q: A 2 kW kettle runs for 6 minutes. How much does this cost at 30 centimes per kWh?
107948.e: 6 minutes is 0.1 hours, so it uses 2 kW times 0.1 h, which gives 0.2 kWh. 0.2 times 30 centimes gives 6 centimes.
107948.m: The cost of electricity is calculated as kWh times the price per kWh.

107949.q: How many joules are equal to one kilowatt-hour?
107949.e: 1 kWh is 1000 watts for 3600 seconds. 1000 times 3600 gives 3,600,000 joules.

107950.q: A device on 230 volts draws a current of 2 amperes. What is its power?
107950.e: Electrical power is voltage times current. 230 V times 2 A gives 460 W.
107950.m: Electrical power is voltage times current.

107951.q: A fridge has an average power of 100 watts. How much electrical energy does it use in a day?
107951.e: A day has 24 hours. 0.1 kW times 24 h gives 2.4 kWh.
107951.m: Devices that are always on use a lot of energy over a day.

107952.q: Which of these devices mainly turns electrical energy into heat?
107952.e: In a kettle, current flows through a heating coil, which gets hot. A dynamo, a solar cell and a wind turbine, on the other hand, produce electrical energy.
107952.m: A kettle turns electricity into heat.

107953.q: Which component stores electrical energy directly in an electric field?
107953.e: A capacitor consists of two conducting plates with an insulating layer between them. Energy is stored in the electric field between the charged plates.
107953.m: A capacitor stores energy in an electric field.

107954.q: Why should you switch devices off completely rather than leaving them on standby?
a: On standby they use electricity all the time
On standby they get cold faster
107954.e: Even in standby mode, a small current flows, day and night. Over a year, this adds up to quite a lot of electrical energy.
107954.m: Standby costs electrical energy all the time.

107955.q: What is thermal energy at the level of particles?
a: The kinetic energy of the particles
107955.e: The particles of a substance are always moving. The warmer a substance is, the more vigorously they move.
107955.m: Heat is the movement of the tiniest particles.

107956.q: Which device takes heat from the outside air or the ground and brings it into the house for heating?
107956.e: A heat pump uses electrical energy to bring heat from the cooler surroundings up to a higher temperature. It is very common in new Swiss houses.
107956.m: A heat pump heats with warmth from the surroundings.

107957.q: How does the heat of a campfire reach you when you sit to one side of it?
107957.e: Warm air rises upwards, not sideways. To the side, you mainly feel the fire’s heat radiation.
107957.m: A campfire warms us mainly by radiation.

107958.q: What is it called when a metal spoon in hot tea also gets warm at the handle?
107958.e: The particles in the metal pass their movement on to the neighbouring particles. In this way, the heat travels through the spoon to the handle.

107959.q: How does a radiator spread heat around the whole room?
a: Only by conduction through the floor
107959.e: The air by the radiator gets warm and rises, and cooler air flows in. This creates an air current that warms the room.
107959.m: Warm air rises and spreads the heat around the room.

107960.q: How much energy is needed to heat 2 kg of water by 10 °C (4.2 kJ per kg and °C)?
107960.e: You calculate mass times temperature change times specific heat capacity: 2 times 10 times 4.2 gives 84 kJ.
107960.m: Water needs a lot of energy to get warm.

107961.q: Which substance is pumped through the radiators in many heating systems to carry heat?
107961.e: Water can take up a great deal of heat and is cheap. It carries the heat from the boiler to the radiators.
107961.m: In heating systems, it is usually water that carries the heat.

107962.q: Why do double or triple-glazed windows keep the heat in the house better?
a: The layer between the panes conducts heat poorly
The panes let no light through
107962.e: Between the panes there is air or a noble gas. Gases conduct heat poorly and so slow down heat loss.

107963.q: Why does less solar radiation reach the ground than outside the Earth’s atmosphere?
a: The atmosphere absorbs and scatters some of it
The Sun is further away there
The ground pushes the radiation away
107963.e: Air, clouds and dust absorb some of the solar radiation or deflect it. That is why it is weaker on the ground than in space.
107963.m: The atmosphere holds back some of the solar radiation.

107964.q: What is it called when an object takes in radiation and turns it into heat, for example?
107964.e: To absorb means to take in. The radiant energy passes into the object, which usually warms up.
107964.m: In absorption, an object takes in radiation.

107965.q: Which of the Sun’s rays cause sunburn?
107965.e: UV radiation is high in energy and can damage skin cells. Sun cream and clothing protect against it.

107966.q: Why are emergency blankets shiny and silvery on one side?
a: They reflect the body’s heat radiation back
107966.e: The shiny metal layer reflects a large part of the heat radiation. This means an injured person loses less body heat.

107967.q: What does a solar thermal collector on the roof of a house do?
a: It heats water with solar radiation
107967.e: A liquid flows through the collector and is warmed by the Sun. This heat is used to make hot water or for heating.
107967.m: Solar collectors turn solar radiation into heat.

107968.q: What is the effect called in which gases in the atmosphere hold back some of the Earth’s heat radiation?
107968.e: The Earth radiates heat into space. Gases such as water vapour and methane hold back some of it and so warm the Earth.
107968.m: The greenhouse effect keeps heat in the atmosphere.

107970.q: Which of these surfaces reflects sunlight most strongly?
107970.e: Fresh snow reflects most of the sunlight. That is why you need sunglasses in the mountains in winter.
107970.m: Bright snow reflects a lot of sunlight.

107971.q: In which form is energy mainly released first during nuclear fission in a reactor?
107971.e: The fragments fly apart at high speed and give off their energy as heat to the surrounding water. Only later is this turned into electricity by steam and a turbine.
107971.m: In a reactor, heat is produced first.

107972.q: Which process gives the Sun its energy?
107972.e: In the hot interior of the Sun, light atomic nuclei fuse into heavier ones. This releases enormous amounts of energy.
107972.m: The Sun gets its energy from nuclear fusion.

107973.q: What does the formula E = mc² tell us about nuclear energy?
a: Even a little mass equals a great deal of energy
107973.e: In nuclear reactions, the resulting nuclei together are slightly lighter than the original nuclei. This tiny difference in mass becomes a lot of energy through the huge factor of the speed of light squared.
107973.m: A small mass equals a huge amount of energy.

107974.q: What is the process called in which each nuclear reaction in a reactor itself triggers further reactions of the same kind?
107974.e: Each reaction releases particles that can in turn trigger new reactions. In a reactor, this reaction is controlled so that it runs steadily.
107974.m: A controlled chain reaction takes place in a reactor.

107975.q: What are the control rods in a nuclear reactor for?
107975.e: Control rods contain substances such as boron or cadmium. The deeper they are lowered in, the fewer nuclear reactions take place.
107975.m: A reactor is regulated with the control rods.

107976.q: Which particle splits a uranium nucleus in a reactor?
107976.e: A neutron enters the uranium nucleus and makes it unstable, so that it breaks apart. This releases new neutrons, which can split further nuclei.

107977.q: Where is Switzerland’s highly radioactive waste one day to be stored for ever?
a: In a hall by the railway station
107977.e: Switzerland is planning a repository deep in the rock. There, the waste is to remain safely sealed in for many thousands of years.
107977.m: Radioactive waste is to be stored deep in the rock.

107978.q: Why must radioactive waste be safely sealed in for so long?
a: It keeps giving off radiation for very many years
It can easily explode like petrol
107978.e: Radioactive substances give off dangerous radiation for thousands of years. That is why they must be kept away from people and the environment.
107978.m: Radioactive waste gives off radiation for a very long time.

107979.q: Which unit appears next to kilocalories on food packaging in Switzerland?
107979.e: On packaging, the energy content is given in kilojoules and in kilocalories. The joule is the official unit of energy, named after James Prescott Joule.
107979.m: The energy content of food is given in kilojoules.

107980.q: How much work do you do if you push a box 4 m with a force of 50 N?
107980.e: Work is force times distance: 50 N times 4 m gives 200 newton-metres. One newton-metre is exactly one joule.
107980.m: One joule equals one newton times one metre.

107981.q: Roughly how much energy do you need to lift a 100 g bar of chocolate one metre?
107981.e: A mass of 100 g has a weight of about 1 newton. 1 newton times 1 metre gives about 1 joule.
107981.m: A joule is quite a small amount of energy.

107982.q: How many joules are equal to one watt-second?
107982.e: One watt means one joule per second. A power of 1 watt for 1 second therefore gives exactly 1 joule.
107982.m: One watt-second is exactly one joule.

107983.q: A 10-watt LED lamp shines for one minute. How much energy does it use?
107983.e: Energy is power times time: 10 W times 60 s gives 600 joules.
107983.m: You get joules from watts times seconds.

107984.q: Which physical quantity is not measured in joules?
107984.e: Energy, work and heat all have the unit joule. Power gives energy per unit of time and is measured in watts.
107984.m: Power is measured in watts, energy in joules.

107985.q: What did James Prescott Joule show with his experiments?
a: Mechanical work can be turned into heat
107985.e: Joule used a falling weight to turn a paddle wheel in water. The water warmed up measurably, so work had turned into heat.
107985.m: Work and heat are two forms of the same energy.

107986.e: One megajoule is 1000 kilojoules. 3.6 times 1000 gives 3600 kJ.
107986.m: One megajoule is a thousand kilojoules.

107987.e: One kilojoule is 1000 joules. 2.5 times 1000 gives 2500 joules.
107987.m: To convert kilojoules into joules, you multiply by a thousand.

107988.q: How was a calorie originally defined?
a: Energy to heat 1 g of water by 1 °C
Energy to melt 1 kg of iron
Energy to boil away 1 litre of water
107988.e: The calorie was defined by heating water. One calorie is the heat that warms 1 g of water by 1 °C.
107988.m: One calorie warms one gram of water by one degree.

107989.q: A yoghurt provides 100 kcal. Roughly how many kilojoules is that?
107989.e: You multiply by about 4.2: 100 times 4.2 gives about 420 kJ. Exactly, it is 418.4 kJ.
107989.m: Kilocalories are converted into kilojoules with a factor of 4.2.

107990.q: A glass of milk contains 7 g of protein. How many kilocalories does this protein provide if 1 g of protein provides about 4 kcal?
107990.e: You calculate 7 times 4 kcal. That gives 28 kcal.
107990.m: Energy content is calculated as the amount times the value per gram.

107991.q: What is usually meant when “calories” are mentioned on a packet or in conversation?
107991.e: In everyday life, people often say “calories” but mean kilocalories. One kilocalorie is 1000 calories.
107991.m: In everyday life, calories usually means kilocalories.

107992.q: A snack contains 20 g of fat. Roughly how many kilocalories does this fat provide if 1 g of fat provides 9 kcal?
107992.e: You calculate 20 times 9 kcal. That gives 180 kcal.
107992.m: For energy content, you multiply the amount by the value per gram.

107993.q: Is the calorie a unit of the International System of Units, SI?
a: No, the SI unit is the joule
No, the SI unit is the watt
107993.e: The calorie is an older unit that is not part of the SI. The official unit of energy is the joule.
107993.m: The official unit of energy is the joule, not the calorie.

a: A substance or means that stores energy
107994.e: Energy carriers contain energy that can be used, for example wood, crude oil or electricity. They can be stored or transported.

107995.q: Which of these energy carriers is a fossil fuel?
107995.e: Fossil fuels formed over millions of years from dead living things. They include coal, crude oil and natural gas.
107995.m: Natural gas is a fossil fuel.

107996.q: Which of these energy carriers is a secondary energy carrier?
107996.e: Secondary energy carriers are made from primary energy carriers. Electricity, for example, is produced in power stations from hydropower or nuclear energy.
107996.m: Electricity is a secondary energy carrier.

107997.q: What did crude oil and natural gas mainly form from?
107997.e: Tiny sea creatures sank to the seabed and were covered by mud. Over millions of years, pressure and heat turned them into crude oil and natural gas.
107997.m: Crude oil formed from ancient marine plankton.

107998.q: Which energy carrier is burned in a pellet heating system?
107998.e: Pellets are small sticks made of pressed sawdust and wood shavings. They are fed into the heating system automatically and burned.
107998.m: Wood pellets are made of pressed wood shavings.

107999.q: Which energy source provides most of the electricity produced in Switzerland?
107999.e: More than half of Swiss electricity comes from hydroelectric power stations in the mountains and on rivers. There are no coal-fired power stations in Switzerland.
107999.m: Switzerland gets most of its electricity from hydropower.

108000.q: Which gas does biogas mainly consist of?
108000.e: Biogas forms when bacteria break down slurry, garden waste or food scraps without oxygen. The main flammable component is methane.

108001.q: Which substance forms when hydrogen is burned as an energy carrier?
108001.e: When it burns, hydrogen combines with oxygen. Only water is produced.

108002.q: Where in Switzerland are dry meadows found particularly often?
108002.e: Dry meadows grow where the soil dries out quickly, for example on steep, sunny south-facing slopes in the Valais or the Jura.
108002.m: Dry meadows are often on sunny south-facing slopes.

108003.q: What is the soil of a dry meadow typically like?
a: Poor in nutrients and well drained
108003.e: On dry meadows, the soil is often shallow and poor in nutrients, and rainwater drains away quickly. That is exactly why many rare plants grow there.
108003.m: Dry meadows have poor, well-drained soils.

108004.q: About how much of Switzerland's dry meadows and pastures has disappeared since 1900?
108004.e: According to the Federal Office for the Environment, more than 95 per cent of dry meadows and pastures have been destroyed since 1900, mainly by fertilising, building and scrub growing over them.
108004.m: Almost all of Switzerland's dry meadows have been lost since 1900.

108005.q: Which habitats does Switzerland's federal inventory “TWW” protect?
108005.e: TWW stands for Trockenwiesen und -weiden, dry meadows and pastures. The inventory of sites of national importance has applied since 2010.
108005.m: The TWW inventory protects Switzerland's most valuable dry meadows.

108006.q: How do many dry meadow plants protect themselves from losing too much water?
a: With aerial roots above the ground
108006.e: Small, hairy or leathery leaves lose less water. That way the plants survive hot, dry summer days.
108006.m: Small, hairy leaves help plants save water.

108007.q: Which low plant with fragrant, small leaves often grows on dry meadows?
108007.e: Wild thyme is a small subshrub that loves warm, dry and poor sites. Its leaves smell strongly of spice.
108007.m: Wild thyme loves dry, warm meadows.

108008.q: Why does a dry meadow become overgrown over time if it is not mown or grazed?
a: The soil becomes saltier and saltier
The rain washes all the plants away
108008.e: Without use, shrubs grow in first and later trees; this is called scrub encroachment. The light-loving meadow plants disappear.
108008.m: Dry meadows need care, or bushes grow over them.

108009.q: Which group of animals is particularly rich in species on dry meadows and easy to hear in summer?
108009.e: Many grasshopper species love warmth and patchy vegetation. Their chirping can be heard everywhere on dry meadows in summer.
108009.m: Many grasshopper species chirp on dry meadows.

108010.q: Which bright green lizard lives on warm, dry slopes in Switzerland, for example in the Valais and Ticino?
108010.e: The western green lizard is the largest lizard in Switzerland and needs very warm, sunny habitats such as dry meadows and rocky steppes.
108010.m: The green lizard loves warm, dry slopes.

108011.q: Which yellow-flowering plant with shiny, roundish leaves flowers in spring on wet meadows?
108011.e: The marsh marigold grows in wet places, in ditches and on wet meadows. It flowers bright yellow as early as March to May.
108011.m: The marsh marigold shows wet ground.

108012.q: How were many wet meadows turned into farmland in the past?
a: By draining them with drainage pipes
108012.e: The water was led away with drainage pipes and ditches. That is how large parts of Switzerland's wetlands disappeared.
108012.m: Drainage has dried out many wet meadows.

108013.q: Which pink-flowering plant with deeply slit petals is typical of wet meadows?
108013.e: Ragged robin has pink petals cut into fringes. It grows on damp meadows that are not too heavily fertilised.
108013.m: Ragged robin flowers on damp meadows.

108014.q: Which bird with a long crest of feathers nests on the ground of wet meadows and has become rare in Switzerland?
108014.e: The lapwing nests on the ground in open, damp areas. Because of drainage and early mowing, it has declined sharply in Switzerland.
108014.m: The lapwing needs damp, open meadows to nest.

108015.q: What does a wet meadow need so that it does not become overgrown with bushes and trees?
108015.e: Without mowing, shrubs and trees grow on a wet meadow over time. Mowing keeps it open, and the typical meadow plants get enough light.
108015.m: Wet meadows stay open because they are mown.

108016.q: Which grass-like plants, often with a three-sided stem, grow frequently in wet meadows?
108016.e: Sedges look like grasses, but usually have a three-sided stem that is not hollow. Many species love wet soils.
108016.m: Sedges can often be recognised by their three-sided stem.

108017.q: Which plant with creamy white, sweet-smelling flower heads grows by ditches and in wet meadows?
108017.e: Meadowsweet grows over a metre tall and is found in wet places. Its many small flowers have a strong scent.
108017.m: Meadowsweet likes to grow by wet ditches.

108018.q: Which grasshopper depends on wet meadows and has its habitat in its name?
108018.e: The large marsh grasshopper needs damp to wet meadows, because its eggs can only develop in damp soil. It is seen as an indicator species for healthy wet meadows.
108018.m: The large marsh grasshopper lives on wet meadows.

108019.q: What did farmers traditionally use the cuttings from litter meadows for?
a: As the main feed for dairy cows
108019.e: The tough, nutrient-poor grass was not good as feed. It was used as litter, that is, as bedding for the animals in the cowshed.
108019.m: Litter meadows provided bedding for the cowshed.

108020.q: In which season are litter meadows usually mown?
108020.e: Litter meadows are only mown late in the year, when the plants have finished flowering and moved their nutrients into their roots.
108020.m: Litter meadows are only mown in autumn.

108021.q: Why may litter meadows only be mown late in the year?
a: So that plants and animals can complete their life cycle
Because the grass is poisonous in summer
Because mowing machines are banned in summer
So that the ground dries out
108021.e: In Switzerland, litter meadows have a late mowing date, usually from 1 September. By then, plants have formed seeds and insects have completed their development.
108021.m: Litter meadows are mown late so that plants and animals can reproduce.

108022.q: What kind of soil are litter meadows usually on?
108022.e: Litter meadows are often on lake shores and in bogs. The soil is wet and poor. Purple moor grass, which turns yellowish brown in autumn, is typical.
108022.m: Litter meadows grow on damp, poor soils.

108023.q: Why are litter meadows not fertilised?
a: So that rare plants of poor soils are not crowded out
Because fertiliser evaporates in wet soil
Because fertiliser freezes there at once
Because the plants there have no roots
108023.e: Fertiliser helps fast-growing grasses. They would overgrow the rare plants adapted to nutrient-poor soils.
108023.m: Without fertiliser, litter meadows stay rich in species.

108024.q: Why are many plants of litter meadows rare today?
a: Many litter meadows were drained or fertilised
108024.e: There used to be many litter meadows. Many were drained or fertilised. Rare species such as the blue marsh gentian lost their habitat as a result.
108024.m: As litter meadows disappear, rare plants disappear too.

108025.q: Why is late mowing in autumn good for the plants of a litter meadow?
a: They have already formed their seeds
They grow twice as fast afterwards
The ground is already frozen then
The grass is most nutritious then
108025.e: By autumn, most plants have flowered and formed seeds. That way they can reproduce again every year.
108025.m: Late mowing gives plants time to form seeds.

108026.q: Which rare plant with blue-violet flowers grows in litter meadows and belongs to the irises?
108026.e: The Siberian iris grows on unfertilised meadows that are sometimes wet and sometimes dry. It has become rare in Switzerland and is protected in many places.
108026.m: The Siberian iris is a treasure of litter meadows.

108027.q: How does a semi-dry grassland differ from a true dry grassland?
a: It has a slightly better water supply
It is under water every winter
It grows only on sandy soils
108027.e: Semi-dry grasslands do not dry out as extremely as dry grasslands. That is why the plant cover grows denser and more closed.
108027.m: Semi-dry grasslands are less dry than dry grasslands.

108028.q: On which type of ground are many semi-dry grasslands found in Switzerland, for example in the Jura?
108028.e: Limestone stores little water and often forms shallow soils. Species-rich semi-dry grasslands develop on them.
108028.m: Many semi-dry grasslands grow on limestone soil.

108029.q: How did most semi-dry grasslands in Central Europe come about?
a: Through centuries of mowing or grazing
108029.e: Semi-dry grasslands are cultural landscapes. They came about because people cleared forests and mowed or grazed the land for a long time without fertilising it.
108029.m: Semi-dry grasslands owe their existence to traditional farming.

108030.q: Which blue-violet flowering plant of the mint family is typical of poor, dry meadows?
108030.e: Meadow clary loves warm, lime-rich and rather dry meadows. Bumblebees like to visit its flowers.
108030.m: Meadow clary grows on warm, poor meadows.

108031.q: Which pink with tightly clustered, bright pink flowers grows on poor, dry meadows?
108031.e: The Carthusian pink has several flowers in one head and grows in sunny, nutrient-poor places.
108031.m: The Carthusian pink flowers on sunny, poor meadows.

108032.q: Why are semi-dry grasslands particularly valuable for butterflies?
a: They offer many different flowering plants
They are wet all year round
108032.e: Semi-dry grasslands are among the most species-rich habitats in Central Europe. Many butterflies find nectar here and food plants for their caterpillars.
108032.m: Species-rich poor meadows are important for butterflies.

108033.q: What happens to biodiversity when a semi-dry grassland is heavily fertilised?
108033.e: Fertiliser helps a few fast-growing species. They crowd out the many small plants adapted to poor soil.
108033.m: Fertilising makes poor meadows poorer in species.

108034.q: Which stemless thistle with shiny silvery bracts grows on poor grassland and closes in damp weather?
108034.e: The stemless carline thistle lies almost flat on the ground. Its silvery bracts close in damp air, which is why it is seen as a weather indicator.
108034.m: The carline thistle closes in damp weather.

108035.q: What does a dense patch of nettles usually indicate?
a: A lot of nitrogen in the soil
108035.e: The common nettle grows lushly where there is a lot of nitrogen, for example near dung heaps or at fertilised edges.

108036.q: Which plant with large leaves, called “Blacke” in Switzerland, indicates over-fertilised meadows?
108036.e: Broad-leaved dock spreads on heavily fertilised meadows, often treated with slurry. Farmers fight it as a weed.
108036.m: Lots of docks on a meadow point to over-fertilising.

108037.q: What can a farmer tell from the plants on her meadow?
a: How wet and nutrient-rich the soil is
What the weather will be like tomorrow
Exactly how deep the groundwater is
108037.e: Indicator plants grow only under certain conditions. Lots of nettles, for example, show a lot of fertiliser, and rushes show wet soil.
108037.m: Plants give away what the soil is like.

108038.e: Heather grows on acidic, poor soils, for example on silicate rock or in bogs. It is usually missing on limestone.
108038.m: Heather grows on acidic, poor soil.

a: A plant that shows certain soil properties
A plant that always grows towards the north
A plant that tells the time
A plant that grows only on signposts
108039.e: Indicator plants prefer to grow under certain conditions. If you know them, you can tell, for example, whether the soil is wet, acidic or rich in nutrients.
108039.m: Indicator plants tell you something about where they grow.

108040.q: What is field horsetail an indicator of?
a: Acidic needle litter in the forest
108040.e: Field horsetail likes to grow where water is held up underground. It is seen as a sign of compacted and waterlogged soil.

108041.q: What is a lot of dandelion on a meadow an indicator of?
108041.e: The common dandelion benefits greatly from fertiliser. Yellow dandelion meadows in spring are usually intensively used, rich meadows.
108041.m: Lots of dandelions show a well-fertilised meadow.

108042.q: What do rushes on a pasture usually indicate?
108042.e: Rushes grow on wet, often compacted soils. Where they are common on pastures, water is standing in the soil.
108042.m: Rushes grow where the soil is wet.

a: Dung and urine from farm animals
108043.e: Slurry is a liquid farm fertiliser made of the dung and urine of cows or pigs, often diluted with water.
108043.m: Slurry is liquid fertiliser made from animal droppings.

108045.q: Which three main plant nutrients does slurry contain?
108045.e: Slurry mainly supplies nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium. These nutrients help feed plants grow.
108045.m: Slurry mainly fertilises with nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium.

108046.q: Which gas escapes when slurry is spread and pollutes the air and sensitive habitats?
108046.e: Ammonia escapes from slurry. With the rain, it gets into forests, bogs and poor meadows and fertilises them without anyone wanting it.

108047.q: What is used to spread slurry close to the ground so that less ammonia escapes?
108047.e: The trailing hose lays the slurry in strips directly on the ground. With the older splash plate, it is sprayed widely, so more ammonia escapes.
108047.m: The trailing hose spreads slurry close to the ground.

108048.q: Why do many meadow flowers disappear when a meadow is often treated with slurry?
a: Slurry makes the ground too cold
108048.e: The many nutrients help strong feed grasses and a few herbs such as dandelion. The smaller meadow flowers no longer get any light.
108048.m: Too much slurry makes meadows poor in species.

108049.q: What can happen if slurry gets into a stream?
a: The stream freezes over at once
108049.e: Slurry contains poisonous ammonia and uses up a lot of oxygen in the water as it breaks down. This can kill fish.
108049.m: Slurry in a stream can kill fish.

108050.q: Why must slurry not be spread on frozen or snow-covered ground?
a: It cannot soak in and is washed into waters
It smells much stronger in winter
It lures wild animals out of the forest
108050.e: On frozen ground, slurry cannot seep away. When it thaws or rains, it runs off and pollutes streams and lakes.
108050.m: You must not spread slurry on frozen ground.

108051.q: Why is climbing into a slurry pit life-threatening?
a: Poisonous gases such as hydrogen sulphide form
The slurry there is boiling hot
108051.e: Gases such as hydrogen sulphide form in slurry pits and can be deadly even in small amounts. That is why you must never climb in without protection.
108051.m: Gases from slurry can be deadly.

108052.q: In Switzerland, what is the hay from a meadow's second cut of the year called?
108052.e: Hay from the first cut is called hay; hay from the second and later cuts is called Emd.
108052.m: Emd is the hay from the second cut.

108053.q: Why is very early mowing bad for many meadow flowers?
108053.e: If a meadow is mown before the seeds are ripe, many flowers can no longer sow themselves. Over time they disappear.
108053.m: Meadow flowers need time to form seeds.

108054.q: Why are meadows often searched with drones carrying thermal cameras before mowing?
108054.e: When in danger, roe deer fawns crouch in the tall grass instead of running away. With a thermal camera, they can be found and taken to safety before mowing.
108054.m: Thermal cameras save fawns from the mower.

108055.q: How can insects such as grasshoppers be spared when mowing?
a: Cut higher and do not mow everything at once
Mow as low and fast as possible
Mow the whole meadow in one day
108055.e: If the grass is cut higher and part of the meadow is left standing, many more insects survive. They can escape into the unmown areas.
108055.m: Mowing high and step by step spares insects.

108056.q: What is a strip of uncut grass?
a: Part of the meadow that is left standing when mowing
A strip of freshly sown lawn
108056.e: A strip of uncut grass is left out when mowing. Insects, spiders and other small animals find shelter and food there.
108056.m: Strips of uncut grass give animals a hiding place after mowing.

108057.q: In which direction should a meadow be mown so that animals can escape?
108057.e: Mowing from the inside outwards leaves animals such as hares or birds an escape route into the open. Mowing from the outside inwards traps them in the middle.
108057.m: If you mow from the inside outwards, animals can escape.

108058.q: Why does early mowing endanger ground-nesting birds such as the whinchat?
a: Their nests with young are destroyed
They can no longer find trees
108058.e: Ground-nesting birds build their nests in tall grass. If mowing happens before the young can fly, the broods are lost.
108058.m: Late mowing protects the nests of meadow birds.

108059.q: What is feed made from freshly mown grass that is fermented airtight called?
108059.e: For silage, grass is preserved without air by lactic acid bacteria. For this, mowing is often early and frequent.

108060.q: Why must Swiss farms set aside part of their land as biodiversity promotion areas?
a: So that animals and plants find habitats
So that hiking trails are created
So that houses can be built
108060.e: Most farms must use at least 7 per cent of their land as biodiversity promotion areas. Wild plants, insects and birds find habitats there.
108060.m: At least 7 per cent of the land is set aside for biodiversity.

108061.q: What do Swiss farmers receive from the federal government if they meet the proof of ecological performance?
108061.e: The proof of ecological performance (PEP) requires, among other things, a balanced use of fertiliser and biodiversity promotion areas. Those who meet it receive direct payments.
108061.m: Without proof of ecological performance, there are no direct payments.

108062.q: Why may extensively used meadows only be mown in summer?
a: So that many plants can flower and form seeds first
So that the grass grows less
So that the cows stay hungry
So that the ground dries out
108062.e: In the lowlands, the earliest cut is allowed from 15 June. That way many plants can flower and form seeds, and insects find food.
108062.m: Extensive meadows in the lowlands are mown in mid-June at the earliest.

108063.q: What is forbidden on an extensively used meadow that is a biodiversity promotion area?
108063.e: Extensively used meadows may not be fertilised. Only then do they stay poor and rich in species.

108064.q: Which feature also counts as a biodiversity promotion area in Switzerland?
108064.e: As well as meadows and hedges, tall-trunk fruit trees also count. They offer birds such as the common redstart nesting places and food.
108064.m: Tall-trunk trees promote biodiversity on the farm.

108065.q: What makes a biodiversity promotion area particularly valuable?
a: Grass that is as short as possible
108065.e: Areas with many typical indicator plants reach quality level II. Farmers receive higher payments for them.
108065.m: Particularly species-rich areas reach quality level II.

108066.q: What is the aim of networking projects for biodiversity promotion areas?
a: To link habitats so that animals can move between them
To connect farms to the internet
108066.e: Single areas are often too small. If they lie cleverly close together, animals and plants can spread and populations can mix.
108066.m: Linked areas help animals to spread.

108067.q: Which of these areas can be a biodiversity promotion area?
108067.e: Biodiversity promotion areas include, for example, hedges, extensive meadows, wildflower fallows and tall-trunk fruit trees. They used to be called ecological compensation areas.

108068.q: What is sown on a wildflower fallow at the edge of a field?
108068.e: A wildflower fallow is sown with native wild flowers and left for several years. It offers insects, hares and birds food and cover.
108068.m: Wildflower fallows bring wild flowers to farmland.

108069.q: Which plant family does sainfoin belong to?
108069.e: Like clover and beans, sainfoin is a legume. It has pea-like flowers and forms pods.
108069.m: Sainfoin is related to clover and beans.

108070.q: What colour are the flowers of sainfoin?
108070.e: Sainfoin carries upright spikes of pink, pea-like flowers with darker stripes.
108070.m: Sainfoin flowers pink with dark veins.

108071.q: Why does sainfoin hardly need any nitrogen fertiliser?
a: Nodule bacteria on its roots capture nitrogen from the air
It takes in nitrogen through its flowers
It needs no nitrogen at all
108071.e: Bacteria live in nodules on the roots and turn nitrogen from the air into a form plants can use.
108071.m: Nodule bacteria supply sainfoin with nitrogen.

108072.e: Sainfoin loves lime and copes well with drought. It is often found in semi-dry grassland and on sunny banks.

108073.q: What was sainfoin traditionally grown for in farming?
a: As a feed plant for animals
108073.e: Sainfoin is an old feed plant. It also grows on poor, dry soils where clover does not do well.
108073.m: Sainfoin is an old feed plant.

108074.q: Which substances in sainfoin can help sheep and goats against intestinal worms?
108074.e: Sainfoin contains a lot of tannins. They can reduce infestation with stomach and intestinal worms and prevent bloating.
108074.m: Tannins make sainfoin a healthy feed.

108075.q: Why is sainfoin very popular with honeybees?
108075.e: Sainfoin flowers offer a lot of nectar and pollen. Beekeepers value it as a valuable source of food for bees.
108075.m: Sainfoin is good forage for bees.

108076.q: How does sainfoin survive dry summers?
a: With water stores in its flowers
By shedding its leaves in summer
With aerial roots on its stem
108076.e: Sainfoin's taproot reaches deep into the soil. That way it reaches water that shallow-rooted grasses cannot get to.
108076.m: Deep roots help sainfoin in dry weather.

108077.q: What kind of plant is upright brome?
108077.e: Upright brome is a grass from the grass family. Its flowers are in loose, branched heads (panicles).

108078.q: What do farmers mostly use poor meadows with a lot of upright brome for?
108078.e: Poor, dry meadows with upright brome are mown late or grazed. That way they stay rich in species.
108078.m: Poor brome meadows provide hay and pasture.

108079.q: How can you tell that upright brome is a grass?
108079.e: Grasses have narrow leaves and round stems divided by joints. Upright brome grows in exactly this way.

108080.q: What does a meadow with a lot of upright brome usually indicate?
a: It is not fertilised, or hardly at all
108080.e: Upright brome grows on poor, unfertilised meadows. If a lot of fertiliser is used, it disappears.
108080.m: Lots of brome shows an unfertilised meadow.

a: As a flat rosette of leaves
108081.e: Upright brome forms dense tufts. From them grow its stiff, upright stems.
108081.m: Upright brome grows in dense tufts.

108082.q: Which soils does upright brome prefer?
a: Lime-rich, poor and rather dry soils
108082.e: Upright brome is an indicator of lime-rich, nutrient-poor and warm places.
108082.m: Upright brome likes poor limestone soil.

108083.q: What happens to upright brome when a poor meadow is heavily fertilised?
a: It is crowded out by vigorous feed grasses
It becomes the most common plant
108083.e: With fertiliser, grasses such as cock's-foot or ryegrass take over. The weakly competing brome then gradually disappears.

108084.q: About how tall does upright brome grow?
108084.e: The stems of upright brome usually grow to between about 30 centimetres and one metre tall.
108084.m: Upright brome grows knee to hip high.

108085.q: Where does the skylark build its nest?
108085.e: The skylark is a ground nester. It makes its nest in a small hollow among grass or cereal crops.
108085.m: The skylark nests on the ground.

108086.q: What is the skylark particularly known for?
a: Its song high in the air
Singing at night in the forest
108086.e: The male rises into the air singing and often trills for minutes high above the field before sinking down again.
108086.m: The skylark sings in flight high above the field.

a: An unsown patch in a cereal field
A nest box on the barn
A window in a bird house
108087.e: Skylark plots are small areas left out when sowing. There the skylark can land and look for food in the dense crop.
108087.m: Skylark plots help the skylark in cereal fields.

108088.q: What does the skylark's plumage look like?
108088.e: Its plain, brown-streaked plumage camouflages the skylark very well on the ground.
108088.m: The skylark is brown-streaked and well camouflaged.

108089.q: What does the skylark feed on?
108089.e: In summer, the skylark mainly eats insects and spiders; in winter, more seeds and parts of plants.
108089.m: The skylark eats insects and seeds.

108090.q: How has the skylark population on the Swiss Plateau developed in recent decades?
108090.e: The Swiss Ornithological Institute in Sempach has recorded a sharp decline for decades. The main reasons are intensive farming and the loss of fallow land and poor meadows.
108090.m: The skylark has become rare in Switzerland.

108091.q: Why does the skylark hardly find nesting places on intensively farmed land?
108091.e: Dense, tall crops are hard for the skylark to get into, and frequent mowing destroys broods. There is also a lack of insects as food.
108091.m: Intensive farming takes away the skylark's habitat.

108092.q: Which feature on its head can the skylark raise?
108092.e: The skylark has slightly longer feathers on the top of its head, which it can raise into a small crest when excited.
108092.m: The skylark can raise a small crest.

108093.q: About how big is a skylark?
a: A little bigger than a house sparrow
As big as a white stork
As big as a carrion crow
108093.e: The skylark is a small songbird, a little bigger and slimmer than a sparrow.
108093.m: The skylark is about the size of a sparrow.

108094.q: On which meadows do particularly many wild orchids grow in Switzerland?
108094.e: Most native orchids love warm, nutrient-poor and lime-rich places, which are common in the Jura and the limestone Alps.
108094.m: Wild orchids like best to grow on poor limestone meadows.

108095.q: How rich in species is the orchid family worldwide?
a: It is one of the most species-rich plant families
It has only about ten species
It is found only in Europe
It consists of a single species
108095.e: There are many thousands of orchid species worldwide, most of them in the tropics. This makes orchids one of the largest plant families of all.
108095.m: Orchids are one of the most species-rich plant families on Earth.

108097.e: An orchid capsule contains a great many dust-fine seeds. They are spread far by the wind.
108097.m: Orchid seeds are as fine as dust.

108098.q: Which native orchid has a flower whose lip looks like a bee?
108098.e: The lip of the bee orchid has velvety brown markings and looks like a bee. It grows on poor limestone meadows.
108098.m: The bee orchid has a flower like a bee.

108099.q: Which orchid with a pink, cone-shaped flower head grows on poor limestone meadows?
108099.e: The pyramidal orchid has a dense flower head that is cone-shaped at first. It looks like a small pyramid.
108099.m: The pyramidal orchid has a cone-shaped flower head.

108100.q: For many native ground orchids, how long does it take from sprouting to the first flower?
108100.e: After sprouting, many ground orchids live underground for years with their fungal partner before they form a green leaf and finally a flower.
108100.m: Orchids often need years before they first flower.

108101.q: What threatens orchid meadows in Switzerland most?
a: Fertilising, building and mowing too early
108101.e: Building, intensive farming and early mowing have made many former orchid sites disappear.
108101.m: Fertilising and early mowing destroy orchid meadows.

108195.q: Which part of the intestine comes directly after the stomach?
108195.e: After the stomach exit, the small intestine begins with the duodenum. There the food mash is mixed with digestive juices.
108195.m: The duodenum is the first part of the small intestine.

108196.q: Where does the duodenum get its name from?
a: It is about twelve finger-widths long
It is about twelve metres long
108196.e: The duodenum is about 25 to 30 centimetres long. That is roughly the width of twelve fingers laid side by side, and its Latin name refers to twelve.
108196.m: The duodenum is about as long as twelve fingers are wide.

108197.q: Which two digestive juices flow into the duodenum?
108197.e: The bile duct and the duct of the pancreas open into the duodenum at a small bump. Their juices help break down fats, proteins and carbohydrates.
108197.m: The bile duct and the pancreatic duct open into the duodenum.

108198.q: What does pancreatic juice do to the acidic food mash in the duodenum?
a: It makes it even more acidic
108198.e: Pancreatic juice contains bicarbonate, which buffers the acid. Only then can the digestive enzymes in the small intestine work properly.
108198.m: Pancreatic juice makes the acidic food mash less acidic.

a: Just after the stomach, at the start of the small intestine
At the end of the large intestine
In the chest next to the heart
In the neck below the larynx
108199.e: The duodenum is the first part of the small intestine. It joins directly onto the stomach exit.
108199.m: The duodenum is the start of the small intestine.

108200.q: Which ring muscle controls when food mash passes from the stomach into the duodenum?
108200.e: The pylorus at the stomach exit keeps opening briefly. This lets the food mash pass into the duodenum in portions.
108200.m: The pylorus lets the food mash into the intestine in portions.

108201.q: What is a common cause of ulcers in the duodenum?
108201.e: A particular bacterium can survive in the lining of the stomach and duodenum and damage it. Then a sore spot forms: an ulcer.
108201.m: Many ulcers in the duodenum are caused by bacteria.

108202.q: Which part of the small intestine follows the duodenum?
108202.e: The small intestine is made up of the duodenum, jejunum and ileum. The jejunum, meaning “empty”, got its name because it was often found empty in people who had died.
108202.m: After the duodenum comes the jejunum.

108203.q: What gives the wall of the duodenum extra protection against acid from the stomach?
108203.e: In the wall of the duodenum there are special glands, Brunner's glands. They make an alkaline mucus that protects the lining from the acid.
108203.m: Alkaline mucus protects the wall of the duodenum.

108204.q: What does the wall of the large intestine look like?
a: It is smooth like a garden hose
It has rings of cartilage like the windpipe
108204.e: The wall of the large intestine is pinched in again and again. In between are pouch-like bulges called haustra.
108204.m: The large intestine has a wall with many bulges.

108205.q: Roughly how long is an adult's large intestine?
108205.e: In adults, the large intestine measures about 1.5 metres. That makes it much shorter but wider than the small intestine.
108205.m: The large intestine is about one and a half metres long.

108206.q: What is the pouch-shaped first part of the large intestine at the lower right of the belly called?
108206.e: The caecum is a pouch-shaped start of the large intestine at the lower right of the belly. This is where the small intestine joins the large intestine.
108206.m: The large intestine begins with the caecum.

108207.q: What is usually actually inflamed in “appendicitis”?
108207.e: In appendicitis, it is almost always the appendix, a small worm-shaped tube on the caecum, that is inflamed. It is then often removed in an operation.
108207.m: In appendicitis, the appendix is inflamed.

108208.q: How does the large intestine run through the belly?
a: Up on the right, across, and down on the left
In many tight loops in the middle
108208.e: The large intestine starts at the lower right, goes up, runs across below the stomach and goes down again on the left. In this way it frames the small intestine.
108208.m: The large intestine runs like a frame around the small intestine.

108209.q: What is the examination called in which a doctor looks at the large intestine with a small camera?
108209.e: In a colonoscopy, a flexible tube with a camera is inserted through the anus. This makes it possible to spot inflammation or growths.
108209.m: A colonoscopy lets you see inside the large intestine.

108210.q: Why is it important that the contents of the large intestine do not flow back into the small intestine?
a: Huge numbers of bacteria live in the large intestine
The large intestine is much hotter
There is stomach acid in the large intestine
The small intestine is already full of air
108210.e: Enormous numbers of bacteria live in the large intestine. A valve at the junction stops them getting back into the small intestine.
108210.m: A valve separates the bacteria-rich large intestine from the small intestine.

108211.q: Besides water, what does the large intestine mainly absorb from its contents?
108211.e: The large intestine mainly absorbs water and mineral salts such as sodium. Most nutrients have already been absorbed in the small intestine.
108211.m: The large intestine takes back water and salts.

108212.q: Roughly where in the belly is the large intestine?
a: It is next to the lungs
108212.e: The large intestine runs like a frame around the loops of the small intestine. It starts at the lower right and ends in the middle of the pelvis.
108212.m: The large intestine lies like a picture frame around the small intestine.

108213.q: Which part of the intestine is the last before the anus?
108213.e: The rectum is the end part of the large intestine. It leads through the anal canal to the anus.
108213.m: The rectum is the last part of the intestine.

108214.q: What job does the rectum do?
a: Store poo until it is passed
108214.e: Poo collects in the rectum until you go to the toilet. It is a stretchy store.
108214.m: The rectum stores poo until you go to the toilet.

108215.q: What is the medical term for the last part of the large intestine, just before the anus?
108215.e: In medicine, this last part is called the rectum. The word comes from the Latin “rectus”, meaning straight.
108215.m: The last part of the large intestine is called the rectum.

108216.q: What triggers the urge to go to the toilet for a poo?
108216.e: When poo collects in the rectum, its wall is stretched. Sensory cells report this to the brain and you feel the urge to go.
108216.m: A full rectum signals the urge to go to the brain.

108217.q: Which sphincter muscle at the anus can be controlled at will?
108217.e: The internal sphincter works automatically. You can tighten the external sphincter on purpose, so you can put off going to the toilet for a while.
108217.m: You can control the external anal sphincter on purpose.

108218.q: Roughly how long is an adult's rectum?
108218.e: The rectum is about 12 to 18 centimetres long. So it is only a short part of the large intestine.
108218.m: The rectum is only about a hand span long.

108219.q: Where in the body is the rectum?
108219.e: The rectum lies in the lower pelvis in front of the sacrum. From there it leads to the anus.
108219.m: The rectum lies low down in the pelvis.

108220.q: Which part of the intestine does the rectum belong to?
108220.e: The rectum is the last piece of the large intestine. In the large intestine, water is taken out of the food mash before the poo collects in the rectum.
108220.m: The rectum is the end part of the large intestine.

a: On the underside of the liver
108221.e: The gall bladder lies in the upper right of the belly on the underside of the liver. It is connected to the liver and intestine by ducts.
108221.m: The gall bladder sits under the liver.

108222.q: What is the job of the gall bladder?
108222.e: The gall bladder collects bile between meals and takes water out of it. This concentrates the bile.
108222.m: The gall bladder is a store for bile.

108223.q: What shape is the gall bladder?
108223.e: The gall bladder is a small, pear-shaped hollow sac. It is about 8 to 10 centimetres long.
108223.m: The gall bladder looks like a small pear.

108224.q: What are the hard deposits called that can form in the gall bladder?
108224.e: Gallstones form when substances in the bile clump together and harden. They can cause severe pain in the upper belly.
108224.m: Gallstones form from substances in the bile.

108225.q: When does the gall bladder contract especially strongly?
108225.e: As soon as fatty food mash reaches the intestine, the gall bladder contracts. Then a lot of bile is released to digest the fat.
108225.m: Fatty food makes the gall bladder empty itself.

108226.q: Can a person live without a gall bladder?
108226.e: With gallstones, the gall bladder is often removed. The liver then releases bile directly and continuously into the intestine.
108226.m: You can live well without a gall bladder.

108227.q: Roughly how much bile can an adult's gall bladder store?
108227.e: The gall bladder is small and holds only about 30 to 50 millilitres. Because it takes water out of the bile, a lot of bile still fits inside.
108227.m: The gall bladder holds only a few tablespoons of bile.

108228.q: What happens to the bile from the gall bladder after a meal?
a: It flows into the small intestine
108228.e: After a meal, the gall bladder contracts. The bile flows into the small intestine and helps digest fat there.
108228.m: Bile helps digest fat in the small intestine.

108229.q: Which component of bile can form gallstones if there is too much of it?
108229.e: Bile contains cholesterol, which is kept dissolved by the bile acids. If there is too much of it, it can crystallise and form stones.
108229.m: Too much cholesterol in the bile can lead to gallstones.

108230.q: How does bile help with digestion?
108230.e: Bile acids break large drops of fat into many small droplets. This lets fat-splitting enzymes work better.
108230.m: Bile makes fat easier to digest.

108231.q: What colour is fresh bile from the liver?
108231.e: Fresh bile is yellow to greenish. The colour comes from bile pigments.

108232.q: What does the body break down when bile pigment is made?
108232.e: Red blood cells live for about four months. When their red pigment is broken down, yellow bile pigment is formed.
108232.m: Bile pigment is made from old red blood cells.

108233.e: Gut bacteria turn the pigments from the bile into brown substances. If bile is missing from the gut, the poo becomes pale.
108233.m: Bile pigments give poo its brown colour.

108234.q: What happens to most of the bile acids after fat has been digested?
a: They go back to the liver
They are stored in the bones
108234.e: Bile acids are absorbed again at the end of the small intestine and carried in the blood to the liver. This cycle is called the enterohepatic circulation.
108234.m: Bile acids are used again and again.

108235.q: What is often the cause when the skin and the whites of the eyes turn yellow (jaundice)?
a: Bile pigment builds up in the body
Too much sugar in the blood
108235.e: If the liver is ill or the bile cannot drain away, bile pigment collects in the blood. It settles in the skin and eyes and turns them yellow.
108235.m: In jaundice, bile pigment builds up in the body.

108236.q: Roughly how much bile does an adult's liver make each day?
108236.e: The liver makes about half a litre to a litre of bile every day. Some of it is stored for a while in the gall bladder.
108236.m: The liver produces about a litre of bile every day.

108237.q: In which organ are the villi found?
108237.e: The lining of the small intestine is covered with millions of villi. There are no villi in the large intestine.
108237.m: Villi are found only in the small intestine.

108238.q: What are the villi in the intestine for?
108238.e: The villi greatly increase the inner surface of the small intestine. This lets far more nutrients be absorbed into the blood.
108238.m: Villi create a huge surface for absorbing nutrients.

108239.e: Villi are small, finger-shaped bumps on the lining. They stand close together like a velvet carpet.

108240.q: What would happen if the small intestine were completely smooth inside, with no villi?
a: It could absorb far fewer nutrients
You would never be hungry again
108240.e: The villi increase the surface of the small intestine enormously. Without them there would be much less surface through which nutrients pass into the blood.
108240.m: Without villi, the body would absorb far fewer nutrients.

108241.q: Where do sugar and amino acids go after the villi have absorbed them?
108241.e: In every villus there are fine blood vessels. They carry sugar and amino acids through the portal vein to the liver.
108241.m: Nutrients from the villi are carried on in the blood.

108242.e: Fine blood vessels and a lymph vessel run through each villus. They carry away the absorbed nutrients.
108242.m: There are fine blood vessels inside the villi.

108243.q: In which disease are the villi damaged by gluten?
108243.e: In coeliac disease, the immune system reacts to gluten from wheat, rye and barley. The villi shrink, and nutrients are absorbed less well.
108243.m: In coeliac disease, gluten harms the villi.

108244.q: Roughly how tall is a single villus?
108244.e: Villi are about 0.5 to 1.5 millimetres tall. With the naked eye you can just about see them as a velvety surface.
108244.m: A villus is only about a millimetre tall.

108245.q: In which part of the intestine do most gut bacteria live?
108245.e: In the large intestine, bacteria find plenty of time and food. That is why by far the most gut bacteria live there.
108245.m: Most gut bacteria live in the large intestine.

108246.q: Which vitamin is made by gut bacteria?
108246.e: Gut bacteria make vitamin K and some B vitamins. The body needs vitamin K for blood clotting.

108247.q: What can gut bacteria break down that our body cannot digest itself?
108247.e: Fibre from plants reaches the large intestine undigested. There bacteria ferment it and make useful substances.
108247.m: Gut bacteria make use of fibre.

108248.q: Which medicines can upset the gut flora and cause diarrhoea?
108248.e: Antibiotics kill not only germs that cause disease but also useful gut bacteria. This can upset the balance of the gut flora.
108248.m: Antibiotics can also hit the good gut bacteria.

108249.q: Roughly how many bacteria live in a person's body compared with their body cells?
108249.e: An estimate from 2016 comes to around 38 trillion bacteria and around 30 trillion human cells. Most of the bacteria live in the gut.
108249.m: About as many bacteria live in the body as it has cells.

108250.q: What are products or foods with live, useful bacteria called?
108250.e: Probiotics contain live microorganisms, for example lactic acid bacteria. They are found in some yoghurts, for instance.

108251.q: How does healthy gut flora protect against germs that cause disease?
a: It leaves them hardly any space or food
108251.e: The many useful bacteria occupy the gut wall and use up the nutrients. So harmful germs find it harder to settle.
108251.m: Good gut bacteria crowd out harmful germs.

108252.q: Which bacterium normally lives harmlessly in every person's gut?
108252.e: Escherichia coli, E. coli for short, is part of the normal gut flora. Only some strains can make you ill.
108252.m: Escherichia coli is a typical resident of the gut.

108253.q: What does it mean to be constipated?
a: Poo comes rarely and is hard
You get tummy ache when eating
You have hiccups all the time
108253.e: When you are constipated, you go to the toilet rarely and the poo is often hard and difficult to pass. This can cause tummy ache and a feeling of fullness.
108253.m: When you are constipated, going to the toilet is rare and difficult.

108254.q: What is most likely to help against constipation?
108254.e: Fibre binds water and makes poo softer and bulkier. Enough fluid supports this effect.
108254.m: Fibre and water help prevent constipation.

108255.q: Which food helps many people with constipation?
108255.e: Prunes contain a lot of fibre and substances that stimulate the gut. White rice, chocolate and rusks tend to make constipation worse.

108256.q: What are medicines called that help you pass poo?
108256.e: Laxatives make poo softer or stimulate the gut. They should only be taken for a short time and on medical advice.
108256.m: Laxatives help with constipation but are not for everyday use.

108257.q: How does exercise help against constipation?
a: It slows the flow of bile
108257.e: Physical activity such as running or cycling gets the gut moving too. People who sit a lot are more likely to get constipated.
108257.m: Exercise gets the gut moving too.

108258.q: From when do people usually speak of constipation in adults?
a: Going for a poo less than 3 times a week
Going for a poo once a day
Going for a poo twice a day
Going for a poo every morning
108258.e: Anything from about three times a day to three times a week is healthy. Less often than three times a week usually counts as constipation.
108258.m: Going for a poo less than three times a week counts as constipation.

108259.q: Why can it lead to constipation if you often hold in the urge to poo?
a: The urge gets weaker over time
108259.e: If you often hold in the urge, the gut gets used to it. The signal gets weaker and the poo stays in the gut for longer.
108259.m: You should go to the toilet soon after you feel the urge.

108260.q: Which foods contain a lot of fibre?
108260.e: Fibre is found in wholegrain products, vegetables, pulses and fruit. Animal foods contain almost none.
108260.m: Wholegrains, vegetables and fruit provide lots of fibre.

108261.q: What is the biggest danger with severe diarrhoea, especially for young children?
108261.e: With diarrhoea, the body loses a lot of water and salts. Young children can become dehydrated quickly.
108261.m: With diarrhoea, the body risks drying out.

108262.q: What should you do above all when you have diarrhoea?
a: Drink plenty, with a little salt and sugar
Drink nothing at all if possible
108262.e: It is important to replace water and salts. Special rehydration drinks from the chemist contain salts and sugar in the right proportions.
108262.m: With diarrhoea, you must replace lost fluid.

108263.q: Which virus often causes contagious vomiting and diarrhoea, especially in winter?
108263.e: Noroviruses are very contagious and suddenly cause vomiting and diarrhoea. Outbreaks often happen in schools, hospitals and on ships.
108263.m: Noroviruses cause contagious vomiting and diarrhoea.

108264.q: Why should you wash your hands especially thoroughly when you have diarrhoea?
a: So you do not pass the germs on
108264.e: Many germs that cause diarrhoea are very contagious and get onto door handles and food via the hands. Washing your hands with soap breaks this path.
108264.m: Hand washing protects others from diarrhoea germs.

108265.q: What is the best way to protect yourself from contagious diarrhoea germs?
108265.e: Many diarrhoea germs are passed on by dirty hands. Washing your hands with soap after the toilet and before eating protects you well.
108265.m: Washing your hands with soap protects against diarrhoea germs.

108266.q: What is the diarrhoea called that people often get in faraway countries from contaminated food or water?
108266.e: Traveller's diarrhoea is the most common illness on trips to hot countries. It is usually caused by bacteria in water or food.
108266.m: Traveller's diarrhoea often comes from contaminated water or food.

108267.q: According to the World Health Organization, from when is it called diarrhoea?
a: Runny poo at least 3 times a day
108267.e: The WHO defines diarrhoea as three or more watery stools a day. So both how often and how runny it is matter.
108267.m: Runny poo three times a day counts as diarrhoea.

108268.q: Which rule of thumb applies to eating in countries with unsafe drinking water?
a: “Boil it, peel it or forget it”
108268.e: Boiling kills germs, and peeling removes the dirty skin. Raw, unpeeled food and ice cubes are risky.
108268.m: When travelling, it is better to skip anything you cannot cook or peel.

a: Stomach acid flows into the oesophagus
Too little saliva in the mouth
108269.e: In heartburn, acidic stomach contents flow back into the oesophagus. Its lining is not protected against acid and burns.
108269.m: Heartburn is caused by stomach acid in the oesophagus.

108270.q: Where do you typically feel heartburn?
108270.e: The burning rises behind the breastbone, sometimes up into the throat. That is where the oesophagus runs.

108271.q: Which muscle normally stops stomach contents from flowing back into the oesophagus?
108271.e: Where the oesophagus joins the stomach there is a sphincter muscle. If it does not close properly, acid can rise up.
108271.m: A sphincter muscle separates the oesophagus and the stomach.

a: Lying down after a big meal
Going for a walk after eating
108272.e: If you lie down with a full stomach, you make it easier for the acid to rise. Big meals also increase the pressure in the stomach.
108272.m: After a big meal, you should not lie down straight away.

108273.q: How do antacids work against heartburn?
108273.e: Antacids contain alkaline substances. These neutralise some of the stomach acid.
108273.m: Antacids make stomach acid less harmful.

108274.q: What is the medical name for stomach contents flowing back into the oesophagus?
108274.e: Reflux comes from the Latin word for flowing back. If it happens often, it is called reflux disease.
108274.m: Stomach contents flowing back is called reflux.

108275.e: Fatty food stays in the stomach for a long time and can loosen the sphincter to the oesophagus. Spicy food, coffee and chocolate can also cause problems.
108275.m: Very fatty food can trigger heartburn.

108276.q: Why does raising the upper body in bed help against heartburn at night?
a: The stomach then makes no acid
108276.e: If the upper body is higher, the acid has to rise against gravity. It manages this much less well.
108276.m: A raised upper body makes it harder for acid to rise.

108277.q: Which acid is in stomach acid?
108277.e: The stomach lining makes hydrochloric acid. It makes the gastric juice strongly acidic.

108278.q: Roughly what pH does the gastric juice in an empty stomach have?
108278.e: With a pH of about 1 to 2, the empty stomach is very acidic. A pH of 7 would be neutral.

108279.q: Which cells in the stomach lining make the acid?
108279.e: The parietal cells sit in the glands of the stomach lining. They release the acid into the inside of the stomach.

108280.q: What protective job does stomach acid do?
108280.e: Many bacteria and other germs do not survive the strong acid. In this way the stomach protects against germs in food.
108280.m: Stomach acid kills many germs in food.

108281.q: Why does stomach acid not digest the stomach wall itself?
a: A layer of mucus protects it
The stomach is made of bone
The stomach wall is made of fat
108281.e: The stomach lining makes a thick layer of mucus. It keeps the acid away from the cells.
108281.m: Mucus protects the stomach wall from its own acid.

108282.q: Which protein-splitting enzyme is activated by stomach acid?
108282.e: The stomach releases an inactive form called pepsinogen. The acid turns it into the active enzyme pepsin.
108282.m: Stomach acid activates the enzyme pepsin.

108283.q: Roughly how much gastric juice does an adult make each day?
108283.e: The stomach lining makes about 2 to 3 litres of gastric juice every day. It contains acid, mucus and enzymes.
108283.m: The stomach makes several litres of gastric juice every day.

108284.q: What does stomach acid do to the proteins in food?
108284.e: The acid destroys the shape of the proteins; they are denatured. Unfolded proteins are easier for enzymes to break down.
108284.m: Stomach acid unfolds proteins for digestion.

108285.q: What can make the stomach produce gastric juice even before you eat?
a: The smell or sight of food
108285.e: Just smelling, seeing or thinking about food stimulates gastric juice through the nerves. The stomach gets ready for the meal in this way.
108285.m: Even the smell of food gets the stomach going.

a: Wave-like muscle movements in the digestive tract
108286.e: In peristalsis, the muscles of the digestive tract contract in waves. This pushes the contents along bit by bit.
108286.m: Peristalsis pushes food through the body in waves.

108287.q: Why can you swallow even when doing a handstand?
a: The stomach sucks the food in
The tongue pushes it all the way to the stomach
108287.e: The muscles of the oesophagus contract in waves. This movement works even against gravity.
108287.m: Thanks to muscle waves, swallowing works even upside down.

108288.q: Which two muscle layers work together in peristalsis?
108288.e: Circular muscles squeeze the gut, longitudinal muscles shorten it. Together they create a continuous wave.
108288.m: Circular and longitudinal muscles create peristalsis.

108289.q: What is the gut's own network of nerves sometimes called?
108289.e: There are many millions of nerve cells in the gut wall. They control the gut's movements on their own and are therefore also called the belly brain or second brain.
108289.m: The gut has its own nervous system.

108290.q: Where do the rumbling and gurgling noises in your tummy come from?
a: Gut movements push gas and liquid along
The ribs rub against each other
The heart beats against the stomach
108290.e: The muscles of the stomach and gut move gas and liquid along. This creates noises, especially when the stomach is nearly empty.
108290.m: Tummy rumbling comes from the movement of the stomach and gut.

108291.q: What is a dangerous condition called in which the contents of the gut can no longer move on?
108291.e: In a bowel obstruction, the gut is blocked or paralysed. It is an emergency that must be treated quickly in hospital.
108291.m: A bowel obstruction is a medical emergency.

108292.q: What happens to the stomach contents when you are sick?
a: They flow into the large intestine
108292.e: When you vomit, the stomach muscles and the diaphragm contract strongly. The stomach contents are pushed upwards, against the normal direction.
108292.m: When you vomit, transport runs in the wrong direction.

108293.q: Roughly how long does a mouthful take to travel down the oesophagus to the stomach?
108293.e: The oesophagus is about 25 centimetres long. The muscle wave carries a mouthful into the stomach in a few seconds.
108293.m: A mouthful reaches the stomach after a few seconds.

108294.q: Which type of muscle moves the gut without us deciding to?
108294.e: The gut wall is made of smooth muscle. It works by itself, without us controlling it consciously.
108294.m: Smooth muscles move the gut without our help.

108295.q: Which energy conversion takes place in a solar collector for hot water on the roof?
108295.e: A solar collector absorbs sunlight with a dark surface. The heat produced warms a liquid, which heats the water in the tank.
108295.m: A solar collector turns sunlight into heat.

108296.q: Which device turns kinetic energy into electrical energy?
108296.e: In a generator, a coil turns in a magnetic field. This turns kinetic energy into electrical energy.
108296.m: A generator produces electrical energy from movement.

108297.q: Which energy conversion happens in a battery while a torch is shining?
108297.e: Chemical reactions take place in the battery. Stored chemical energy is given off as electrical energy.
108297.m: A battery supplies electrical energy from chemical energy.

108298.q: Which form of energy do plants take in during photosynthesis?
108298.e: Plants use sunlight to make sugar from water and carbon dioxide. The light energy is stored as chemical energy.
108298.m: Plants store light energy as chemical energy.

108299.q: Into which form of energy does a kettle mainly turn electrical energy?
108299.e: Current flows through the kettle’s heating element and makes it very hot. This heat passes into the water.
108299.m: A kettle turns electrical energy into heat.

108300.q: Which energy conversion happens in the water wheel of an old mill?
a: Potential energy of the water into turning motion
108300.e: The water falls or flows onto the paddles of the wheel and drives it. Its potential and kinetic energy becomes the turning motion that drives the millstone.
108300.m: A water wheel uses the energy of flowing water.

108301.q: Where do our muscles get the energy for movement?
a: From the chemical energy in food
108301.e: The nutrients in food contain chemical energy. The muscle cells turn it into kinetic energy and heat.
108301.m: Muscles use the chemical energy in food.

108302.q: Which energy conversion happens when an arrow flies off in archery?
108302.e: When the bow is drawn, energy is stored in it. When released, it passes to the arrow and makes it fly fast.
108302.m: A drawn bow passes its energy to the arrow.

108303.q: Which energy conversion does an electric car use when braking to charge its battery?
108303.e: When braking, the electric motor works as a generator. In this way, some of the kinetic energy is recovered and stored in the battery.
108303.m: Electric cars can recover energy when braking.

108304.q: A bicycle light with a dynamo is shining. Where does the energy for the light come from?
a: From the movement of the legs when pedalling
From the air in the tyre
108304.e: Energy never comes from nothing. The muscles drive the wheel, the dynamo turns kinetic energy into electrical energy, and the lamp turns this into light.
108304.m: Energy is only converted, never created from nothing.

108305.q: Why does a dropped ball never bounce higher than the height it fell from?
a: It never has more energy than at the start
The Earth pulls it more strongly
The ground is always too soft
108305.e: To reach a greater height, the ball would need more potential energy than it had at the start. Without extra energy, that is impossible.
108305.m: Without extra energy, a ball never gets back to its starting height.

108306.q: A ball has 10 J of potential energy at a height of 2 m. How great is its kinetic energy just before it hits the ground, ignoring air resistance?
108306.e: Without air resistance, no energy is lost. All 10 J of potential energy is turned into kinetic energy.
108306.m: Without losses, all the potential energy becomes kinetic energy.

108307.q: A 5 kg rucksack is lifted onto a 3 m high shelf (g equals 10 N/kg). How much potential energy does it gain?
108307.e: Potential energy is calculated as m times g times h. 5 kg times 10 N/kg times 3 m gives 150 J.
108307.m: Potential energy is the product of mass, gravitational field strength and height.

108308.q: What happens to the total energy in a closed system over time?
a: At some point it becomes zero
108308.e: In a closed system, no energy is added and none is lost. That is why the sum of all forms of energy stays constant.
108308.m: In a closed system, the total energy stays constant.
